6.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
6.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

6.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a care agency that will provide personal care at home. The patient has capacity but has not been asked yet. Who in the organisation is responsible for advising on difficult decisions about confidential information?
o: The ward matron on duty
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The Data Protection Officer at the ICO
The Caldicott Guardian
6.w: The Caldicott Guardian is the senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient information and enabling appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions. The first step remains asking the patient.

n.0: The matron can support the team but is not the designated lead for confidentiality decisions.
n.1: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns; they do not advise on confidentiality decisions.
n.2: The ICO is the external regulator; it does not advise on individual sharing decisions within a trust.

6.q: Simon, 66, is an acutely ill medical inpatient on enoxaparin prophylaxis. On day 4 he is walking again and asks to stop the injections. He remains in hospital. What is the minimum NICE duration of pharmacological prophylaxis for him?
o: At least 7 days
At least 3 days
At least 28 days
Until he walks unaided
6.w: NICE NG89 1.4.6: offer pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days to acutely ill medical patients whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk. The patient's concerns are explored and any decision is made with him.

n.1: NICE sets a minimum of 7 days in acutely ill medical patients.
n.2: 28 days is not the NG89 minimum for medical patients.
n.3: The NG89 minimum is a time period, not a mobility milestone.

6.q: Jason, 26, attends the emergency department for the third time this year with injuries after drinking heavily. He tells the nurse that as a child he lived with domestic violence and that his father misused alcohol. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to use this information?
o: Refer him to children's social care about what happened in his childhood
Tell him his drinking is a choice that is unrelated to his childhood
Recognise that early adversity may underlie his current risks, and offer support
Treat his injuries and avoid discussing his past, as it is not relevant now
6.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): adults with 4+ ACEs were more likely to be high-risk drinkers and victims of violence. NMC P2.6: understand the importance of early years and childhood experiences on later physical, mental and behavioural health and wellbeing.

n.0: Jason is an adult; children's social care is for current concerns about children.
n.1: This is dismissive and contradicts evidence linking ACEs with high-risk drinking.
n.3: The ACE evidence links childhood adversity with health-harming behaviours, so it is relevant to his care.

6.q: Gwen, 70, is in the last days of life with metastatic cancer and new bone pain. She has not taken opioids before. The team agree to start subcutaneous morphine for symptom control, and the nurse is planning her care. Which approach to dosing is recommended?
o: Wait until her pain is severe before giving the first dose of morphine
Start with the lowest effective dose and titrate to her symptoms
Start at the top of the prescribed range so that she is comfortable quickly
Give a loading dose by intramuscular injection, then change to subcutaneous
6.w: NICE NG31 (2015) recs 1.5.7 and 1.5.8: for people starting treatment who have not previously had medicines for symptom management, start with the lowest effective dose and titrate as clinically indicated, reassessing symptoms at least daily.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.11 asks for pain to be managed promptly and effectively once identified.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.7 recommends starting with the lowest effective dose for people not previously given symptom-control medicines.
n.3: Intramuscular injections should be avoided in the last days of life (NG31 rec 1.5.5).

6.q: Ahmed, 28, is distressed and tearful after hearing bad news. Which skill is the cornerstone of mental health first aid in this situation?
o: Offering a sedative medicine
Distracting him with other topics
Listening non-judgementally
Giving clear advice on solutions
6.w: Mental health first aid centres on approaching the person, listening non-judgementally, giving support and information, and encouraging appropriate professional help (Annexe B 2.14).

n.0: Medication is not a first aid response to normal distress.
n.1: Distraction can invalidate his feelings and block disclosure.
n.3: Jumping to advice can feel dismissive before the person feels heard.

6.q: Callum, 29, attends a minor illness clinic with a 3-day history of a runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. He is well with normal observations and asks for antibiotics 'to be safe'. The nurse prescriber judges this a self-limiting viral illness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain antibiotics will not help, and give safety-netting advice
Advise him to take the leftover antibiotics he has at home
Suggest he buys antibiotics from a community pharmacy
Prescribe a 3-day course so that he does not need to come back
6.w: NICE NG15 recs 1.1.31 and 1.1.33: discuss why an antimicrobial may not be the best option and what to do if the condition deteriorates, and do not issue an immediate antimicrobial prescription for a likely self-limiting condition. Self-care advice is appropriate.

n.1: Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and their use drives resistance.
n.2: Systemic antibiotics are prescription-only medicines, and a community pharmacy would not supply them for a self-limiting viral illness.
n.3: NG15 says do not issue an immediate prescription for a likely self-limiting condition.

6.q: Wearing non-sterile gloves and an apron, Sam has just emptied the stoma bag of Kofi, 47. Sam now needs to give Kofi mouth care before leaving the bed space. What should Sam do before starting the mouth care?
o: Pull a second pair of gloves over the first pair and continue
Keep the same gloves, as both tasks are for the same patient
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene and put on new gloves
Apply alcohol handrub over the gloves, then continue with mouth care
6.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves must be changed after completing a procedure or task even on the same patient, and hand hygiene must be performed between glove changes. Gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub.

n.0: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and still leaves the contaminated outer layer touching the mouth.
n.1: Gloves are changed between tasks on the same patient, so contamination from the stoma is not carried to the mouth.
n.3: NIPCM states gloves are not decontaminated with handrub or soap and water between uses.

6.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
6.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

6.q: Walter, 79, has a ReSPECT form recommending ward-based treatment but not admission to intensive care. He becomes acutely unwell and cannot express his views. A student nurse asks what status the ReSPECT form has. Which statement is correct?
o: Its recommendations guide the clinicians present but are not legally binding
It is a legally binding refusal of treatment that clinicians must follow
It replaces the need for clinicians to assess what treatment would benefit him
It becomes valid once Walter has also registered a lasting power of attorney
6.w: Resuscitation Council UK (ReSPECT; RCUK 2025 Ethics guidelines): ReSPECT creates personalised recommendations for a future emergency in which the person cannot make or express choices. Preferences and recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; the final decision rests with clinicians present unless a legally binding document applies.

n.1: RCUK states ReSPECT recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; only documents such as a valid ADRT are binding.
n.2: Clinicians still make treatment decisions at the time, using the recommendations to inform them.
n.3: A ReSPECT form does not depend on an LPA; it records recommendations from conversations with the person and clinicians.

6.q: Edith, 84, has type 2 diabetes, moderate frailty, two falls this year and a lying-to-standing systolic drop of 22 mmHg. She takes modified-release metformin; HbA1c is 60 mmol/mol. The team considers adding an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Add an SGLT-2 inhibitor and aim for an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol
Add an SGLT-2 inhibitor and aim for HbA1c 53 mmol/mol
Switch to gliclazide and aim for HbA1c 53 mmol/mol
Continue metformin and agree a relaxed individual HbA1c target
6.w: Two steps: NG28 (1.19.1) offers an SGLT-2 inhibitor in frailty only if it will not cause adverse events such as volume depletion or hypotension, which Edith already has. NG28 (1.5.9) supports relaxing the HbA1c target in older, frailer people at risk of falls.

n.0: An SGLT-2 inhibitor risks volume depletion with her postural drop, and a tight target raises hypo and falls risk.
n.1: The SGLT-2 inhibitor remains unsafe given her postural hypotension and falls.
n.2: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia, which increases falls risk in frailty.

6.q: Mary, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, says she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action is most appropriate first?
o: Restrict her fluids until she passes urine
Give her a laxative to relieve the discomfort
Insert a catheter without discussing it with her
Assess her bladder volume with a bladder scanner
6.w: Annexe B 6.4: recognise and respond to retention. A bladder scan assesses residual volume to guide whether catheterisation is needed, which is then performed with her consent and in line with local policy.

n.0: Restricting fluids does not treat retention and risks dehydration.
n.1: A laxative does not address urinary retention.
n.2: Catheterisation needs assessment and valid consent (Code 4.2).

6.q: Mr Gray, 70, has capacity and a physical disability. He discloses that his son pushes him when angry, but asks the nurse to do nothing. The nurse discusses the options, and there is no apparent risk to anyone else. Which of the six adult safeguarding principles requires the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk?
o: Empowerment
Protection
Accountability
Proportionality
6.w: The six principles (Care Act statutory guidance ch 14) are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability. Proportionality means the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented.

n.0: Empowerment concerns person-led decisions and informed consent, not the scale of response.
n.1: Protection concerns support and representation for those in greatest need.
n.2: Accountability concerns accountability and transparency in delivering safeguarding, not the scale of the response.

6.q: A nurse is preparing for a structured multimorbidity review with Ahmed, 77, who takes 13 regular medicines. Following the NICE NG56 sequence, which step should come before reviewing his medicines?
o: Deciding who will coordinate his ongoing care
Arranging the timing of his follow-up review
Agreeing his individualised management plan
Establishing his goals, values and priorities
6.w: NG56 1.5.2 order: discuss the purpose of the approach, establish disease and treatment burden, establish goals, values and priorities, review medicines and other treatments, then agree an individualised plan (including coordination and follow-up).

n.0: Coordination of care is set within the final management plan.
n.1: Follow-up timing is part of the plan agreed at the end.
n.2: The management plan is agreed after the medicines review.

6.q: Agnes, 79, has type 2 diabetes with reduced sensation in her feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks you to cut them during her bath. What is the most appropriate action?
o: File her nails down after soaking her feet for 20 minutes
Explain the risk and refer her to the podiatry service
Ask a healthcare support worker to cut them carefully
Cut her nails straight across with sterile nail clippers
6.w: People with diabetes and reduced sensation are at high risk of foot ulceration from minor trauma, so thickened nails should be cut by a podiatrist. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during nail care.

n.0: Prolonged soaking softens skin and can cause maceration in a person with diabetes.
n.2: Delegating a task that needs specialist assessment does not reduce the risk.
n.3: Cutting thickened nails in a person with diabetic neuropathy risks injury and ulceration.

6.q: A red cell transfusion for Graham, 66, started at 14:00. Baseline pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate were recorded at 13:30 and were normal. According to BSH guidance, when should the next set of observations be taken?
o: At 14:30, 30 minutes after the start
At 15:00, 1 hour after the start
At 14:15, 15 minutes after the start
At the end of the unit, within 60 minutes
6.w: BSH (2017) observations: baseline no more than 60 minutes before starting, then pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, and again no more than 60 minutes after the end. Severe reactions often occur early in the unit.

n.0: The BSH timepoint is 15 minutes, not 30.
n.1: Waiting an hour misses the early period when serious reactions usually start.
n.3: End-of-unit observations are needed, but an observation at 15 minutes comes first.

6.q: Doris, 78, has type 2 diabetes and is drowsy and dehydrated. Glucose is 42 mmol/L, ketones 0.8 mmol/L, pH 7.36, calculated osmolality 345 mOsm/kg. HHS is diagnosed. Which initial treatment is most appropriate?
o: Fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour with 0.9% sodium chloride
0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour, insulin held while glucose falls
10% glucose at 125 mL/hour with a variable rate insulin infusion
0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour, then insulin
6.w: JBDS 06 (2022): HHS is treated with fluid first, using 0.9% sodium chloride (1 L over the first hour), aiming for gradual falls in osmolality (3.0 to 8.0 mOsm/kg/hour) and glucose (no more than 5 mmol/L/hour). Insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) starts once glucose stops falling with fluids alone, unless significantly ketonaemic.

n.0: Early insulin at the DKA rate causes rapid osmotic shifts; HHS uses fluid first and a lower insulin rate.
n.2: Glucose and VRIII are not initial HHS treatment; the priority is replacing lost fluid.
n.3: 0.45% sodium chloride is used only if osmolality is not falling despite adequate positive fluid balance.

6.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Send them by WhatsApp to the community nurse's phone
Print them and post them by second class mail
Email them from her personal account as it is faster
Send them through an approved, secure NHS system
6.w: Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; Caldicott principles; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

n.0: Personal messaging apps are not approved secure systems for clinical data.
n.1: Post is slower and less secure than approved electronic routes.
n.2: Personal email breaches data security (Code 10.5).

6.q: Mr Mensah, 59, has Black African heritage and is recovering from pneumonia. His pulse oximeter reads 94% on air. He is a little more breathless than earlier. Which consideration is most important when interpreting this reading?
o: Oximeters underestimate saturations in people with dark skin
Oximeters can overestimate saturations in people with dark skin
His reading is within target, so his breathlessness is not significant
An SpO2 of 94% on air means oxygen therapy should be started
6.w: NICE NG253 (practical information on pulse oximeters): some oximeters underestimate or overestimate saturations, especially when borderline, and overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. His true saturation may be lower, so the reading should be interpreted with his clinical picture and escalated if concerned.

n.0: The reported error in people with dark skin is overestimation, not underestimation.
n.2: Increasing breathlessness is significant even when the oximeter reading is within target.
n.3: 94% on air is within the 94-98% target for most adults; starting oxygen is not indicated by the number alone.

6.q: A ward manager is reviewing last month's incident reports with the team. She explains that some incidents are classed as Never Events because strong national safety barriers exist to prevent them. Which of the following incidents is classed as a Never Event in NHS England?
o: A fall resulting in a hip fracture on a ward
A missed dose of a prescribed antibiotic
Misplaced nasogastric tube not detected before use
A category 3 pressure ulcer acquired in hospital
6.w: The NHS England Never Events list (2018, updated 2021, still active) includes misplaced naso- or oro-gastric tubes not detected before use, as strong national barriers (pH testing and X-ray protocols) exist.

n.0: Inpatient falls are serious incidents but are not on the Never Events list.
n.1: Missed doses are medication incidents but are not Never Events.
n.3: Pressure ulcers are reported as incidents but are not Never Events.

6.q: A district nursing team wants to find out how patients rate their new evening visiting service, with no benchmark to compare against, by asking current patients to complete a short questionnaire. What type of project is this?
o: Qualitative research study
Clinical audit
Randomised controlled trial
Service evaluation
6.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): service evaluation asks 'What standard does this service achieve?', measures the current service without reference to a standard and does not need REC review.

n.0: It aims to judge the current service, not to generate generalisable knowledge.
n.1: Audit compares practice with a predetermined standard; here there is no standard.
n.2: There is no allocation to interventions or randomisation.

6.q: Leah, 34, attends the emergency department after self-harm. A colleague completes a self-harm risk scale, which places her at low risk, and suggests she can be discharged on that basis. According to NICE NG225, what should happen?
o: Assess Leah's needs and agree a safety plan with her, not using the scale
Repeat the scale in four hours and discharge Leah if it is unchanged
Discharge Leah, as the scale places her in the low-risk group
Admit Leah for observation until a medium-risk score can be ruled out
6.w: NICE NG225 (2022) advises not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Care is based on a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan developed with the person.

n.1: Repeating an invalid tool does not make it a valid basis for discharge.
n.2: NG225 says scales must not be used to decide discharge; a low score gives false reassurance.
n.3: NG225 advises against global low, medium or high risk stratification; admission is decided by assessed needs, not a score band.

6.q: Margaret, 83, has mixed dementia and no history of epilepsy or bipolar disorder. She has become verbally aggressive in the evenings. A locum doctor suggests starting sodium valproate to calm her. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as NICE advises against valproate for agitation in dementia
Give it, as valproate is safer than antipsychotics in older people
Give it, then check her valproate blood level after the first week
Give it, as mood stabilisers are first-line for agitation in dementia
6.w: NG97 1.7.10: do not offer valproate to manage agitation or aggression in people living with dementia, unless it is indicated for another condition. Code 18 and 19 require nurses to question medicines that may cause harm.

n.1: NICE does not recommend valproate as an alternative to antipsychotics for this purpose.
n.2: Monitoring levels does not address that valproate should not be started for this indication.
n.3: First-line management is a structured assessment and psychosocial interventions, not mood stabilisers.

6.q: Simon, 38, has anaphylaxis after an iodinated contrast injection in the radiology department. The nurse opens the emergency drug box, which contains several adrenaline preparations. Which preparation should be drawn up for his intramuscular injection?
o: 5 mg/mL (1 in 200)
10 micrograms/mL (1 in 100,000)
100 micrograms/mL (1 in 10,000)
6.w: RCUK: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) preparation, for example 0.5 mL = 500 micrograms in an adult.

n.0: 5 mg/mL is not a standard adrenaline preparation for anaphylaxis.
n.1: 1 in 100,000 is a dilution used by specialists for IV infusion, not IM.
n.2: 1 in 10,000 is the IV preparation used in cardiac arrest, not for IM anaphylaxis treatment.

6.q: Mrs Ellis, 81, has advanced heart failure and full capacity. A doctor completes a DNACPR form overnight and asks the nurse not to mention it to her because 'it will only upset her'. Mrs Ellis has said she wants to be involved in all decisions. Which statement best reflects the legal position?
o: She should be consulted unless this is likely to cause her physical or psychological harm
She should be told once the decision has been reviewed by a second consultant
She need not be told because a DNACPR decision is a clinical decision for the doctor
Her husband should be told instead, as the decision affects the whole family
6.w: In R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014] EWCA Civ 822, the Court of Appeal held that Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions and that there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Possible upset is not enough.

n.1: A second opinion does not replace the duty to consult her before the notice is placed; delaying her involvement is not lawful on these facts.
n.2: Tracey held that although CPR is a clinical decision, the patient must be involved and consulted; the clinical nature of the decision does not remove that duty.
n.3: Mrs Ellis has capacity, so the duty to consult is owed to her; informing her husband in her place breaches her Article 8 rights and confidentiality.

6.q: Daniel, 45, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain haemorrhage. Treatment is to be withdrawn. He has lived in England all his life and has not recorded a donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. What happens about organ donation?
o: His organs are retrieved without discussion because his consent is deemed
His family are approached to find out whether he held any views about donation
The consultant decides on donation at a best interests meeting
Donation cannot proceed because he did not register as an organ donor
6.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England (opt out from 20 May 2020): adults are considered to agree to donate unless they recorded a decision not to donate or are in an excluded group, and families are still consulted when donation is a possibility, to share any knowledge of the person's decision.

n.0: Under the opt-out law the family are still consulted when donation is possible; retrieval does not proceed without that discussion.
n.2: Donation decisions follow the deemed consent law and the person's known views, not a clinical best interests meeting.
n.3: In England, adults not in an excluded group are considered to agree unless they opted out; registration is not required.

6.q: On a surgical ward, Femi asks the ward manager about the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 because a new bariatric care pathway is being written. Which step do the regulations require the employer to take first?
o: Set a maximum weight that any member of staff may lift on the ward
Reduce the risk of injury to the lowest level by providing equipment
Avoid hazardous manual handling so far as is reasonably practicable
Assess the risk of injury from every manual handling task on the ward
6.w: The Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 set out a hierarchy for employers: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; assess the risk of injury from any hazardous operations that cannot be avoided; and reduce that risk to as low as reasonably practicable (HSE, Manual handling at work).

n.0: The HSE states that the law does not set specific weight limits; weight is one factor in the risk assessment.
n.1: Reducing risk is the third step, after avoidance and assessment.
n.3: Assessment is the second step and applies to hazardous handling that cannot be avoided, not to every task.

6.q: A hospital is reviewing how it meets the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605). Which patient's need falls within the scope of the standard?
o: A patient whose first language is Romanian
A patient who wants a copy of their clinic letter
A Deaf patient who uses British Sign Language
A patient who prefers appointments by email
6.w: Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025): covers information and communication needs relating to disability, impairment or sensory loss, through six stages: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review.

n.0: Language needs without a disability are met through interpreting services, not the AIS.
n.1: Receiving copies is an access right, not an AIS communication need.
n.3: A general preference unrelated to disability or sensory loss is outside the AIS.

6.q: Leah, 27, has type 1 diabetes. She phones the ward helpline saying she has had diarrhoea and vomiting since last night, is not eating and her glucose is 16 mmol/L. She plans to skip her insulin until she can eat. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop insulin until vomiting settles, sipping sugary drinks meanwhile
Keep taking insulin, check blood ketones and seek urgent help if raised
Omit long-acting insulin and continue mealtime doses with fluids
Halve all insulin doses and recheck glucose in 24 hours
6.w: Insulin must not be stopped during illness: insulin deficiency drives ketone production. NICE NG17 (1.7.23, 1.10.1) recommends sick-day rules including ketone monitoring, and vomiting with raised ketones needs urgent assessment for DKA.

n.0: Stopping insulin while vomiting is a classic route into diabetic ketoacidosis.
n.2: Basal insulin is the dose that suppresses ketogenesis; omitting it is the most dangerous change.
n.3: Halving doses with a 24-hour wait ignores rising glucose and the need to check ketones now.

6.q: Paula, 38, has a reversibility test. Her FEV1 is 2.0 L before and 2.3 L after a bronchodilator. How should this result be interpreted?
o: Negative, as FEV1 needs to rise by 20%
Positive, as FEV1 rose by 15% and 300 mL
Positive, as FEV1 rose by 10% and 200 mL
Negative, as FEV1 needs to rise by 400 mL
6.w: Two steps: change = 2.3 - 2.0 = 0.3 L (300 mL); 0.3 / 2.0 x 100 = 15%. NG245 counts an FEV1 increase of 12% or more AND 200 mL or more as a positive bronchodilator reversibility test.

n.0: The NG245 threshold is 12%, not 20%.
n.2: The rise is 300 mL (15%), not 200 mL (10%); the working is wrong.
n.3: 400 mL is not the NG245 threshold; the test needs 12% and 200 mL or more.

6.q: Lisa, 45, has had widespread pain for 8 months with poor sleep and low mood. Blood tests and imaging are normal and no injury or disease explains the pain or its impact. Using NICE NG193 terms, how is her pain best classified?
o: Neuropathic pain, as it is widespread and has no visible cause or injury
Chronic primary pain, as no condition adequately accounts for it
Chronic secondary pain, as it has lasted more than 3 months
Acute pain, as it began less than 12 months ago
6.w: NG193: chronic pain persists or recurs for more than 3 months. Chronic primary pain is where no underlying condition adequately accounts for the pain or its impact; chronic secondary pain is where one does. The two can coexist.

n.0: Neuropathic pain arises from nerve damage or disease, which has not been identified here.
n.2: Secondary pain requires an underlying condition that accounts for it, which has not been found.
n.3: Pain lasting more than 3 months is chronic, not acute.

6.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
6.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

6.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
6.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

6.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
6.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

6.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
6.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

6.q: Mrs Turner, 72, had a hip replacement two days ago. Her son tells the nurse at visiting time that his mother 'seems confused and is seeing things on the curtains', which started this afternoon. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the son to stay with her to settle her for the night
Note it and ask the night staff to see if it continues
Reassure the son that this is common after an anaesthetic
Assess her for delirium and record the reported change
6.w: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1-1.5.2: recent changes or fluctuations (including hallucinations) may be reported by relatives and should prompt assessment with an appropriate tool; changes must be documented.

n.0: Family presence can help, but it does not replace assessment of a new change.
n.1: Deferring to night staff delays assessment of an acute change.
n.2: Dismissing a new change risks missing delirium and its cause.

6.q: Hassan, 54, is prescribed 7.5 mg of an intramuscular medicine. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 2 mL. The nurse works out the volume to draw up and a colleague is available. What volume is needed, and what should happen before administration?
o: 1.5 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
2.67 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
0.75 mL, then give it straight away as the colleague is busy
3.75 mL, then record the calculation in the notes and give it
6.w: Volume = (dose required / stock strength) x stock volume = (7.5 / 10) x 2 = 1.5 mL. RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 says any calculations needed are double checked, where practicable, by a second person.

n.1: 2.67 mL inverts the fraction (10 / 7.5 x 2); a check would catch it, but the volume is wrong.
n.2: 0.75 mL omits multiplying by the 2 mL volume, and skipping an available second check is unsafe.
n.3: 3.75 mL comes from dividing the dose by the stock volume (7.5 / 2) instead of using the formula, and no second check is made.

6.q: Following radiotherapy, the team judges that Joe's spine, affected by metastases, is likely to be stable. He starts graded sitting. When the bed head is raised to 60 degrees his back pain increases sharply and his legs feel weaker. What should the nurse do?
o: Stand him with a frame, as standing can relieve back pain
Give breakthrough analgesia and continue sitting him upright
Continue to 90 degrees, as pain is expected when sitting up
Lower him until the changes reverse, then seek reassessment
6.w: NG234 1.6.2-1.6.4: monitor neurological symptoms and pain continuously during mobilisation; if pain or neurological symptoms significantly increase, return the person to a position where these changes reverse and reassess spinal stability.

n.0: Standing increases spinal loading when there are signs of instability.
n.1: Analgesia may mask warning signs; the new weakness needs reassessment.
n.2: Progressing despite increasing pain and weakness risks further cord damage.

6.q: A community nurse is supporting Elsie, 82, who lives alone, to plan her care. Public Health England's life course guidance identifies a main outcome to aim for across life, including in older age. What is it?
o: Reducing the number of medicines prescribed
Planning an early move into residential care
Maintaining good functional ability
Increasing the total number of years lived
6.w: Public Health England, Health matters: prevention, a life course approach (2019): maintaining good functional ability is the main outcome of the life course approach to health, and functional ability can be enhanced throughout life by a supportive environment.

n.0: Medicine reduction may help some people but is not the main outcome named.
n.1: Moving into care is not an outcome measure of the life course approach.
n.3: The guidance identifies functional ability as the main outcome, not length of life.

6.q: Ahmed, 47, has type 2 diabetes managed with modified-release metformin and dapagliflozin. He does not drive for work and has never had a hypo. He asks for a glucose meter to test daily. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Advise testing once a week to track his response to treatment
Explain routine self-testing is not recommended on his medicines
Provide a meter and advise testing before each main meal
Provide a meter and advise testing each morning before breakfast
6.w: NICE NG28 (1.6.2) does not routinely recommend capillary self-monitoring in type 2 diabetes unless the person uses insulin, has hypoglycaemia, takes oral medicines that may cause hypos while driving or operating machinery, or is pregnant or planning pregnancy. HbA1c monitors his control.

n.0: Weekly snapshots do not reliably show response; HbA1c is the monitoring measure.
n.2: Pre-meal testing suits insulin dose adjustment, which Ahmed does not need.
n.3: Daily fasting checks are not routinely indicated on medicines that do not cause hypoglycaemia.

6.q: Linda, 59, had breast cancer treated 4 years ago. At a clinic visit she reports 3 weeks of progressive back pain that wakes her at night and worsens when she coughs. Her strength, sensation, bladder and bowel function are normal. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours
Reassure her that this sounds like mechanical back pain
Request a plain spinal X-ray before any specialist referral
Refer her for a routine outpatient MRI within 6 weeks
6.w: NG234 1.3.3: seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours if a person with a past or current cancer diagnosis has pain with characteristics suggesting spinal metastases (progressive, night pain, pain on straining), without cord compression signs.

n.1: Night pain and pain on straining in someone with previous cancer are red flags for spinal metastases.
n.2: NG234 1.5.9 says do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases.
n.3: A 6-week routine wait is too slow for pain suggesting spinal metastases.

6.q: Mr Daly, 80, has capacity. When the nurse begins to explain his scan results, he says, "I don't want the details. Just tell my daughter." What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain the results fully, as he has a legal right to know them all
Respect his wish, check what he wants to know and his consent to share
Tell his daughter everything and give him no information himself
Delay the conversation until he is ready for all the details
6.w: Code 2.4: respect the level to which people want to be involved in decisions about their care. Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows, with consent.

n.0: Code 2.4 requires respect for the level of involvement he wants.
n.2: He should be asked what he does want to know, and his consent confirmed first.
n.3: He has stated his wish now; delaying ignores it.

6.q: Sheila, 72, arrives in the recovery room after a 3-hour hip replacement. Her temperature is 35.6 C and she is shivering. The ward has called to collect her. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her temperature in recovery in 1 hour
Transfer her with two warm blankets and recheck on the ward
Transfer her and start forced-air warming on the ward
Use forced-air warming and transfer once 36.0 C or above
6.w: NICE CG65 (1.4.1): measure temperature on arrival in recovery and every 15 minutes; do not arrange ward transfer unless temperature is 36.0 C or above; if below 36.0 C, actively warm with forced-air warming until discharged from recovery or comfortably warm.

n.0: CG65 asks for temperature every 15 minutes in recovery and active warming now, not a 1-hour wait.
n.1: Blankets are passive warming, and CG65 advises against ward transfer below 36.0 C.
n.2: Warming should start in recovery, and transfer waits until she is 36.0 C or above.

6.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
6.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

6.q: Hannah, a staff nurse, is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Derek Lowe, 58. At the bedside he tells her he is allergic to penicillin. His allergy band was missing and the chart says 'no known allergies'. No dose was given. What should Hannah do about reporting?
o: Report herself to the NMC, as she nearly gave a contraindicated drug
Record it as a near miss on the trust's patient safety reporting system
Tell the ward manager verbally, as no harm reached the patient
Correct the chart and allergy band, as no report is needed without harm
6.w: Near misses are patient safety events and must be recorded so the system can learn, whether or not harm occurred (P6.8; Code 14 and NMC/GMC candour guidance 2024, which covers reporting near misses). Local systems feed the national Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service. The chart and band must also be corrected and the prescriber informed.

n.0: Self-referral to the regulator is not the response to a near miss caught by correct checks; this is a system issue for local reporting.
n.2: Verbal reporting alone loses the learning; near misses are formally recorded on the local system.
n.3: Correcting the records is needed, but near misses are reported because they reveal weaknesses before harm occurs.

6.q: Ada, 76, has an upper GI bleed and continues to pass fresh melaena. Her platelet count is 42 x 10^9/L and her INR is 1.2. Which blood component is indicated now under NICE guidance?
o: Fresh frozen plasma
Cryoprecipitate
Prothrombin complex concentrate
Platelet transfusion
6.w: Two steps: she is actively bleeding, and her platelet count is below 50 x 10^9/L. NICE CG141 (1.2.4) says offer platelet transfusion to patients who are actively bleeding with platelets below 50 x 10^9/L. Her INR is not above 1.5 times normal, so FFP is not indicated.

n.0: FFP is for active bleeding with PT/INR or APTT above 1.5 times normal; her INR is 1.2.
n.1: Cryoprecipitate is added when fibrinogen stays below 1.5 g/L despite FFP.
n.2: Prothrombin complex concentrate is for actively bleeding patients taking warfarin.

6.q: Ruth, 68, has type 2 diabetes and is being referred for an elective hip replacement. Her HbA1c measured last month is 74 mmol/mol. According to the JBDS perioperative guideline, what should happen?
o: Proceed with surgery and use a variable rate insulin infusion
Proceed with surgery, as HbA1c is not relevant to elective surgery
Optimise her diabetes before surgery, as HbA1c is above 69 mmol/mol
Cancel the referral until her HbA1c is below 48 mmol/mol
6.w: Two steps: JBDS 03 (CPOC, 2022) asks for an HbA1c within 3 months before referral and advises optimising diabetes before elective surgery if HbA1c is above 69 mmol/mol (8.5%), because poor control increases complications such as infection.

n.0: A VRIII manages glucose on the day but does not address the risk from poor preoperative control.
n.1: Raised HbA1c is linked with more postoperative complications, so it is relevant to elective surgery.
n.3: 48 mmol/mol is a long-term target, not the threshold for proceeding with surgery.

6.q: On discharge, several patients offer gifts to the ward team. According to the Code, which gift would it be acceptable to accept, subject to local policy?
o: A £50 gift voucher for the nurse who cared for her
A £100 cheque for the nurse's personal use
A designer handbag for the nurse in charge
A box of chocolates for the whole team to share
6.w: Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality, as accepting them could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment.

n.0: A voucher of this value is not trivial; Code 21.1 says refuse all but the most trivial gifts.
n.1: Money for personal use is not a trivial gift and may be seen as an inducement.
n.2: An expensive gift could be seen as seeking preferential treatment and breaches Code 21.1.

6.q: During a late shift on an adult surgical ward, a healthcare assistant tells Ruby, the nurse in charge, that Mr Peter Grant, 70, asked for analgesia 45 minutes ago and has still not received it because both nurses in his bay are busy. What should Ruby do?
o: Complete an incident report at the end of the shift and continue with the current allocation
Record the delay in Mr Grant's notes and discuss the bay workload at the next team meeting
Arrange for Mr Grant's analgesia to be given now and escalate the red flag on staffing
Ask the healthcare assistant to tell Mr Grant that a nurse will come once the bay is quieter
6.w: NICE SG1 Safe staffing for nursing in adult inpatient wards (2014) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in providing pain relief as a nursing red flag. A red flag should prompt an immediate escalation response by the registered nurse in charge, for example allocating additional staff (rec 1.4.3, Box 2). Mr Grant's pain is dealt with first.

n.0: Reporting is useful but does not relieve his pain or address the staffing problem now.
n.1: Documenting and deferring discussion does not meet the immediate escalation response that SG1 requires.
n.3: This prolongs his pain and treats a recognised red flag as routine.

6.q: A newly qualified nurse is learning which ward medicines must be entered in the controlled drugs register. Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, which of these medicines is a Schedule 2 controlled drug?
o: Diazepam 5 mg tablets
Oxycodone 5 mg in 5 mL oral solution
Tramadol 50 mg capsules
Midazolam injection 10 mg in 2 mL
6.w: Under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001 (Home Office controlled drugs list), oxycodone is in Schedule 2, alongside morphine, diamorphine and fentanyl, and needs a CD register entry (NICE NG46). Midazolam and tramadol are Schedule 3; diazepam is Schedule 4 Part 1.

n.0: Diazepam is a Schedule 4 Part 1 benzodiazepine.
n.2: Tramadol is in Schedule 3.
n.3: Midazolam is a Schedule 3 controlled drug, although many hospitals record it in the register by local policy.

6.q: At a team meeting, a district nursing team leader explains the integrated care partnership (ICP) in her area. Which statement about the ICP is correct?
o: It inspects and rates the quality of local health services
It is the NHS body that commissions hospital and GP services
It is a joint committee that develops the integrated care strategy
It employs the community nurses who work in the local area
6.w: The ICP is a joint committee run by the NHS organisations and upper-tier local authorities in each ICS, with wider partners such as the voluntary sector. It must develop a long-term integrated care strategy to improve health, care and wellbeing (NHS England, What is integrated care?; P7.1).

n.0: Inspection and rating are carried out by the Care Quality Commission in England.
n.1: Planning NHS services and managing the budget is the role of the integrated care board.
n.3: Community nurses are employed by provider organisations, not by the ICP.

6.q: At a retirement celebration on the ward, a nurse takes a team photograph. A patient sitting in a bay is visible in the background. The nurse wants to post it on her public social media account. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Post the photograph after blurring the patient's face
Post the photograph with no names or ward details
Post the photograph using strict privacy settings
Post a version without the patient, who has not consented
6.w: NMC social media guidance: do not post pictures of patients and people receiving care without their consent, regardless of whether you believe they could be identified. Code 5.1 and 20.10.

n.0: NMC guidance requires consent before posting images of patients, whether or not you believe they could be identified.
n.1: Removing names does not remove the need for the patient's consent to the image being shared.
n.2: Privacy settings do not replace consent and content can still be shared onward.

6.q: An integrated frailty service involves a hospital, community nursing, social care and a voluntary sector partner. The service lead, Ade, wants to evaluate the quality of people's experience of care across the whole pathway. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Measure the average length of hospital stay for people in the service
Compare each organisation's complaint numbers separately for the past year
Ask people and families for feedback on their whole journey across services
Survey staff in each organisation about how well they work together
6.w: Evaluating the experience of complex care means asking the people who receive it, and their families, about the whole journey, including transitions between services (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Length of stay is an efficiency measure, not a measure of people's experience.
n.1: Complaints in separate organisations show only part of the picture and miss the transitions between services.
n.3: Staff views are useful but do not describe the experience of people using the service.

6.q: Under regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations, an apology must be given as part of the duty of candour. Which statement to a patient best meets the regulation's definition of an apology?
o: "Errors like this are rare and are usually harmless."
"The trust accepts legal liability for the error."
"I am very sorry that this happened to you."
"An investigation will decide who was responsible."
6.w: Reg 20(7): 'apology' means an expression of sorrow or regret in respect of a notifiable safety incident. Code 14.2 requires the nurse to apologise to the person affected.

n.0: This minimises the incident and does not express sorrow or regret.
n.1: An admission of liability is not what the regulation means by an apology; it means an expression of sorrow or regret.
n.3: This explains process but contains no expression of sorrow or regret.

6.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
6.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

6.q: Charlie, a mental health nurse in England, asks in October 2026 whether the Mental Health Act 2025 has replaced the 1983 Act for detentions on his ward. Which statement is correct?
o: The 2025 Act received Royal Assent, but most provisions are not yet in force
The 2025 Act applies to new detentions; the 1983 Act applies to existing ones
The 2025 Act is still a Bill and has not yet completed its parliamentary stages
The 2025 Act is fully in force and has replaced the 1983 Act in England
6.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions (including changes to sections 3 and 4) were not in force at October 2026. The Mental Health Act 1983 as amended remains the current law for detention (BUILD-PLAN unsettled law note; P7.4 implications of current and future health policy).

n.1: There is no rule of this kind; detentions continue under the 1983 Act as amended until provisions are commenced.
n.2: The Act completed its passage and received Royal Assent in December 2025.
n.3: Most provisions of the 2025 Act await commencement, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies.

6.q: Kieran, 45, is shouting in a corridor after being told his discharge is delayed. He is pacing and red-faced but has not threatened anyone. Which approach is the best first step?
o: Call security to remove him from the ward straight away
Stand close and tell him firmly to lower his voice immediately
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and acknowledge his frustration
Walk away and leave him until he has calmed himself down
6.w: De-escalation (Annexe A 3.5; NICE NG10) is the first-line response to agitation: a calm, non-threatening stance at a safe distance, active listening and acknowledging feelings, offering choices and reducing stimulation. Restrictive options are a last resort.

n.0: Removal by security is restrictive and premature when de-escalation has not been tried.
n.1: Standing close and issuing commands can feel threatening and escalate the situation.
n.3: Leaving an agitated person unsupported misses the chance to de-escalate and to keep others safe.

6.q: Victor, 81, has been taking clindamycin for 5 days for cellulitis. He now has four episodes of watery diarrhoea in 12 hours and is in a four-bed bay. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop the clindamycin and keep him in the bay with curtains drawn
Isolate him, send a stool sample and ask for an antibiotic review
Give loperamide and review his bowels at the end of the day
Send a stool sample and keep him in the bay until the result returns
6.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.35 highlights the risk of selecting for C. difficile with certain antibiotics. New diarrhoea on antibiotics should prompt isolation on suspicion (NIPCM ch 2.1), a stool sample and a prescriber review of the antibiotic.

n.0: Changing antibiotics is a prescriber decision, and staying in the bay exposes other patients.
n.2: Antimotility drugs are inappropriate in suspected C. difficile and delay diagnosis.
n.3: Isolation should not wait for the result, as C. difficile spreads to others in the bay.

6.q: Pauline, 72, has a sudden urge to pass urine and often leaks before reaching the toilet. She passes urine every hour and drinks six cups of strong coffee a day. Infection has been excluded. Which plan follows NICE NG123?
o: An indwelling urinary catheter while waiting for urodynamic studies
Immediate-release oxybutynin with a review at 6 months
Supervised pelvic floor training for 3 months, with pads
Bladder training for at least 6 weeks, with caffeine reduction
6.w: NG123 1.4.11: offer bladder training lasting a minimum of 6 weeks as first-line treatment for urgency or mixed incontinence; 1.4.1 recommends a trial of caffeine reduction in overactive bladder.

n.0: Catheterisation is not a treatment for overactive bladder, and urodynamics are not routine before conservative treatment.
n.1: Drug treatment follows conservative measures, review is due at 4 weeks (1.4.38), and IR oxybutynin is cautioned in older women.
n.2: Pelvic floor training is first-line for stress or mixed incontinence; her picture is urgency.

6.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
6.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

6.q: Ellen, 77, who had C. difficile infection, has been discharged home from a single room. The domestic team asks the nurse what terminal cleaning is required. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Use detergent wipes on surfaces and send the curtains as used linen
Clean with a 10,000 ppm available chlorine solution and leave the curtains in place
Clean with neutral detergent and change the curtains at the next routine change
Remove the curtains as infectious linen and clean with 1,000 ppm available chlorine
6.w: NIPCM ch 2.3 terminal decontamination: bag and remove waste, manage curtains and bedding as infectious linen, decontaminate equipment, then clean with a combined detergent and 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or detergent followed by 1,000 ppm), working from high to low and least to most contaminated.

n.0: Curtains from an infectious patient's room are infectious linen, and wipes alone are not a terminal clean.
n.1: 10,000 ppm is the strength for blood spills; terminal cleaning uses 1,000 ppm, and curtains are removed.
n.2: Detergent alone does not meet the terminal clean standard, and curtains from an isolation room are removed as infectious linen.

6.q: Fiona, 26, knows her best peak flow is 500 L/min. During an attack her PEF is 150 L/min. She can speak in full sentences and her SpO2 is 95%. What is her PEF as a percentage of best, and how is this classified?
o: 30%, which is life-threatening
30%, which is classed as acute severe
33%, which is classed as acute severe
40%, which is classed as acute severe
6.w: Two steps: 150 / 500 x 100 = 30%. SIGN 158: PEF below 33% best or predicted is a life-threatening feature.

n.1: Acute severe is PEF 33-50%; 30% is below 33% and so is life-threatening.
n.3: The calculation is wrong: 150/500 x 100 = 30%.

6.q: Mr Osei, 80, has mild cognitive impairment. The nurse explains the options for his discharge. He understands, weighs the options and chooses home with carers, but 20 minutes later he cannot recall the details of the conversation. What should the nurse conclude?
o: He lacks capacity, because his cognitive impairment is lifelong
His capacity must be reassessed by a psychiatrist before discharge
He lacks capacity, because he could not recall the information
He can still make the decision, as retaining it briefly is enough
6.w: MCA 2005 s3(3): the fact that a person can retain information for a short period only does not prevent him from being regarded as able to make the decision. Mr Osei retained it long enough to make his choice.

n.0: A condition cannot establish incapacity (s2(3)); the test is functional and decision-specific.
n.1: Any suitably skilled decision maker can assess capacity; a psychiatrist is not required when the s3 test is already met.
n.2: s3(3) states that short-term retention is sufficient; later forgetting does not mean he lacked capacity.

6.q: On admission, Derek, 59, says he is 'allergic' to codeine. When asked, he explains that it made him nauseated and constipated, with no rash, swelling or breathing problems. How should the nurse record this?
o: Record a morphine allergy, as it is in the same group
Record a codeine allergy and apply a red allergy wristband
Record a codeine intolerance, noting nausea and constipation
Record no reaction, as nausea is not clinically relevant
6.w: Responding to adverse reactions (AnnexB.11.10) includes accurate documentation: the drug, the reaction and its nature. Nausea and constipation are predictable side effects (intolerance), not an immune allergy; labelling them as allergy can deny appropriate analgesia later.

n.0: Extending an inaccurate label to morphine compounds the error.
n.1: An allergy label for a side effect is inaccurate and may restrict future treatment.
n.3: The reaction still matters to future prescribing and should be documented.

6.q: What is the standard UK in-hospital telephone number for calling the cardiac arrest team?
6.w: RCUK 2025 in-hospital resuscitation: 2222 is the standard UK internal number for cardiac arrest and medical emergency calls.

n.0: 3333 is not the standardised UK cardiac arrest number.
n.1: 999 is the external emergency number, used out of hospital.
n.3: 111 is the NHS non-emergency advice line.

6.q: An occupational health nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin skin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms that the injection has been placed correctly?
o: The fluid flows freely and leaves no mark on the skin
Blood flashback is seen in the hub of the syringe
A small pale bleb forms raising the skin at the site
A bruise appears at the site within a few minutes
6.w: Intradermal injections are given at a shallow angle of about 10-15 degrees with the bevel up, just under the epidermis; correct placement raises a small pale bleb (AnnexB.11.7). No bleb suggests a deeper, subcutaneous injection.

n.0: Free flow with no bleb suggests the fluid has gone into subcutaneous tissue.
n.1: Flashback indicates the needle is in a blood vessel, not the dermis.
n.3: Bruising suggests trauma to vessels, not correct dermal placement.

6.q: Priya, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant and attends her antenatal appointment in October, during the flu season. She has had no vaccines in this pregnancy. According to the UKHSA schedule, which vaccines should she be offered now?
o: Flu, pertussis and RSV vaccines, all at this appointment
Pertussis vaccine now, with the flu vaccine after the birth
RSV vaccine now, with the pertussis vaccine from 28 weeks
Inactivated flu vaccine and the pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
6.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: in pregnancy, inactivated flu vaccine at any stage during the flu season; pertussis (Tdap) from 16 weeks (ideally before 32 weeks but may be given later); RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks.

n.0: RSV vaccine is offered from 28 weeks of pregnancy, so it is not due at 20 weeks.
n.1: Inactivated flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season.
n.2: This reverses the timings: pertussis is from 16 weeks and RSV from 28 weeks.

7.q: Mr Grant, 72, has COPD and is admitted with breathlessness. His SpO2 is 89% on air. No target saturation range has been prescribed or documented. A colleague says to use NEWS2 SpO2 Scale 2 because he has COPD. What should the nurse do?
o: Use Scale 2, because a diagnosis of COPD is sufficient
Use Scale 1 and ask the medical team to prescribe a target range
Use Scale 2 and give oxygen to reach 94-98% saturations
Leave the SpO2 parameter unscored until a target range is prescribed
7.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): Scale 2 (target 88-92%) is for people with hypercapnic respiratory failure and is used when a clinician has prescribed that target. Until then Scale 1 applies (89% scores 3), and the team should be asked to set a target.

n.0: COPD alone does not authorise Scale 2; it must be prescribed by a clinician.
n.2: Scale 2 corresponds to a target of 88-92%, not 94-98%.
n.3: Leaving the parameter unscored gives a falsely low NEWS2 and delays escalation.

7.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
7.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.

7.q: Linda, 59, had breast cancer treated 4 years ago. At a clinic visit she reports 3 weeks of progressive back pain that wakes her at night and worsens when she coughs. Her strength, sensation, bladder and bowel function are normal. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours
Reassure her that this sounds like mechanical back pain
Request a plain spinal X-ray before any specialist referral
Refer her for a routine outpatient MRI within 6 weeks
7.w: NG234 1.3.3: seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours if a person with a past or current cancer diagnosis has pain with characteristics suggesting spinal metastases (progressive, night pain, pain on straining), without cord compression signs.

n.1: Night pain and pain on straining in someone with previous cancer are red flags for spinal metastases.
n.2: NG234 1.5.9 says do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases.
n.3: A 6-week routine wait is too slow for pain suggesting spinal metastases.

7.q: Two staff nurses begin arguing loudly at the nurses' station about who should admit a new patient. Patients and visitors nearby are watching. Lorna is the nurse in charge. What should Lorna do first?
o: Admit the new patient herself so that the disagreement is no longer relevant
Calmly ask them both to step into the office and talk the issue through there
Tell both nurses firmly that they will each be reported to the ward manager
Leave them to resolve it between themselves, as they are both experienced nurses
7.w: A calm presence and moving the conflict to a private place protects patients' dignity and the team's professionalism and allows the issue to be resolved (AnnexA.4.2.3 calm presence when dealing with conflict; Code 20.1 and 20.3). The admission can then be allocated clearly.

n.0: Taking the task herself avoids the conflict without addressing it and adds to her workload.
n.2: Threatening sanctions in public escalates the conflict and does not resolve the allocation.
n.3: A public argument is affecting patients now; the nurse in charge needs to intervene.

7.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
7.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

7.q: Ian, 35, has type 1 diabetes and is shaky and sweaty at a community clinic. He is alert and able to swallow. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. After giving 15-20 g of glucose tablets, his symptoms are no better at 15 minutes. What should you do?
o: Give a further 15-20 g of oral glucose
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give him a meal containing complex carbohydrate
Recheck his blood glucose again in 30 minutes
7.w: RCUK first aid 2025: treat hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L) in a person who can swallow with 15-20 g glucose; repeat if symptoms persist after 15 minutes; give a snack once recovered.

n.1: He is alert and swallowing, so oral treatment is repeated before an emergency call.
n.2: A snack follows recovery; complex carbohydrate alone is too slow while still hypoglycaemic.
n.3: Waiting another 30 minutes leaves hypoglycaemia untreated.

7.q: Iris, 76, is awaiting emergency laparotomy for a perforated bowel. She is dehydrated, with a pulse of 110, and has diabetes and heart failure. Her chart includes regular ibuprofen for pain. What should the nurse do?
o: Swap the ibuprofen for a COX-2 inhibitor such as celecoxib
Give the ibuprofen, as NSAIDs reduce opioid requirements
Query the ibuprofen because NSAIDs raise her risk of AKI
Give the ibuprofen with food to protect her stomach
7.w: NICE NG148 (1.1.13) lists emergency surgery with sepsis or hypovolaemia, intraperitoneal surgery, diabetes, heart failure, age 65 or over and NSAIDs among AKI risk factors in surgical patients. NSAIDs in a dehydrated patient should be queried with the prescriber.

n.0: COX-2 inhibitors carry the same renal risk, and substituting a medicine is for the prescriber.
n.1: The opioid-sparing benefit does not outweigh the AKI risk in a dehydrated high-risk patient.
n.3: Food does not reduce the effect of NSAIDs on renal blood flow, and she is nil by mouth for theatre.

7.q: Stanley, 67, arrives in the emergency department with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 90% on a 28% Venturi mask. A colleague says blood gases are unnecessary because his saturation is within the target. Which reply is best?
o: Blood gases are needed because his saturation is above target
Blood gases are needed to measure his haemoglobin level
Oximetry tells us nothing about his carbon dioxide or pH
Blood gases are needed before any nebuliser can be given
7.w: NICE NG115: pulse oximetry gives no information about PaCO2 or pH, so measure arterial blood gases (noting the inspired oxygen) in everyone arriving at hospital with an exacerbation.

n.0: His saturation of 90% is within the 88-92% target; the reason for gases is the missing CO2 and pH data.
n.1: Haemoglobin is not the reason NICE gives for measuring gases in exacerbations.
n.3: Bronchodilators are not delayed for gas results; the gas guides oxygen and ventilation.

7.q: Linda, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric infusion pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should you check first?
o: The line, clamps and cannula site for a blockage
The pump's battery level and mains connection
The fluid bag for an air bubble near the top
The prescription chart for the next bag due
7.w: A downstream occlusion means resistance between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing and the cannula site (phlebitis, infiltration or a positional cannula) before restarting (Annexe B 5.9).

n.1: Battery alarms are separate from occlusion alarms.
n.2: Air at the top of the bag is above the pump and does not cause a downstream occlusion.
n.3: The prescription does not explain an occlusion alarm.

7.q: Chloe, 19, has type 1 diabetes and presents with vomiting and abdominal pain. Four sets of venous results are reviewed during the shift. Which set meets the JBDS criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis?
o: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 1.4 mmol/L, pH 7.34
Glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones 0.9 mmol/L, pH 7.36
Glucose 9 mmol/L, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, pH 7.29
Glucose 18 mmol/L, ketones 4.2 mmol/L, pH 7.21
7.w: JBDS 02 (2023) requires all three: glucose above 11.0 mmol/L or known diabetes, blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L (or ketonuria 2+), and bicarbonate below 15.0 mmol/L and/or venous pH below 7.3.

n.0: Ketones of 1.4 mmol/L and a pH of 7.34 do not meet the ketonaemia or acidosis criteria.
n.1: Very high glucose with low ketones and normal pH suggests HHS, not DKA.
n.2: There is no ketonaemia; the low pH needs another explanation.

7.q: Tara, 22, tells the nurse, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which technique is this?
o: A cognitive behavioural therapy method
A motivational interviewing technique
A distraction and diversion technique
A reminiscence therapy based technique
7.w: Annexe A 3.6: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques. Examining evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is cognitive restructuring.

n.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not evidence for thoughts.
n.2: Distraction moves attention away; this examines the thought directly.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories for wellbeing, not testing thoughts.

7.q: Which contemporary tool is most widely used in UK adult care settings to screen for malnutrition?
o: The Braden scale for predicting risk
The 4AT rapid assessment test
The Waterlow risk assessment score
The 'MUST' screening tool
7.w: 'MUST' (BAPEN) combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect to give a low, medium or high risk of malnutrition, with a management plan for each (Annexe B 5.2).

n.0: Braden assesses pressure ulcer risk.
n.1: The 4AT screens for delirium.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

7.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is concerned that a planned reduction in local district nursing posts will affect housebound patients. He wants to use his professional knowledge to influence the decision. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Refuse to accept new referrals until the reduction in posts is withdrawn
Share named patients' stories with a local newspaper to raise awareness
Write to his MP with anonymised evidence about the impact on care
Tell his patients during home visits that they should vote against the council
7.w: Political awareness and influence are part of the nurse's role (P7.13; P5.12). Engaging with elected representatives using anonymised evidence is legitimate, while the Code requires confidentiality (Code 5) and that personal political views are not expressed inappropriately to people in his care (Code 20.7).

n.0: Refusing referrals puts patients at risk and is not a professional way to influence policy.
n.1: Sharing identifiable patient information breaches confidentiality (Code 5).
n.3: Expressing personal political views to patients during care breaches Code 20.7.

7.q: After Ivan Novak, 79, fell and fractured his hip on a medical ward, the trust begins a learning response under PSIRF. His wife asks whether she can contribute her account of the evening and ask questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Advise her to wait for the final report and then decide whether to make a complaint
Explain that incident reviews are internal and that she will receive a summary letter
Welcome her involvement and arrange for her account and questions to inform the review
Ask her to raise her concerns through the Patient Advice and Liaison Service instead
7.w: Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected is one of PSIRF's four aims; families are invited to share their account and questions so the learning response reflects their perspective (NHS England PSIRF, Engaging and involving patients, families and staff). This applies P6.9, working with people and families on improvement.

n.0: Delaying her involvement until the report is final excludes her perspective from the learning.
n.1: PSIRF expects meaningful involvement of those affected, not a summary sent after the event.
n.3: PALS can support families, but it does not replace involving her directly in the learning response.

7.q: Gordon, 66, dies unexpectedly on a surgical ward on the day after a planned procedure. There are no suspicious circumstances, but his death will be referred to the coroner to investigate the cause. He has a peripheral cannula and a urinary catheter. How should the nurse manage these devices during care after death?
o: Leave the cannula in place and spigot the urinary catheter
Remove both and send them with him in a labelled bag
Remove the cannula and catheter before washing him
Remove the cannula but leave the catheter bag attached
7.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause and there are no suspicious circumstances, leave IV cannulae and lines in situ and catheters spigotted; personal care can then be given. Deaths that may be related to a medical procedure or treatment require coroner referral.

n.1: Removing devices could affect the coroner's investigation of a death that may relate to a procedure.
n.2: Devices are left in situ when the death is referred to the coroner to investigate the cause.
n.3: The cannula must stay in situ; the catheter is spigotted, and the bag contents may be discarded per policy.

7.q: A ward manager is introducing the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) to her team. Which of the following is one of PSIRF's four stated aims?
o: Identifying the member of staff responsible for each incident
Reporting every patient safety incident directly to the regulator
A root cause analysis for every incident within a fixed timescale
Compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected
7.w: PSIRF (NHS England 2022, replacing the Serious Incident Framework 2015) has four aims: compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight focused on strengthening the response system (S-PSIRF).
