n.3: Low mood may cause withdrawal, but slowed responses and drowsiness developing over days point to delirium first.

8.q: A new community nursing team has been formed by merging two teams. In the first few weeks there are disagreements about who covers which visits and how handovers should run. What should the team leader, Fiona, do first?
o: Allocate the visits herself and ask the team to follow the new system
Meet the whole team to clarify roles and agree ways of working together
Wait for the team to settle, as early disagreement usually fades with time
Ask the two former team leaders to decide the arrangements between them
8.w: In newly formed groups, uncertainty about roles commonly causes conflict. Leaders help by bringing the team together to clarify roles and agree shared ways of working, which builds cohesion and safe handovers (P5.1 group dynamics; AnnexA.4.2.2 active listening to team concerns).

n.0: Imposing a system without involving the team misses their knowledge and may prolong conflict.
n.2: Leaving role confusion unresolved risks missed visits and unsafe handovers.
n.3: Delegating to the former leaders may entrench the two old teams rather than build one team.

8.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
8.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

8.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
8.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

8.q: Martin, 35, has an acute asthma attack. His PEF is 40% of predicted and his SpO2 is 90% on air. He is talking in short phrases. Which classification applies?
o: Life-threatening asthma
Near-fatal asthma
Moderate asthma attack
Acute severe asthma
8.w: SIGN 158: any one life-threatening feature in a person with severe asthma, including SpO2 below 92%, PEF below 33%, silent chest, cyanosis or exhaustion, makes the attack life-threatening.

n.1: Near-fatal asthma needs a raised PaCO2 or mechanical ventilation.
n.2: Moderate attacks have PEF above 50% and no severe or life-threatening features.
n.3: His PEF fits acute severe, but SpO2 below 92% is a life-threatening feature.

8.q: Maeve, 79, has dementia and lacks capacity. When she had capacity she made a written, signed and witnessed advance decision refusing antipsychotic medication. The team confirms it is valid and applicable. She is now refusing a newly prescribed antipsychotic. Her family ask for it to be given covertly. What applies?
o: Respect the advance decision and do not give the antipsychotic
Give it covertly, as a best interests meeting overrides the advance decision
Give it covertly until a court decides on the advance decision
Give it covertly if her family and the GP both agree
8.w: Under the MCA 2005 ss24-26, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same effect as a capacitous refusal and binds professionals. Best interests decisions cannot override it, so the antipsychotic cannot be given, covertly or otherwise.

n.1: A best interests decision cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
n.2: Treatment may be given to prevent serious deterioration while a court decides on validity, but here validity is confirmed.
n.3: Family and GP agreement does not override a binding advance refusal.

8.q: Jean, 58, has just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She is anxious about what changes she needs to make and asks how she can learn to manage the condition. According to NICE, what should the nurse offer first?
o: A printed leaflet, with education offered if HbA1c rises
Referral to a dietitian for a low-sugar meal plan
A group structured education programme, reinforced each year
Advice to buy foods marketed for people with diabetes
8.w: NICE NG28 (1.2.1, 1.2.4) says offer structured education at diagnosis with annual reinforcement and review, with group programmes as the preferred option and an equivalent alternative for those who cannot attend.

n.0: Education is an integral part of care from diagnosis, not something offered after deterioration.
n.1: Dietary advice is individualised and integrated, but it is not a substitute for structured education.
n.3: NG28 (1.3.8) discourages the use of foods marketed specifically for people with diabetes.

8.q: Joseph, 52, is in a high-dependency unit on day 2 of severe acute pancreatitis. He has not eaten since admission and is not expected to manage oral intake soon. Which nutrition plan is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Parenteral nutrition started as soon as possible after admission
Clear oral fluids for 7 days, then a light diet
Nil by mouth until his pain has settled
Enteral nutrition started within 72 hours of presentation
8.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.6-1.2.7): offer enteral nutrition to anyone with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis, starting within 72 hours of presentation; parenteral nutrition is for when enteral nutrition has failed or is contraindicated.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for when enteral feeding fails or is contraindicated.
n.1: A week of clear fluids would leave a patient with severe illness malnourished.
n.2: Waiting for pain to settle risks malnutrition; NG104 sets a 72-hour start for enteral feeding.

8.q: Mrs Ivy Turner, 86, is admitted with a chest infection and has urinary incontinence at night. A colleague suggests inserting a urinary catheter so her bed stays dry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Insert the catheter and review it after one week
Use continence pads overnight until she is discharged
Insert the catheter overnight and remove it each morning
Carry out a continence assessment and plan alternatives
8.w: Catheters carry risks of infection and loss of continence function and should not be used for staff convenience. A continence assessment identifies causes and less invasive options such as prompted toileting (P7.8 avoid unnecessary interventions; NICE CG139 urinary catheter use only after considering alternatives).

n.0: Catheterising for convenience exposes her to infection risk without a clinical indication.
n.1: Pads without a continence assessment leave the cause unidentified and may reduce continence and dignity.
n.2: Repeated insertion increases infection and trauma risk and is not a continence plan.

8.q: At 08:00 nurse Ollie gives Mrs Brown, 72, her 10:00 dose of paracetamol 1 g in error, two hours early. She is alert and well, and the next dose has not yet been given. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her, apologise, inform the prescriber and report it as an incident
Tell her and apologise, then retime later doses without reporting
Inform the prescriber and record the error in the medicines chart
Report it as an incident and tell her if harm develops later
8.w: Code 14.1-14.3: put the situation right, explain fully and promptly and apologise, then document and escalate. The NMC/GMC duty of candour guidance (Dec 2024) also covers reporting incidents and near misses.

n.1: Adjusting doses is right, but Code 14.3 also requires the event to be documented and escalated.
n.2: This omits explaining and apologising to Mrs Brown, which the professional duty requires.
n.3: Code 14 applies when an incident had the potential for harm; candour does not wait for harm to occur.

8.q: Monica, 55, had abdominal surgery five days ago. Her wound edges are now red and swollen, the area is hot and tender, and there is cloudy discharge. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Which conclusion best fits these findings?
o: The wound is in the normal maturation phase
The wound is showing signs of a moisture lesion
The wound shows a normal inflammatory response
The wound shows signs of infection
8.w: Increasing redness, swelling, heat, pain, purulent or cloudy exudate and fever at day 5 indicate wound infection, which needs escalation and review. Mild early inflammation in the first few days is normal, but it should be settling, not worsening (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Maturation (remodelling) is a late phase lasting months and does not cause fever and pus.
n.1: Moisture lesions are caused by incontinence or sweat on the skin, not surgical wound infection.
n.2: Normal inflammation is mild and settles early; worsening signs with fever suggest infection.

8.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
8.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

8.q: In a GP surgery waiting room, the practice nurse notices Colin, 56, coughing repeatedly into his hands. He has a fever and says he has no tissues. Other patients are seated close by. Which action best applies respiratory and cough hygiene?
o: Give tissues, a bin and a facemask, and seat him at least 1 metre from others
Ask him to cough into his hands and seat him at least 2 metres from others
Give him an FFP3 respirator to wear until he is called in for his appointment
Ask him to wait outside the building in his car until the nurse is ready to see him
8.w: NIPCM ch 1.3 and ch 2: cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue, dispose of it promptly and clean hands; outpatients with respiratory symptoms should be asked to wear a facemask if tolerated and be separated from others by at least 1 metre. Prioritising his appointment also helps.

n.1: Coughing into hands contaminates them; the crook of the arm is the fallback, and the NIPCM distance is 1 metre, not the pandemic-era 2 metres.
n.2: NIPCM states an FFP3 respirator must not be worn by an infectious patient, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
n.3: Sending a febrile patient to wait outside delays assessment and is not a standard respiratory hygiene measure.

8.q: Tessa, 45, is admitted with mild acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. She is not vomiting and says she is hungry. Her care plan was written as nil by mouth by default. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Request parenteral nutrition while she is in hospital
Offer clear fluids for 48 hours before any food
Ask for review, as food is not withheld without a clear reason
Keep her nil by mouth until her amylase level has returned to normal
8.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.5) says ensure people with acute pancreatitis are not made nil by mouth and do not have food withheld unless there is a clear reason, such as vomiting.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is for severe disease where enteral feeding has failed or is contraindicated.
n.1: Routine restriction to clear fluids is still withholding food without a clear reason.
n.3: NG104 advises against routine nil by mouth; normalising amylase is not a condition for eating.

8.q: Zara, a first-year student nurse, asks to insert a urinary catheter for a patient. She has not yet been taught or practised the procedure. Her practice supervisor, Ama, is busy. What is the most appropriate response from Ama?
o: Carry out the procedure with Zara observing and explain each step
Ask a healthcare assistant to supervise Zara during the catheterisation
Ask Zara to read the procedure policy and then insert the catheter
Let Zara insert the catheter while Ama finishes her other tasks nearby
8.w: Delegation must be within the person's competence (Code 11.1). A student who has not been taught a procedure should first observe and then practise under direct supervision. Ama can use the opportunity to teach (P5.8 support and supervise students; AnnexA.4.1.1 clear explanations when teaching).

n.1: Supervision must come from someone competent in the procedure and in supporting the student; this does not meet the student's learning needs.
n.2: Reading a policy does not provide the skill and assessed competence needed.
n.3: Indirect supervision is unsafe for an aseptic invasive procedure the student has not learned.

8.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
8.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

8.q: Mrs Brennan, 66, has heart failure and wants to stay well at home. Which nursing action best supports her self-management?
o: Agree a written plan with her, including when to seek help
Tell her to rest and avoid activity until her next review
Arrange for a carer to manage her medicines at home
Ask her to phone the ward whenever she feels unwell
8.w: Proficiency P4.2: work in partnership to encourage shared decision making and support people to manage their own care. Code 2.1-2.3.

n.1: This is not person-centred and may not reflect her condition or goals.
n.2: Taking over her medicines reduces self-management without a reason to do so.
n.3: This keeps her dependent and does not build her own management skills.

8.q: A urinal has been knocked over, spilling urine across the floor of a bay. The urine contains no visible blood. The nurse wears gloves and an apron. Which approach to managing this spill is correct?
o: Sprinkle chlorine-releasing granules directly on the urine
Pour 10,000 ppm chlorine solution directly on the urine first
Soak up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Leave it for the domestic team to clean at the next routine round
8.w: NIPCM appendix 9: do not use a chlorine-releasing agent directly on a urine spill (it can release chlorine gas). Soak up with disposable paper towels (a gelling agent may be used), then decontaminate with 1,000 ppm available chlorine or a combined detergent and chlorine product, then wash and dry.

n.0: Granules are for blood and high-risk body fluids; on urine they risk releasing chlorine gas.
n.1: Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine, and 10,000 ppm is the blood-spill strength.
n.3: Spills are treated immediately by trained staff, not left as a slip and infection hazard.

9.q: A major incident is declared at Sophie's hospital after a factory fire. Sophie is the nurse in charge of a medical ward. The ward's major incident action card is in the office. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Follow the action card, for example by identifying patients fit for discharge
Phone off-duty colleagues personally and ask them to come in to work
Carry on with routine ward work until casualties start arriving on the ward
Send two of her nurses straight to the emergency department to help
9.w: In a hospital major incident, staff follow their role-specific action cards and the trust's command structure. Ward nurses in charge typically help create capacity, for example by identifying patients who can safely be discharged or moved, and release staff only when the incident control team requests them (P6.12 roles at different levels of seniority).

n.1: Calling in staff is coordinated centrally through the trust's call-in procedure to avoid exhausting the workforce for later phases.
n.2: Waiting passively loses time to create the capacity the hospital will need.
n.3: Self-deploying staff disrupts the coordinated response and leaves the ward short; staff are released when requested by incident control.

9.q: Ivy, 75, has heart failure and takes ramipril and spironolactone. Today's blood results show potassium 5.8 mmol/L; it was 4.9 a month ago. Her spironolactone is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose and advise foods rich in potassium
Inform the prescriber before giving the next spironolactone dose
Give the dose and recheck her electrolytes in 3 months
Give the dose, as 5.8 mmol/L is expected with these two drugs
9.w: Assess then act: potassium has risen above 5.5 mmol/L on an ACE inhibitor and an MRA, both of which raise potassium. NICE NG106 (2025) says follow local guidance if potassium exceeds 5.5 mmol/L, so the prescriber must review before more spironolactone is given.

n.0: Increasing potassium intake would make hyperkalaemia worse.
n.2: A potassium above 5.5 needs action now under NG106 monitoring advice.
n.3: NICE sets 5.5 mmol/L as the level that triggers action.

9.q: George, 71, has known COPD with previous hypercapnic respiratory failure. He arrives breathless with SpO2 84% on air. Blood gas results are awaited. What target saturation range is appropriate?
9.w: BTS guideline: for people with known COPD or other risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, aim for 88-92% pending blood gas results; NEWS2 Scale 2 is then used if this target is prescribed (RCP 2017).

n.0: 85-88% leaves him below the recommended lower limit of 88%.
n.1: 92-95% overshoots the 88-92% target for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.2: 94-98% risks worsening hypercapnia in someone with previous hypercapnic failure.

9.q: Dorothy, 90, is in the last days of life on a care of older people ward. Her chart still includes daily blood tests, which were requested a week ago when she was admitted. She is comfortable and settled. What should the nurse do about the blood tests?
o: Ask the team to review whether the daily blood tests will change her care
Ask Dorothy's daughter to give consent for the tests to be stopped
Take the blood tests as charted because the request is still active
Leave the tests undone and record that Dorothy declined them
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.1.4: avoid investigations that are unlikely to affect care in the last few days of life unless there is a clinical need, for example a blood count to guide platelet transfusion to prevent catastrophic bleeding. The nurse should prompt a team review rather than act alone.

n.1: Relatives cannot consent for an adult; the clinical team should review whether the tests are needed.
n.2: Continuing a test that is unlikely to change care causes discomfort; NG31 rec 1.1.4 says avoid such investigations.
n.3: Recording a refusal that did not happen is falsifying the record (Code 10.3) and does not resolve the plan.

9.q: Frank, 68, returned to the ward after bowel surgery 6 hours ago. On his 4-hourly observations his temperature has fallen to 35.8 C and he says he feels cold. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give paracetamol and recheck his temperature in 1 hour
Add a blanket and recheck at his next 4-hourly observations
Use forced-air warming, checking temperature every 30 minutes
Report it at handover as an expected effect of anaesthesia
9.w: NICE CG65 (1.4.3): if a patient's temperature falls below 36.0 C on the ward, warm them with forced-air warming until comfortably warm (36.5 to 37.5 C), measuring and documenting temperature at least every 30 minutes during warming.

n.0: Paracetamol lowers temperature and does nothing to warm him.
n.1: A blanket is passive, and a 4-hour wait leaves hypothermia untreated.
n.3: Postoperative hypothermia increases complications and needs treating now, not reporting later.

9.q: Maureen, 70, has multiple myeloma and takes no opioids. Over three days she has become very thirsty, is passing large volumes of urine, is constipated and is now newly confused. Her blood glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. What is the nurse's most appropriate interpretation and action?
o: Possible hyperkalaemia; arrange an urgent 12-lead ECG
Possible hyponatraemia; restrict her fluid intake today
Possible hypercalcaemia; escalate for an urgent calcium level
Possible dehydration from poor intake; encourage more oral fluids
9.w: Thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion in a person with myeloma or bone metastases suggest hypercalcaemia of malignancy, an oncological emergency that needs urgent blood calcium measurement and medical review (Cancer Research UK guidance on high calcium in cancer; recognition-level).

n.0: Hyperkalaemia does not explain thirst, polyuria and constipation.
n.1: Fluid restriction would worsen dehydration caused by polyuria.
n.3: Poor intake does not explain large urine volumes; this cluster points to high calcium.

9.q: Eileen, 72, had 20 minutes of slurred speech yesterday afternoon that fully resolved. She attends her GP today. She has not had aspirin. Which statement about her assessment timing is correct?
o: She needs specialist assessment within 7 days as symptoms resolved
She needs a carotid ultrasound before any referral is made
She needs specialist assessment within 24 hours of her symptom onset
She needs specialist assessment within 24 hours of today's visit
9.w: NICE NG128 1.1.5: refer immediately people who have had a suspected TIA for specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset of symptoms (and give aspirin 300 mg unless contraindicated).

n.0: Resolution does not change the 24-hour standard for recent TIA.
n.1: Imaging is arranged by the specialist service and must not delay referral.
n.3: The 24-hour clock runs from symptom onset, not from presentation.

9.q: Frank, 68, has heart failure. He attends the practice in October 2026 and asks whether he is eligible for the RSV vaccine. Which answer is accurate under the UKHSA schedule from September 2026?
o: No; the RSV vaccine is offered in pregnancy and to care home residents
Yes; people aged 65 to 74 with heart failure are now offered it
No; the RSV vaccine is offered to older adults from age 75
No; RSV vaccine is offered to care home residents aged 80 or over
9.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) at 75 years and for all adult residents of care homes for older adults; from September 2026, also for people aged 65 to 74 with chronic respiratory or heart conditions (for example severe asthma, chronic pulmonary disease, heart failure) or immunosuppression; and in pregnancy from 28 weeks.

n.0: These groups are eligible, but the 2026 schedule also includes 65 to 74 year olds with heart failure.
n.2: The age-75 programme continues, but from September 2026 people aged 65 to 74 with chronic heart conditions are also eligible.
n.3: The care home programme covers all adult residents of care homes for older adults, and Frank is eligible anyway.

9.q: Cyril, 82, has not opened his bowels for 6 days despite oral laxatives and is uncomfortable. The doctor has prescribed a phosphate enema, and Cyril has given consent after you explained the procedure. In what position should he be placed for administration?
o: Supine with legs raised
Right lateral with legs straight
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Left lateral with knees flexed
9.w: The left lateral position follows the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum, allowing the enema to flow along the bowel by gravity (Annexe B 6.5).

n.0: Supine makes insertion and retention difficult.
n.1: Right lateral works against the anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon.
n.2: Prone is uncomfortable and does not aid flow into the sigmoid colon.

9.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
9.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

9.q: Mrs Hart, 83, has dementia and lacks capacity. For three nights she has called out repeatedly, disturbing other patients. A colleague suggests asking for regular night-time lorazepam 'so everyone gets some sleep'. She has not been reviewed for pain or constipation. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Move her to a side room and close the door at night
Assess for pain, constipation and delirium before considering medication
Request regular lorazepam, as other patients on the bay also need sleep
Give PRN lorazepam tonight and review tomorrow whether it helped her
9.w: Using sedation to control behaviour for others' convenience is chemical restraint and must be in her best interests and the least restrictive option (MCA s1(5)-(6)). NICE NG97 rec 1.7.1: before any treatment for distress in dementia, assess for and address causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care, so she should be assessed first.

n.0: Isolating her behind a closed door is restrictive and does not address the cause of her distress.
n.2: Medication for the benefit of others is not in her best interests and is a restrictive practice.
n.3: Giving sedation before assessing for treatable causes skips the least restrictive approach.

9.q: Vera, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and is keen to return home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker suggests giving her a full bed bath to save time. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone her wash until she can manage it without help
Set her up to wash what she can and help with the rest
Give her a full bed bath so that she can rest afterwards
Ask her daughter to wash her during the afternoon visit
9.w: Annexe B 4.3: assist with washing and dressing in a way that promotes independence. Encouraging Vera to do what she can, with help for the rest, maintains her abilities and dignity and supports her goal of going home (Code 1.2, 2.1).

n.0: Postponing hygiene leaves her needs unmet and risks skin problems.
n.2: A full bed bath removes the independence she needs to regain.
n.3: Hygiene is a fundamental of care that the nursing team is responsible for providing.

9.q: Winston, 69, has a long-term urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker is about to empty his drainage bag into a single-use jug. There is a small risk of splashing. Which PPE is most appropriate for this task?
o: Sterile gloves and a disposable apron to protect the closed system
A disposable apron, with hand hygiene once the bag is emptied
Non-sterile gloves, a long-sleeved gown and an FFP3 respirator
Non-sterile gloves and apron, plus eye protection if splashing is likely
9.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves are worn when exposure to body fluids is anticipated, aprons protect clothing when contamination is likely, and eye or face protection is worn when splashing to the face is anticipated. Sterility is not needed to empty a drainage bag.

n.0: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures; emptying a bag via the outlet needs non-sterile gloves.
n.1: Contact with urine is anticipated, so gloves are needed as well as the apron.
n.2: Gowns are for extensive splashing and FFP3 respirators for airborne risks; neither applies to emptying a catheter bag.

9.q: Before giving the first dose of oral amoxicillin to Stanley, 67, the nurse notices he is wearing a red allergy wristband labelled 'penicillin'. The allergy section of his drug chart is blank and the prescriber has gone home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose with an antihistamine to cover any possible reaction
Withhold it, clarify the allergy with Stanley and contact a prescriber
Give the dose, as the drug chart has no allergy recorded
Give half the dose and observe Stanley closely for any reaction
9.w: RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 requires the person administering to check allergies or previous adverse drug reactions, and to raise ambiguities with the prescriber or pharmacy without delay. Amoxicillin is a penicillin, so the dose is withheld, the reaction history clarified, the chart updated and an alternative sought.

n.0: An antihistamine would not prevent anaphylaxis and the nurse cannot add a medicine.
n.2: The wristband is a warning that must be resolved; a blank chart is an omission, not evidence of no allergy.
n.3: Altering the prescribed dose is not within the nurse's role, and any dose risks anaphylaxis.

9.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, has capacity and wants to return home after a fall. In a meeting her son says firmly that she must go to a care home and answers every question put to her. What is the most appropriate next step for the nurse?
o: Refer for a best interests meeting to settle the disagreement
Ask the son to put his concerns in writing for the discharge team
Speak with Mrs Lewis privately to explore her own views and wishes
Arrange a care home placement as her son holds strong views
9.w: NMC proficiency P1.9 requires decisions based on people's needs and preferences, recognising and addressing factors that may unduly influence them. Speaking with her alone lets her express her wishes freely (Code 2.3, 2.4, 4.1).

n.0: Best interests decisions apply when a person lacks capacity (MCA s4); Mrs Lewis has capacity, so the decision is hers.
n.1: This may record his concerns but leaves the undue influence unaddressed and does not establish what Mrs Lewis wants.
n.3: The son's views do not replace the decision of a person with capacity; Code 1.3 and P1.9 require decisions based on her needs and preferences.

9.q: Before starting apixaban for Leonard, 70, who has atrial fibrillation, the team assesses his bleeding risk. Which tool does NICE NG196 recommend for this?
o: HAS-BLED
ABCD2
CHA2DS2-VASc
ORBIT
9.w: NICE NG196 1.3: use the ORBIT bleeding risk score to assess bleeding risk in people with AF, alongside CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk.

n.0: NG196 replaced HAS-BLED with ORBIT as the preferred bleeding risk tool.
n.1: ABCD2 was a TIA risk score and is not used for bleeding risk.
n.2: CHA2DS2-VASc assesses stroke risk, not bleeding risk.

9.q: Before giving Mrs Okoro, 54, the results of her scan, the doctor and nurse want to check what she already understands. Which opening question is most appropriate?
o: "Have you prepared yourself for some bad news today?"
"What have you been told so far about the scan?"
"Do you know what a malignant tumour is?"
"Shall I go straight to the results for you?"
9.w: Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations; Code 7.4 check understanding; Code 7.1 use terms people understand.

n.0: This alarms her without finding out what she knows.
n.2: This uses jargon and jumps ahead before her understanding is known.
n.3: Going straight to results skips checking her understanding first.

9.q: Morris, 64, has newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. He has no contraindications. Which combination does NICE NG106 (2025) recommend as first-line treatment?
o: ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor together
ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, loop diuretic and digoxin
Beta-blocker and SGLT2 inhibitor, adding an ACE inhibitor if needed
ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker, adding an MRA months later
9.w: NICE NG106 (updated Sep 2025): for HFrEF offer an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor; it is not necessary to optimise one before starting the next.

n.1: Diuretics relieve congestion and digoxin is not a first-line pillar.
n.2: The ACE inhibitor (or ARNI) is one of the four first-line drugs.
n.3: The 2025 update offers all four together rather than one after another.

9.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
9.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

9.q: Ivan, 72, has COPD and is prescribed salbutamol 2 puffs via a pressurised metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. He tells the nurse he usually sprays both puffs into the spacer and then takes one big breath. What should the nurse advise?
o: Spray one puff and breathe it in, then repeat for the second
Spray both puffs together, then take several slow breaths
Spray one puff, wait a full minute, then breathe it in
Spray both puffs together, then take one breath and hold it
9.w: With a spacer, one actuation is given at a time and inhaled straight away (by a slow deep breath or several tidal breaths), then the process is repeated for the next puff after shaking (AnnexB.11.8). Multiple actuations into the spacer reduce the dose delivered.

n.1: Firing two puffs together causes the drug to stick to the spacer walls, reducing the dose reaching the lungs.
n.2: Delaying inhalation lets the drug settle on the spacer walls.
n.3: This repeats his current error of firing both puffs into the spacer at once.

9.q: Mr Albert King, 81, has heart failure, type 2 diabetes, COPD and osteoarthritis. He takes 14 different medicines and has had two falls this month. The community nurse visits. What is the most appropriate next step to address his complex needs?
o: Remove the medicines he finds hardest to swallow from his list
Advise him to stop his diuretic on days when he feels dizzy
Request a structured medication review with his GP or pharmacist
Refer him to the falls clinic and leave the medicines unchanged
9.w: Polypharmacy with multiple long-term conditions increases the risk of falls and adverse effects. A structured medication review, including psychotropic and cardiovascular drugs, is part of falls assessment (NICE NG249; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; P7.5 comorbidities and complex needs).

n.0: Nurses without prescribing responsibility for him must not stop prescribed medicines on swallowing difficulty alone; the issue needs review.
n.1: Advising him to stop a diuretic without prescriber review risks fluid overload.
n.3: A falls referral is reasonable, but leaving medicines unreviewed ignores a likely contributing factor.

9.q: Ms Okoro, 24, has type 1 diabetes and has been vomiting since last night. Her urinalysis shows glucose 3+ and ketones 3+. She is breathing quickly and her capillary glucose is 22.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage oral fluids and recheck her urine in 4 hours
Check her blood ketones and inform the doctor urgently
Record the results and send the urine for culture
Give her usual insulin dose and recheck in the morning
9.w: High glucose with heavy ketonuria, vomiting and rapid breathing in type 1 diabetes suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency. The nurse should check capillary blood ketones per local protocol and escalate urgently (P3.11, P3.12; Annexe B 2.10).

n.0: Oral fluids and a 4-hour recheck delay treatment of possible ketoacidosis.
n.2: Culture does not address the immediate danger shown by the results.
n.3: Her usual dose does not treat ketoacidosis, and waiting until morning is unsafe.

9.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
9.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

9.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
9.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

9.q: Joyce, 74, is admitted with pneumonia. Her VTE risk outweighs her bleeding risk and enoxaparin is prescribed. Within what time of the decision to admit should the first dose be given?
o: Within 14 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 4 hours
Within 48 hours
9.w: NICE NG89: start pharmacological VTE prophylaxis as soon as possible and within 14 hours of admission (decision to admit) for people whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk.

n.1: 24 hours is later than the NICE timeframe for starting prophylaxis.
n.2: 4 hours is the DVT ultrasound timeframe, not the LMWH start time.
n.3: 48 hours is far later than NICE recommends.

9.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
9.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

9.q: Gladys, 88, died at home this morning and her death has been verified. Her daughter, Pam, wants to help the community nurse with washing her. As they turn Gladys, there is a sighing sound from her mouth. Pam becomes frightened and asks whether her mother is still alive. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Explain gently that air can escape from the body when it is moved
Recheck Gladys's pulse and breathing and then call 999 for help
Call the GP to come and verify the death a second time
Ask Pam to leave the room while the nurse completes the washing
9.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): when moving the deceased, air can be released and this should not be mistaken for breathing; share this sensitively with the key contact or carer assisting. Prepare key contacts sensitively for changes to the body after death.

n.1: Death has been verified; the guidance says released air should not be mistaken for breathing.
n.2: The death was properly verified; a sound from released air is expected and is not a reason to re-verify.
n.3: Pam wishes to take part; the guidance is to prepare and support key contacts, not exclude them.

9.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
9.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

9.q: Kamala, 54, has CKD with an ACR of 95 mg/mmol. Her clinic blood pressure is 136/84 mmHg on current treatment. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: It is within her target of below 150/90 for proteinuric CKD
It is above her target of below 130/80, so treatment review is needed
It is within her target of below 140/90, so no change is needed
It needs confirming by home readings above 145/85 first
9.w: NICE NG203 sets a target systolic below 130 mmHg (range 120 to 129) and diastolic below 80 mmHg when ACR is 70 mg/mmol or more. At 136/84 she is above target.

n.0: Below 150/90 is not a CKD target.
n.2: Below 140/90 applies to people with an ACR below 70 mg/mmol.
n.3: Her clinic reading already exceeds her target; 145/85 is an ABPM figure for people aged 80 and over.

9.q: Irene, 84, has an indwelling urinary catheter and new confusion with a fever of 38.4°C. The doctor requests a catheter specimen of urine (CSU) before antibiotics are started. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
o: Decontaminate hands and aspirate from the sampling port aseptically
Disconnect the bag and collect urine from the end of the catheter
Collect urine from the drainage bag outlet into a sterile pot
Replace the catheter and send a sample from the new catheter
9.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate hands and wear new non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and obtain urine samples from the sampling port using an aseptic technique, keeping the drainage system closed.

n.1: Breaking the closed drainage system raises the risk of introducing infection.
n.2: Urine in the bag has stood and may be colonised, so it does not reflect bladder urine.
n.3: Catheters are changed when clinically necessary; changing it just to obtain a sample is not the CG139 method.

9.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
9.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

9.q: A student nurse sets up a simple face mask at 3 L/min for Faisal, 55, whose prescribed target is 94-98%. Which explanation should you give the student before adjusting the flow?
o: Below 5 L/min a simple mask can cause carbon dioxide rebreathing
Simple masks deliver 100% oxygen at any flow rate
Simple masks are designed to run between 1 and 2 L/min
A simple mask needs 15 L/min to keep its reservoir bag inflated
9.w: BTS 2017: simple face masks are used at 5-10 L/min. At lower flows exhaled carbon dioxide may be rebreathed from the mask, so a nasal cannula is preferable if low flow is needed.

n.1: Simple masks give a variable, lower concentration; they do not deliver 100% oxygen.
n.2: 1-2 L/min is a nasal cannula range for at-risk patients, not a simple mask setting.
n.3: A simple mask has no reservoir bag; 15 L/min applies to the reservoir mask.

9.q: Nadia is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound for Doreen, 81. Splashing of wound fluid towards her face is likely. There are no full-face visors on the ward. Which facial protection should Nadia wear?
o: A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection
A Type II surgical mask and her own prescription glasses
A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask without eye protection
An FFP3 respirator without separate eye protection
9.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: where splashing of blood or body fluids onto the face is anticipated and a full-face visor is not available, wear a Type IIR FRSM with eye protection. Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.

n.1: A Type II mask is not fluid resistant, and corrective spectacles do not count as eye protection.
n.2: The mask protects the nose and mouth, but the eyes remain exposed to the expected splashes.
n.3: An FFP3 respirator protects against airborne particles; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.

9.q: At a training session on restrictive practice, a nurse asks which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 is engaged when a person who lacks capacity is deprived of their liberty in a care home. Which Article should the trainer name?
o: Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
9.w: Article 5 (HRA 1998 Sch 1) protects the right to liberty and security and requires lawful procedures for any deprivation of liberty. DoLS exist to provide those safeguards for people lacking capacity.

n.0: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of other rights; it is not the liberty right itself.
n.1: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not lawful authority for deprivation of liberty.
n.3: Article 8 may be relevant to care arrangements, but deprivation of liberty engages Article 5.

9.q: A community nurse is identifying people on her caseload who meet the NICE NG56 definition of multimorbidity. Which person meets the definition?
o: Carol, 58, who has well-controlled type 1 diabetes
Derek, 71, recovering from a wrist fracture and a chest infection
Elaine, 63, who has hypertension treated with three medicines
Brian, 66, who has hearing loss and chronic back pain
9.w: NG56 1.1.1: multimorbidity is 2 or more long-term health conditions, which can include sensory impairment such as hearing loss and symptom complexes such as chronic pain. Brian has two long-term conditions.

n.0: Carol has one long-term condition.
n.1: A healing fracture and a chest infection are acute problems, not long-term conditions.
n.2: Several medicines for one condition is still a single long-term condition.

9.q: Mrs Brennan, 66, has heart failure and wants to stay well at home. Which nursing action best supports her self-management?
o: Agree a written plan with her, including when to seek help
Tell her to rest and avoid activity until her next review
Arrange for a carer to manage her medicines at home
Ask her to phone the ward whenever she feels unwell
9.w: Proficiency P4.2: work in partnership to encourage shared decision making and support people to manage their own care. Code 2.1-2.3.

n.1: This is not person-centred and may not reflect her condition or goals.
n.2: Taking over her medicines reduces self-management without a reason to do so.
n.3: This keeps her dependent and does not build her own management skills.

9.q: Margaret, 83, has mixed dementia and no history of epilepsy or bipolar disorder. She has become verbally aggressive in the evenings. A locum doctor suggests starting sodium valproate to calm her. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as NICE advises against valproate for agitation in dementia
Give it, as valproate is safer than antipsychotics in older people
Give it, then check her valproate blood level after the first week
Give it, as mood stabilisers are first-line for agitation in dementia
9.w: NG97 1.7.10: do not offer valproate to manage agitation or aggression in people living with dementia, unless it is indicated for another condition. Code 18 and 19 require nurses to question medicines that may cause harm.

n.1: NICE does not recommend valproate as an alternative to antipsychotics for this purpose.
n.2: Monitoring levels does not address that valproate should not be started for this indication.
n.3: First-line management is a structured assessment and psychosocial interventions, not mood stabilisers.

9.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
9.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

9.q: Mrs Anita Rao, 68, is admitted for elective surgery. She is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. Her 12-year-old grandson has come with her and offers to interpret. What should the admitting nurse do?
o: Record and flag her need for a BSL interpreter and arrange one to attend
Rely on lip reading by facing Mrs Rao and speaking slowly and clearly
Accept the grandson's offer, as Mrs Rao is comfortable with him interpreting
Use written notes for the admission, as she can read English well
9.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs arising from disability or sensory loss. A qualified BSL interpreter ensures accurate information and valid consent; children should not be used to interpret clinical information (Code 7.2; P7.9).

n.1: Lip reading is unreliable for complex clinical information and is not her preferred communication method.
n.2: A child interpreter may mistranslate clinical information and is placed in an inappropriate role, risking invalid consent.
n.3: Written English may not be fully accessible to a first-language BSL user, and the standard requires her preferred format.

9.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?
o: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Proliferation, haemostasis, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
9.w: Wounds heal through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (clearing debris and bacteria), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelialisation) and maturation or remodelling (collagen reorganisation, which can last months).

n.0: Haemostasis comes first, and proliferation precedes maturation.
n.1: Proliferation follows inflammation; it does not begin the process.
n.2: Inflammation precedes proliferation, not the other way round.

9.q: Ms Ford, 50, is due to have surgery this afternoon. She is restless, keeps asking the same questions and says she cannot stop thinking she will not wake up. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
o: Give her a leaflet about the operation and leave her to rest
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe a sedative premedication
Tell her that modern anaesthetics are very safe and move on
Sit with her, explore her fears and explain what will happen
9.w: NMC proficiency P4.8 requires nurses to initiate interventions for common symptoms including anxiety. Listening, exploring specific fears and giving clear information are first-line, person-centred interventions for pre-operative anxiety.

n.0: A leaflet without discussion leaves her specific fears unexplored.
n.1: Medication may be considered later, but non-drug measures come first for anxiety with normal observations.
n.2: Brief reassurance without exploring her fears does not address her anxiety.

9.q: On admission, Gemma, 35, lists citalopram as her only regular medicine. When asked about other products, she says she has been taking St John's wort from a health food shop for low mood. What should the nurse do?
o: Record it as a herbal product that needs no further review or action
Remove it from her locker and dispose of it in the sharps bin
Record it and inform the prescriber, as it interacts with citalopram
Advise her to double her citalopram dose instead of using it
9.w: Medicines reconciliation includes over-the-counter and herbal products (NICE NG5; P4.15). St John's wort taken with an SSRI such as citalopram increases the risk of serotonin syndrome and interacts with many other drugs, so it is documented and the prescriber or pharmacist informed.

n.0: Herbal products can cause significant interactions and must be reviewed.
n.1: Patients' own products are not removed without consent, and sharps bins are not for medicines.
n.3: Changing a prescribed dose is not the nurse's decision and could cause toxicity.

9.q: Mary, 84, has moderate dementia and cannot reliably describe pain. Using the Abbey pain scale, the nurse finds signs of pain linked to her arthritic knee and gives her prescribed paracetamol. What should happen next, according to NICE NG97?
o: Repeat the observational pain assessment after the analgesia
Reassess her pain at the next weekly multidisciplinary review
Use her verbal self-report from now on as she seems calmer
Record the pain as resolved once she stops calling out
9.w: NG97 1.8.3-1.8.5: use a structured observational pain tool alongside standard assessment, and repeat pain assessments after any pain management intervention and when behaviour changes may be caused by pain.

n.1: Waiting a week fails to evaluate the intervention promptly.
n.2: In moderate dementia an observational tool is used alongside self-report, which is unreliable for her.
n.3: Quietness is not proof of pain relief; the assessment should be repeated with the tool.

9.q: Harold, 70, is being discharged after major abdominal surgery for colon cancer. He is surprised to be sent home with LMWH injections for nearly 4 weeks. Which explanation reflects NICE guidance?
o: The injections treat a clot found during his operation
LMWH is continued for 3 months after major abdominal surgery
LMWH is given at home because he cannot wear stockings
28-day prophylaxis is considered after abdominal cancer surgery
9.w: NICE NG89 (1.14.3-1.14.4): pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 7 days after abdominal surgery when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, and consider extending it to 28 days after major cancer surgery in the abdomen.

n.0: This is prophylaxis; there is no information that a clot was found.
n.1: 3 months is the minimum treatment duration for confirmed DVT or PE, not prophylaxis after surgery.
n.2: Extended prophylaxis relates to his cancer surgery, not to stocking intolerance.

9.q: Rhys, 34, with type 1 diabetes, is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion for DKA. At 21:00 his usual subcutaneous insulin glargine is due. A colleague suggests leaving it as he is already receiving IV insulin. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give his usual glargine dose at the normal time
Withhold the glargine until the infusion is stopped
Withhold the glargine and increase the infusion rate
Give half the glargine dose and record the reason
9.w: JBDS 02 (2023) and its nursing guide state that the person's usual long-acting basal insulin should continue alongside the FRIII. This prevents rebound ketosis when the infusion stops and smooths the transition back to subcutaneous insulin.

n.1: Stopping basal insulin causes rebound hyperglycaemia and ketosis when the IV infusion is discontinued.
n.2: The infusion rate is fixed by weight; withholding basal insulin to compensate is not the protocol.
n.3: JBDS advises continuing the usual basal dose; an unprescribed reduction is not appropriate.

9.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
9.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

9.q: Ray, 58, smokes, drinks about 30 units a week and takes little exercise. He tells the nurse he wants to be healthier but feels overwhelmed by everything he 'should' change. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise him to stop smoking and drinking on the same day
Tell him to start with alcohol, as it carries the greatest risk
Give leaflets on all three topics and review him in six months
Ask which change he feels most motivated to tackle first
9.w: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) rec 8: tailor interventions by assessing the person's behaviour, capability, context and how motivated they are to change; if many behaviours need to change, assess which one or ones the person is most motivated to tackle. NMC Annexe A 2.7: assess motivation and capacity for behaviour change.

n.0: Tackling several behaviours at once when he feels overwhelmed may reduce his chance of success; PH49 asks which he is most motivated to change.
n.1: Choosing for him ignores his motivation; PH49 recommends assessing which behaviour he is most motivated to tackle.
n.2: Leaflets without a plan miss the chance to agree goals; PH49 recommends goals, action plans and planned review.

9.q: Joan, 87, is wearing anti-embolism stockings after surgery. She has significantly reduced mobility and spends most of the day in bed. Under NICE NG89, how often should her skin be inspected?
o: When she reports pain or discomfort in her legs
Once a day when the stockings are removed for washing
Once a week when the stockings are changed for new ones
2 or 3 times a day, especially heels and bony prominences
9.w: NICE NG89: remove stockings daily for hygiene and skin inspection; in people with significantly reduced mobility, poor skin integrity or sensory loss, inspect the skin 2 or 3 times a day, particularly over heels and bony prominences. Stop stockings if there is marking, blistering or discolouration.

n.0: Waiting for symptoms misses early damage; NG89 sets routine checks 2 or 3 times a day for people with significantly reduced mobility.
n.1: Daily removal and inspection is the minimum for everyone; she needs more frequent checks because of her significantly reduced mobility.
n.2: Weekly inspection would miss pressure damage.

9.q: Tara, 22, tells the nurse, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which technique is this?
o: A cognitive behavioural therapy method
A motivational interviewing technique
A distraction and diversion technique
A reminiscence therapy based technique
9.w: Annexe A 3.6: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques. Examining evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is cognitive restructuring.

n.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not evidence for thoughts.
n.2: Distraction moves attention away; this examines the thought directly.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories for wellbeing, not testing thoughts.

9.q: Hamid, 74, takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. His INR today is 8.5 (target 2.5 to 3.5). He has no bleeding, bruising or other symptoms, and his 18:00 dose is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the usual dose, as he has no signs of bleeding
Give oral vitamin K from ward stock to lower the INR
Withhold the warfarin and inform the prescriber urgently
Give half the usual dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
9.w: An INR well above target raises the risk of serious bleeding. Anticoagulants are high-risk medicines (P4.15): the dose is withheld and the prescriber informed promptly, who decides on dose changes or reversal such as vitamin K.

n.0: No bleeding now does not remove the high bleeding risk at INR 8.5.
n.1: Vitamin K must be prescribed; giving it from stock without a prescription is unlawful.
n.3: Altering the warfarin dose is a prescriber decision.

9.q: Ruth, a practice supervisor, observed her student speak abruptly to a patient who was slow to answer during an admission assessment. The rest of the student's admission work was thorough. How should Ruth give feedback?
o: Wait until the final interview so the feedback is part of the formal assessment
Discuss it privately and soon, naming the strengths and the behaviour, then agree next steps
Write it in the student's document without discussion so that there is a clear record
Mention it to the student briefly at the bedside so that the patient hears the correction
9.w: Constructive feedback is timely, private, specific about the behaviour and its effect, balanced with genuine strengths, and ends with agreed actions (AnnexA.4.1.3 unambiguous, constructive feedback on strengths, weaknesses and potential; P5.9).

n.0: Delaying feedback to the end of placement denies the student time to improve.
n.2: Records should reflect feedback that has been discussed; writing it without discussion is not constructive.
n.3: Correcting a student in front of a patient is humiliating and undermines the therapeutic relationship.

9.q: Cyril, 79, is admitted for elective knee replacement surgery tomorrow. He is orientated and well, but is over 65 and has mild cognitive impairment. When should a tailored delirium prevention package begin, according to NICE CG103?
o: After a 4AT score of 4 or more has been recorded on the surgical ward
Within 24 hours of admission, after assessing contributing factors
When the first signs of confusion appear on the ward
After surgery, once he has returned to the orthopaedic ward
9.w: CG103 1.4.2: within 24 hours of admission, assess people at risk for clinical factors contributing to delirium and provide a tailored multicomponent intervention package. Age 65+ and cognitive impairment are risk factors (1.2).

n.0: A 4AT of 4 or more indicates possible delirium; prevention should start before this.
n.2: Prevention begins before delirium appears; waiting for confusion means it has already developed.
n.3: Delaying until after surgery loses the pre-operative window for prevention.

9.q: Bethany, 33, has had asthma for years. She uses a salbutamol inhaler about three times a week and takes no other asthma medicine. At her annual review, what is the recommended change?
o: Continue salbutamol as her asthma sounds well controlled
Add a regular long-acting beta2 agonist on its own
Add a daily leukotriene receptor antagonist to salbutamol
Switch her to as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol
9.w: NG245 (2024): people with asthma treated with a SABA alone should be moved to as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol.

n.0: SABA-only treatment leaves inflammation untreated; NG245 recommends moving these people on.
n.1: A LABA without an inhaled corticosteroid is unsafe in asthma.
n.2: This is not the NG245 recommendation for SABA-only users.

9.q: Leonard, 77, has heart failure and advanced bowel cancer with bowel obstruction. He is in the last days of life with persistent nausea and vomiting. Subcutaneous hyoscine butylbromide was started 24 hours ago, but his symptoms have not improved. Which action should the nurse discuss with the prescriber?
o: Continuing the same hyoscine dose for 72 hours more
Changing hyoscine to the intramuscular route
Adding cyclizine as the next option
Considering octreotide as the next option
9.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.22: for nausea or vomiting with obstructive bowel disorders in the last days of life, consider hyoscine butylbromide first line, then octreotide if symptoms do not improve within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.3: take into account risks such as cyclizine exacerbating heart failure.

n.0: NG31 rec 1.5.22 says consider octreotide if symptoms have not improved within 24 hours.
n.1: NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life.
n.2: NG31 rec 1.5.3 notes that cyclizine may exacerbate heart failure, which Leonard has; octreotide is the NG31 next step.

9.q: Graham, 61, has central chest pain and a suspected acute coronary syndrome. He has no lung disease. A healthcare assistant has started oxygen at 15 L/min via a reservoir mask. His SpO2 on air before this was 97%. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue high-flow oxygen to limit the size of any infarct
Remove the oxygen and continue to monitor his saturation
Switch to a 28% Venturi mask aiming for 88-92%
Change to nasal cannulae at 2 L/min as a precaution
9.w: NICE CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen in suspected ACS; monitor SpO2 and give oxygen only if it falls below 94% (target 94-98%). BTS 2017 notes unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may increase infarct size.

n.0: Unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may increase infarct size; it is not a protective treatment.
n.2: The 88-92% range is for people at risk of hypercapnia; he is not, and he is not hypoxaemic.
n.3: Low-flow oxygen is still not indicated when SpO2 is 94% or above in suspected ACS.

9.q: A nurse is admitting four people to an acute medical unit. Using the risk factors in NICE CG103, which person is at increased risk of developing delirium and should be observed for it?
o: Mr Green, 45, admitted for a planned endoscopy
Mrs Young, 78, admitted with a urinary infection
Ms Black, 30, admitted with a simple ankle fracture
Mr White, 52, admitted for blood pressure review
9.w: NICE CG103 (updated 2023) lists risk factors including age 65 or over, past or present cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness. Mrs Young is 78, so she should be observed at least daily for indicators of delirium.

n.0: At 45 and admitted for a planned procedure, Mr Green has none of the CG103 risk factors described.
n.2: An ankle fracture is not a CG103 risk factor; current hip fracture is.
n.3: At 52 with no listed risk factor, Mr White is not identified as at risk by CG103.

9.q: After several months of tension and two formal grievances, a mental health ward manager wants to help the team learn from difficult experiences and improve how they work together. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Hold a single team-building social event outside of working hours
Set up regular facilitated team reflection sessions to discuss practice
Ask each team member to send any concerns to her by email in confidence
Rotate staff with other wards for six months to reduce the tension
9.w: Regular, facilitated group reflection allows staff to share experiences, understand each other's perspectives and agree improvements, which supports team relationships and learning (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; AnnexA.4.1.4 encouraging reflection).

n.0: A one-off social event may help morale but is not a structured way to reflect on practice.
n.2: Individual emails may surface concerns but do not support shared team learning.
n.3: Rotating staff disrupts continuity of care and avoids rather than addresses team issues.

9.q: Dorothy, 86, has Alzheimer's disease and lives in a care home. For three afternoons she has been shouting, pacing and pushing staff away during personal care. She cannot explain what is wrong. According to NICE NG97, what should the nurse do first?
o: Move her to a quieter unit within the home for the afternoons
Increase checks to every 15 minutes and record each episode
Assess for causes such as pain, delirium or unsuitable care
Ask the GP for as-required risperidone to use in the afternoons
9.w: NG97 1.7.1: before any non-drug or drug treatment for distress, carry out a structured assessment to explore reasons for distress and check for clinical or environmental causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care. Psychosocial and environmental interventions come next (1.7.2).

n.0: Moving her may add disorientation and does not identify the cause of her distress.
n.1: Recording episodes without looking for the cause leaves pain or delirium untreated.
n.3: Antipsychotics are for risk of harm or severe distress after causes are explored (NG97 1.7.3).

9.q: Kai, 34, is on an intensive care unit, and the team have decided to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. The bedside nurse thinks organ donation may be possible and Kai's parents are at the bedside. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Raise donation with Kai's parents yourself at the bedside straight away
Contact the specialist nurse for organ donation to lead the approach
Wait to see whether Kai's parents ask about organ donation
Ask Kai's GP to discuss donation with his parents by phone
9.w: NHS Blood and Transplant / British Transplantation Society best practice: the specialist nurse for organ donation is the main professional who makes the family approach, in collaboration with the hospital team, after checking the NHS Organ Donor Register for a recorded decision or nominated representative. Families are always approached if donation is possible.

n.0: The family approach is planned jointly and led by the specialist nurse, who checks the Organ Donor Register first.
n.2: Families are approached whenever donation is possible; waiting may lose the chance to honour Kai's decision.
n.3: The GP is not part of the donation pathway; the specialist nurse for organ donation leads it.

9.q: Doreen, 70, started an anticholinergic medicine for overactive bladder a week ago. She tells the nurse her mouth is dry and her symptoms are no better yet, so she wants to stop it. Which response is consistent with NICE NG123?
o: Stop it now, as a dry mouth shows the medicine is unsuitable for her
Ask her GP to double the dose so that it works more quickly
Benefits can take 4 weeks, and dry mouth may show it is working
Ask her GP to switch her to immediate-release oxybutynin
9.w: NG123 1.4.25: explain that dry mouth and constipation may indicate the medicine is starting to work and that substantial benefit may take at least 4 weeks; review at 4 weeks (1.4.38), or sooner if adverse effects are intolerable (1.4.39).

n.0: Dry mouth is an expected effect; stopping at one week abandons treatment before benefit can appear.
n.1: Increasing the dose early increases side effects before the 4-week review.
n.3: Switching after a week is premature, and NG123 cautions against IR oxybutynin in older women at risk.

9.q: A newly qualified nurse asks which abbreviation practice best supports safe record keeping when documenting medicines and care in the notes. Which approach should she follow?
o: Write terms in full unless the trust approves the abbreviation
Use abbreviations for drug names to save time in busy shifts
Use the abbreviations she learned during her training abroad
Use any abbreviation that colleagues on the ward understand
9.w: Code 10.4: records must be clearly written and not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. Annexe A 1.8 accurate, clear, legible records.

n.1: Abbreviating drug names risks medication errors and breaches Code 10.4.
n.2: Abbreviations vary between countries and may not be understood here.
n.3: Local shorthand may be misread by others; Code 10.4 says no unnecessary abbreviations.

9.q: Peter, 81, is found in cardiac arrest in a hospital bed with a pressure-relieving mattress. CPR is needed. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start CPR on the bed, compressing deeper if needed
Wait for the arrest team to bring a backboard
Move him to the floor before starting compressions
Start rescue breaths until the mattress is deflated
9.w: RCUK 2025: do not move a person from a bed to the floor to do CPR; start compressions on the bed and compress deeper if needed to compensate for the mattress, deploying CPR mode on the mattress where available.

n.1: Waiting delays the start of compressions.
n.2: Moving him to the floor delays compressions and risks injury to staff.
n.3: Compressions take priority; breaths before compressions delay circulation.

9.q: Isaac, 47, has been in hospital for a week. His wife says his breathing has worsened and she raised this with the ward team twice today without response. She asks how she can get a different team to review him. Under Martha's Rule, what should you tell her?
o: She should ask his consultant to arrange a formal second opinion
She can request a transfer to another hospital through the GP
She can request an urgent review by a different clinical team herself
She needs to submit a written complaint to the Patient Advice and Liaison Service
9.w: Martha's Rule (NHS England) lets patients, families and carers request an urgent review from a different team, usually critical care outreach, if they are worried about deterioration and feel they are not being heard. It is a rapid review, not a second opinion.

n.0: Martha's Rule escalation is distinct from a formal second opinion by another consultant.
n.1: Transfer through the GP is not the route for an urgent inpatient review.
n.3: PALS and complaints are not designed for urgent clinical deterioration and would delay review.

9.q: Lillian, 89, has dementia and gets out of bed at night. Her son asks for bed rails to be put up to stop her falling. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Assess the risks first, as rails can harm her if she climbs
Put the rails up and add a lap belt in her chair by day
Refuse the request because bed rails are not allowed
Put the rails up straight away, as her son has asked
9.w: Annexe B 7.4: use safety devices appropriately. Bed rails must be individually risk-assessed; for a person with dementia who mobilises, they may cause entrapment or a higher fall from climbing over. Alternatives include a low bed, crash mat or sensor alarm, discussed with her and her family.

n.1: A lap belt is a restriction needing capacity and best-interests consideration, not a routine add-on.
n.2: Bed rails can be used after individual assessment.
n.3: A relative's request does not replace an individual risk assessment.

9.q: Over two months, Zara has noticed her usually cheerful colleague has become withdrawn, irritable with patients and has had several short-term absences. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Speak to her privately, voice concern and signpost support
Avoid raising it in case it causes her more stress
Suggest she takes annual leave to recover from stress
Report her absence pattern to the ward manager at once
9.w: Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to health. Code 8.7 support colleagues; escalate if patient safety becomes affected.

n.1: Avoiding the issue fails to support a colleague showing signs of vulnerability (P1.5).
