n.2: Advising leave without understanding the problem may not meet her needs.
n.3: Raising it with the manager may follow, but a supportive conversation is the appropriate first step when there is no immediate safety risk.

9.q: A journalist telephones a medical ward asking how a well-known footballer admitted that morning is doing. The admission has already been reported on local news. The nurse who answers is the most senior person on the ward. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm that he is a patient but share no clinical details
Decline to comment and refer the caller to the communications team
Give a brief general update, as the admission is already public
Ask the patient's consultant to call the journalist back later
9.w: Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, always protecting the confidentiality and dignity of people receiving care. Code 5.1 respects privacy; trust communications teams handle media enquiries with the patient's consent.

n.0: Confirming that someone is a patient is itself a disclosure of confidential information (Code 5).
n.2: Media reports do not remove the duty of confidentiality (Code 5.1); no information should be shared without consent and agreed process.
n.3: Passing the request to a clinician bypasses the trust's media process; media contact goes through the communications team.

9.q: A ward manager has designed a new bedside safety checklist and wants every ward in the hospital to start using it next Monday. Arjun, the ward's quality improvement lead, is asked for advice. Which approach best reflects improvement methodology?
o: Pilot it on one ward for a year before deciding whether to use it more widely
Introduce it on all wards on Monday and audit compliance in six months
Test it with a few patients on one ward, measure, adapt and then scale up
Ask each ward manager to decide whether to adopt the checklist locally
9.w: The Model for Improvement uses rapid, small-scale PDSA cycles: test a change with a few patients or one shift, measure the effect, adapt, and build up to wider implementation once it works. This limits risk and builds learning and ownership (NHS England improvement guidance; P6.4, P6.6).

n.0: A single year-long pilot is slow; PDSA relies on short, repeated cycles that allow rapid adaptation.
n.1: Hospital-wide launch without testing risks spreading an untested change, and a six-month delay in measurement slows learning.
n.3: Leaving adoption to individual choice produces inconsistent practice without any evidence that the checklist works.

9.q: Carol, 41, tells the nurse at a health check that she drinks most weekends: about 7 units on Friday night and 7 units on Saturday night, and nothing during the week. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Her drinking is above the weekly guideline, which is 10 units for women
Her drinking is low risk because her weekly total is within 14 units
Spread drinking over 3 or more days, as heavy sessions raise her risk
She should drink a small amount daily, as this protects her heart
9.w: UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016): it is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, for men and women; if drinking as much as 14 units a week, spread it evenly over 3 or more days, as one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase the risk of death from long-term illness and from accidents and injuries.

n.0: The CMO guideline is 14 units a week for both men and women.
n.1: The CMOs advise that one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase risks of long-term illness, accidents and injuries.
n.3: The CMOs do not advise drinking for health; risk rises with regular drinking.

9.q: Kezia, a second-year adult nursing student, is ending her placement on a surgical ward. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment (SSSA), who conducts the assessment that confirms her achievement of proficiencies for this placement?
o: Her practice assessor, informed by feedback from her supervisors
Her practice supervisor, who has worked most shifts with her
Her academic assessor, who visits the ward at the end of placement
The ward manager, who signs off all students on the ward
9.w: Under the SSSA (NMC 2018), practice supervisors support and supervise and contribute feedback; the practice assessor conducts the assessment and confirms achievement of practice proficiencies, drawing on that feedback; the academic assessor works with the practice assessor on progression decisions (P5.8).

n.1: Practice supervisors contribute to assessment through feedback but do not confirm achievement of proficiencies.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement for progression with the practice assessor, but does not assess practice on the ward.
n.3: SSSA roles are defined by function, not by management position; the ward manager has no automatic assessment role.

9.q: A ward is running an improvement project to discharge more patients before midday. The team is already measuring the percentage of discharges before 12:00. Which additional measure would act as a balancing measure?
o: Number of patients discharged before 12:00 each day
Average time that discharge letters are completed
Number of take-home prescriptions ready the evening before
Readmission rate within 30 days of discharge
9.w: Balancing measures check whether improving one part of a system causes problems elsewhere. Rushing discharges could increase readmissions, so 30-day readmission is a balancing measure. The other options are outcome or process measures for the same aim (Model for Improvement measures: outcome, process, balancing; P6.4, P6.7). Two steps: classify each measure, then identify the one that detects unintended harm.

n.0: This is the outcome measure itself, restated as a count.
n.1: Discharge letter timing is a process measure that supports the aim, not a check for unintended harm.
n.2: Prescriptions ready in advance is a process measure on the route to earlier discharge.

9.q: Daniel, 52, is on a surgical ward breathing room air. His observations are: RR 18, SpO2 97%, BP 124/78, pulse 86, alert, temperature 37.4°C. His NEWS2 is 0. What is the minimum frequency of his observations under NEWS2?
o: Hourly
12-hourly
Every 30 minutes
4-6 hourly
9.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017) chart 4: an aggregate score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for a single parameter scoring 3 or a total of 5 or more.
n.2: Every 30 minutes is not a NEWS2 chart 4 frequency; it is the NG253 recalculation interval for high sepsis risk.
n.3: 4-6 hourly is the minimum for a total score of 1-4.

9.q: Mr Price, 79, was alert this morning. At 14:00 his eyes are closed and he opens them and answers when the nurse speaks to him, but then drifts off again. His other observations are unchanged from earlier. How should his level of consciousness be recorded and scored on NEWS2?
o: V on ACVPU, scoring 1
V on ACVPU, scoring 3
A on ACVPU, scoring 0
P on ACVPU, scoring 3
9.w: ACVPU: Alert, new Confusion, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive. He responds to voice, so V. NEWS2 Chart 1 scores any of C, V, P or U as 3, which also triggers at least hourly monitoring and informing the medical team.

n.0: V is correct, but any score other than Alert scores 3 on NEWS2, not 1.
n.2: He is not alert, as his eyes are closed until he is spoken to.
n.3: He responds to voice, so a pain stimulus was not needed; P overstates the level.

9.q: At 03:00 Mr Fry, 58, recently diagnosed with motor neurone disease, is awake and tearful and says, "What's the point of carrying on?" What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure him that things will look brighter in the morning light
Offer him a sleeping tablet so that he can rest
Tell him the doctor will talk it through with him on the ward round
Sit with him, explore his meaning and ask about self-harm thoughts
9.w: Proficiency P1.12: support people who are emotionally vulnerable; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; Code 17.1 protect people at risk. NICE NG225: assess and support with a safety plan, not risk tools.

n.0: False reassurance dismisses possible suicidal thoughts that need exploring.
n.1: Sedation does not address his distress or assess his safety.
n.2: Delaying leaves a possibly at-risk person unsupported now.

9.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
9.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

9.q: Ms Hunt, 55, has had the same leg ulcer care plan for three weeks. Measurements show the wound has not reduced in size, and she says the dressing leaks and stops her going out. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassess the wound with her and revise the plan, referring if needed
Ask her to stay at home more until the leaking settles down
Continue the plan, as wounds can take several months to heal
Change to a more absorbent dressing without discussing it with her
9.w: P3.15: work in partnership to monitor, evaluate and reassess care plans, readjusting goals and documenting progress. Lack of progress and a poor experience for the person mean the plan should be reviewed with her, with referral (for example to tissue viability) if needed (P3.16).

n.1: Restricting her life to suit the dressing is not person-centred and does not address the problem.
n.2: Continuing an unchanged plan ignores evidence that it is not working.
n.3: Changing the plan without her involvement is not partnership working.

9.q: Grace, 70, has had an open bowel resection and is nil by mouth with an ileus. She cannot take oral medicines and her pain is severe. According to NICE, what should she be offered for pain relief?
o: Regular intramuscular morphine every 4 hours
Oral immediate-release morphine as needed
A choice of PCA or a continuous epidural
Intravenous ibuprofen as the main analgesic
9.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.11): for people who cannot take oral opioids, offer a choice of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) or a continuous epidural, taking into account the benefits of an epidural after major open-torso surgery or with expected severe pain.

n.0: Intramuscular injections are painful, give erratic absorption and are not the NG180 option.
n.1: She cannot take oral medicines.
n.3: IV NSAIDs are adjuncts in multimodal analgesia and are not enough alone for severe pain.

9.q: Victor, 67, had 30 minutes of left arm weakness this morning that has fully resolved. He has no contraindication to aspirin and no bleeding disorder. Which actions are recommended?
o: Aspirin 75 mg now and a specialist clinic within 7 days
No aspirin until a CT scan has been done
Calculate an ABCD2 score to decide on referral timing
Aspirin 300 mg now and specialist assessment within 24 hours
9.w: NICE NG128 1.1.4-1.1.5: offer aspirin 300 mg immediately to people with suspected TIA (unless contraindicated) and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours of symptom onset.

n.0: NICE recommends 300 mg and assessment within 24 hours of onset.
n.1: For suspected TIA with resolved symptoms, NICE advises aspirin 300 mg straight away.
n.2: NICE no longer uses ABCD2; all suspected TIAs are seen within 24 hours.

9.q: Brenda, 58, had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy yesterday and is going home today with dressings over her port sites. She asks when she can safely have a shower. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: After 24 hours, once the dressings are dry
After 48 hours from the end of surgery
After 7 days, once sutures are removed
After 10 days, once the wounds are fully healed
9.w: NICE NG125 (1.4.3) advises telling patients that they may shower safely 48 hours after surgery.

n.0: 24 hours is earlier than the NG125 advice.
n.2: There is no need to wait for suture removal; showering is safe from 48 hours.
n.3: Waiting 10 days is unnecessary and affects hygiene and comfort.

9.q: In theatre, Callum, a newly registered scrub nurse, sees the surgeon pick up the scalpel before the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist time out has been done. The team seems not to have noticed. What should Callum do?
o: Complete an incident report after the operation so the omission is recorded
Note the omission and raise it at the team debrief at the end of the list
Quietly tell the anaesthetist so that the surgeon is not challenged openly
Say clearly that the time out has not been done and ask the team to pause
9.w: Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and Code 19 (preserve safety) require nurses to intervene. Checklists work only if anyone can stop the process; speaking up clearly and directly at the moment of risk is the safest action, whatever the speaker's seniority (P6.6; P5.2).

n.0: Reporting is appropriate later, but the immediate risk must be addressed before the incision.
n.1: Raising it afterwards allows the operation to proceed without the safety check that prevents wrong site and wrong patient surgery.
n.2: An indirect approach delays action and may not stop the procedure in time.

9.q: Asif, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He needs routine IV maintenance fluids. Using NICE CG174, what is the appropriate total daily water range?
9.w: NICE CG174: 25-30 mL/kg/day. 70 kg x 25 = 1,750 mL; 70 kg x 30 = 2,100 mL. CG174 also notes that intake rarely needs to exceed 3 L/day.

n.0: 700-1,050 mL uses 10-15 mL/kg/day, below CG174 maintenance.
n.2: 3,500-4,200 mL is well above maintenance and risks overload.
n.3: 2,800-3,500 mL uses 40-50 mL/kg/day, above maintenance.

9.q: Kofi raised a patient safety concern with his manager and then with the trust's director of nursing. Three months later nothing has changed and patients remain at risk. Under NMC guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record his concerns in his reflective accounts for revalidation
Raise the concern again with his manager in writing
Contact a national newspaper to make the risk public
Raise the concern with a regulator such as the CQC
9.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance stage 4: if internal routes have not worked, raise the concern with a regulator or helpline, for example the CQC in England. Code 16.1.

n.0: Reflection does not escalate the risk to anyone able to act.
n.1: He has already used the internal stages without result; repeating stage 1 delays action.
n.2: Media disclosure is not a stage in NMC guidance and may lose legal protection.

9.q: Mavis, 70, has AKI. Despite medical treatment her potassium remains 6.9 mmol/L, she is breathless with bilateral crackles and her urine output is minimal. Which escalation is most appropriate?
o: Ask for referral to the renal outpatient clinic after discharge
Ask for a low-dose dopamine infusion to improve renal blood flow
Ask for immediate referral for renal replacement therapy assessment
Ask for a loop diuretic and recheck urea and electrolytes tomorrow
9.w: NICE NG148 (1.5.8, 1.5.11): refer immediately for renal replacement therapy, to a nephrologist or critical care specialist, if hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema are not responding to medical management.

n.0: Outpatient referral ignores life-threatening complications needing urgent renal replacement therapy.
n.1: NG148 (1.5.5) says do not offer low-dose dopamine to treat AKI.
n.3: Refractory hyperkalaemia with pulmonary oedema needs immediate escalation, not a next-day recheck.

9.q: Reviewing the night's charts, Nurse Hana sees that a healthcare assistant recorded hourly observations for a patient who was off the ward in theatre for three of those hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Mention it informally to the healthcare assistant next week
Amend the entries herself so the chart is accurate
Leave it, as the patient has now returned safely
Escalate it to the nurse in charge straight away
9.w: Code 10.3: complete records without falsification, taking immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to these requirements. Code 16.1 escalate concerns.

n.0: Falsified observations are a safety concern; Code 10.3 requires immediate action.
n.1: Altering another person's entries is itself inappropriate; the concern must be escalated.
n.2: The patient's safety now does not remove the falsification; it must be acted upon.

9.q: Martina, a staff nurse, has just finished three consecutive 12-hour night shifts and feels exhausted. The ward manager phones asking her to work an extra day shift starting in four hours because of sickness. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the shift and ask a colleague to second-check her medicines
Accept a shorter shift and leave as soon as cover can be found
Accept the shift and plan to rest during her break in the afternoon
Decline the shift, explaining that fatigue would make her practice unsafe
9.w: Fatigue is a key human factor that impairs judgement and increases error. Code 20.9 requires registrants to maintain the level of health needed to carry out their role, and Code 19.1 requires them to take measures to reduce mistakes. Martina should explain the safety risk so the manager can seek other cover (P5.2).

n.0: A second check does not make an exhausted nurse safe across all her tasks on a full shift.
n.1: Working even part of the shift while exhausted creates the same risk, and the time cover arrives is uncertain.
n.2: A short break does not offset the fatigue from three night shifts; she would still start the shift unsafe.

9.q: Colin, 64, had a myocardial infarction two years ago and is now diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c 66 mmol/mol. He tolerates metformin. Which initial medicines plan does the 2026 NICE guideline recommend?
o: Metformin, a DPP-4 inhibitor and weekly semaglutide
Modified-release metformin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor and weekly semaglutide
Metformin and an SGLT-2 inhibitor, adding semaglutide if HbA1c stays above 58
Modified-release metformin with pioglitazone for cardiac protection
9.w: NICE NG28 (1.15.1, 2026) recommends that adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease are offered modified-release metformin, an SGLT-2 inhibitor and subcutaneous semaglutide up to 1 mg weekly for cardiovascular, renal and glycaemic benefit from the start.

n.0: NG28 1.24.6 advises against combining a GLP-1 receptor agonist with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
n.2: Semaglutide is offered at the outset for its cardiovascular benefit, not held back until HbA1c fails to fall.
n.3: Pioglitazone is not part of the recommended initial regimen in cardiovascular disease.

9.q: Leonard, 80, has dementia with Lewy bodies and has developed delirium with a chest infection. He is frightened and hitting out. Verbal and non-verbal de-escalation has not worked. The junior doctor plans to prescribe haloperidol. What should the nurse do first?
o: Apply bed rails and mittens to stop him hitting out at staff
Suggest regular lorazepam instead, as it is safer in delirium in older people
Alert the prescriber to his Lewy body dementia before any dose
Give the first dose and observe him for drowsiness afterwards
9.w: NICE CG103 1.7.4: if de-escalation fails, consider short-term haloperidol at the lowest dose, taking account of MHRA advice on cardiac and neurological risks, especially in Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies. NG97 1.7.4 warns of severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions in Lewy body dementia, so the prescriber must weigh this first.

n.0: Mechanical restraint is not a CG103 intervention and increases distress and injury risk.
n.1: CG103 does not recommend benzodiazepines as first-line for delirium distress, and they can worsen confusion.
n.3: Giving it without raising the Lewy body risk exposes him to a possible severe sensitivity reaction.

9.q: Mr Burke, 64, has capacity and is waiting for biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer, as 'it would destroy him'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer the decision to the consultant to settle with his wife
Tell her that her request is unlawful and end the conversation there
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Agree, and record her request on the front of the notes
9.w: Code 2.4 respect the level of involvement a person wants; Code 5.5 share with the person the information they want or need to know. Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations.

n.0: The decision about what he is told rests with him, not with his wife and the consultant.
n.1: This dismisses her distress; her worries need exploring with compassion.
n.3: He has capacity; withholding his diagnosis at another's request breaches his right to information.

9.q: Tom, 30, has type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus regimen and is admitted with leg cellulitis. He is alert, eating normally and has managed his insulin for 15 years. He asks to keep giving his own injections. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion while he is unwell
Explain that ward nurses must give all insulin while he is an inpatient
Withhold his mealtime insulin until the infection is controlled
Check he is willing, able and safe, then support self-administration
9.w: NICE NG17 (1.13.6, 1.13.8) says inpatients with type 1 diabetes should be enabled to self-administer subcutaneous insulin if willing and able and it is safe, respecting their personal expertise. Because he is eating, subcutaneous insulin is appropriate (1.13.5).

n.0: IV insulin is for people unable to eat, missing more than one meal or with unpredictable glucose; Tom is eating.
n.1: This removes self-management from a capable adult, against NG17 recommendations on inpatient care.
n.2: Infection usually raises glucose; omitting mealtime insulin risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis.

9.q: Before entering the room of Margaret, 71, who has influenza and needs help to wash, Ade gathers an apron, a fluid-resistant surgical mask, goggles and non-sterile gloves. In which order should Ade put this equipment on?
o: Mask, eye protection, gloves, then apron
Apron, mask, eye protection, then gloves
Apron, gloves, eye protection, then mask
Gloves, apron, mask, then eye protection
9.w: NIPCM appendix 6 sets the order for putting on PPE as apron or gown, FRSM or respirator, eye protection, then gloves. Gloves go on last so that they are not contaminated while the other items are adjusted.

n.0: The apron goes on first; putting it on last means pulling it over gloves and face protection.
n.2: The mask is fitted before eye protection and gloves; adjusting a mask with gloved hands risks contamination.
n.3: Putting gloves on first means they touch the apron ties, mask and goggles while fitting them.

9.q: Callum, 39, has an asthma attack. His PEF is 55% of best, respiratory rate 22/min, heart rate 114/min and he completes sentences. SpO2 is 96%. How should this attack be classified?
o: Acute severe asthma
Mild asthma with no severe features
Moderate asthma attack
Life-threatening asthma
9.w: SIGN 158: any one feature (PEF 33-50%, RR 25/min or more, HR 110/min or more, unable to complete sentences) classifies an attack as acute severe.

n.1: His heart rate of 114/min is a severe feature.
n.2: His PEF fits moderate, but a heart rate of 110/min or more is an acute severe feature.
n.3: There are no life-threatening features such as SpO2 below 92% or PEF below 33%.

9.q: A district nurse visits Mr Shaw, 68, whose wife died recently. He has given his dog to a neighbour, written letters to his children and says calmly that 'everything is sorted now'. He denies any physical symptoms. How should the nurse interpret these signs?
o: They are warning signs of suicidal intent needing direct enquiry
They suggest early dementia, so a memory screen is the priority
They show he is adjusting well and needs routine follow-up
They suggest normal grief, so a bereavement leaflet is enough
9.w: Giving away possessions, putting affairs in order and sudden calm after loss can signal suicidal intent (NMC Annexe B 1.1.6: recognise signs of self-harm and suicidal ideation). NICE NG225 supports asking about suicidal thoughts and acting on immediate safety concerns.

n.1: Nothing suggests cognitive decline; the behaviour points to risk of suicide.
n.2: Settling affairs after recent bereavement with sudden calm is a recognised warning sign, not evidence of adjustment.
n.3: A leaflet does not address possible suicidal intent, which needs direct enquiry.

9.q: Victor, 66, has COPD. He tells you he has to stop for breath after walking about 100 metres on level ground but can still dress himself and leave the house. What is his MRC dyspnoea grade?
o: Grade 5
Grade 2
Grade 3
Grade 4
9.w: NICE NG115 Table 1 (MRC dyspnoea scale): grade 4 = stops for breath after walking about 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground.

n.0: Grade 5 is too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing.
n.1: Grade 2 is breathlessness when hurrying or walking up a slight hill.
n.2: Grade 3 is walking slower than contemporaries or stopping at own pace on the level.

9.q: Ada, 88, has been sleeping poorly. She dozes most of the afternoon, is woken for observations at 02:00 and 06:00, and has a NEWS2 of 0. She says she is tired all day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Review her observation times with the team to protect her sleep
Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her to take at night
Wake her more often in the afternoon so that she sleeps at night
Leave her plan unchanged, as observations have to be done at night
9.w: With a NEWS2 of 0 the minimum frequency is 12-hourly (RCP 2017), so night-time waking may be avoidable. Reviewing the care plan to cluster care and protect sleep supports rest (Annexe B 3.1, 3.6).

n.1: Sedatives are not first line and increase falls risk in older people.
n.2: Repeatedly waking her during the day adds fatigue rather than addressing the night-time disturbance.
n.3: Observation timing is a clinical decision and can be reviewed when the score is 0.

9.q: Mr Price, 69, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and depression. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on air and he is struggling to finish sentences; his capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L. Which need should the nurse prioritise first?
o: His dietary intake and weight
His raised blood glucose
His low mood and anxiety
His breathing and oxygenation
9.w: When prioritising care for a person with comorbidities (P3.13), immediate threats to life come first. Severe hypoxaemia and breathlessness are an airway and breathing priority needing escalation and oxygen to a prescribed target; the other needs are addressed once he is stable.

n.0: Nutrition is important for recovery but is not the immediate priority.
n.1: A glucose of 11.2 mmol/L needs monitoring but is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxaemia.
n.2: His mood matters but is not the most urgent need while he is hypoxic.

9.q: A nurse joining a care home finds that Ada, 90, has been given her medicines covertly for 10 months. The best interests decision and management plan are filed, but there is no record of any review since. What should the nurse do?
o: Continue, as a plan is in place and signed
Ask Ada's daughter to confirm she still agrees with the plan
Stop all covert medicines until the GP's next visit
Arrange a review of the plan with the multidisciplinary team
9.w: Covert administration requires a documented management plan that is reviewed regularly (NICE SC1 1.15; RPS/RCN 2019 paras 21-23). Ada's capacity, the need for each medicine and the method should be reconsidered by the team, including the prescriber and pharmacist.

n.0: A plan without review may be out of date; review is a required safeguard.
n.1: Family views are part of the review, but the daughter cannot authorise continuation alone.
n.2: Abruptly stopping all medicines could cause harm; a prompt review is needed instead.

9.q: Cyril, 82, has heart failure and is on intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily. His morning bloods show potassium 3.1 mmol/L (previously 4.0). He feels weak. What best explains this result, and what should the nurse do?
o: IV furosemide dilutes the blood; increase his oral fluid intake
Loop diuretics cause potassium retention; repeat the bloods tomorrow
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; inform the prescriber now
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; give a banana with lunch
9.w: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urinary sodium and potassium excretion, so hypokalaemia is an expected effect (P4.17, applying pharmacology). A fall to 3.1 mmol/L with weakness needs prompt prescriber review for replacement and dose review; low potassium increases arrhythmia risk in heart failure.

n.0: Dilution is not the mechanism, and extra fluid may worsen heart failure.
n.1: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, not retention, and a day's delay is unsafe.
n.3: Dietary potassium will not correct this promptly and the prescriber still needs to know.

9.q: Ama is due to revalidate next month. Her CPD log shows 35 hours: 18 hours at a study day and team workshops, and 17 hours reading journal articles on her own. What is the position on her CPD requirement?
o: She needs five more hours of any type of CPD
She needs two more hours of participatory learning
She needs fifteen more hours of participatory learning
She meets it, as she has 35 hours in total
9.w: NMC revalidation CPD requirement (updated 08/09/2021): 35 hours of CPD in three years, of which at least 20 must include participatory learning. 20 - 18 = 2 participatory hours still needed.

n.0: Her total of 35 is already met; the shortfall is in participatory hours, not overall hours.
n.2: She needs 20 participatory hours in total; with 18 already logged, the gap is two hours.
n.3: The total is met, but at least 20 of the 35 hours must be participatory; she has 18.

9.q: Douglas, 61, has CKD with an eGFR of 48 and an ACR of 40 mg/mmol. Ramipril is to be started. His potassium today is 4.6 mmol/L. Which monitoring plan should the nurse arrange?
o: Potassium and eGFR every 3 months for the first year
Potassium and eGFR 1 to 2 weeks after starting and after dose rises
Potassium and eGFR at the next annual CKD review
Blood pressure checks at 1 week, with bloods if he feels unwell
9.w: NICE NG203 (1.6.14) says measure serum potassium and eGFR before starting renin-angiotensin system antagonists in CKD and repeat between 1 and 2 weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

n.0: 3-monthly checks miss the early changes that NG203 asks to be detected at 1 to 2 weeks.
n.2: Waiting a year could miss hyperkalaemia or a large fall in eGFR after starting the drug.
n.3: Hyperkalaemia and falling eGFR are often symptomless, so bloods are needed regardless of symptoms.

9.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to secure and cover the site. Which type of dressing is recommended so that the site can be inspected?
o: A sterile hydrocolloid dressing over the hub
A sterile gauze dressing and crepe bandage
Non-sterile adhesive tape over a gauze square
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
9.w: Vascular access device care (NICE CG139 and the IPC facts sheet) uses a sterile, transparent, semipermeable membrane dressing so the insertion site can be observed for signs of infection or phlebitis without removing it.

n.0: Hydrocolloid dressings are for wounds; they are opaque and not designed for cannula sites.
n.1: A bandage over gauze prevents regular inspection of the insertion site.
n.2: Non-sterile tape and gauze hide the site and are not a sterile covering for a Key-Site.

9.q: On a medical ward the early shift requires 40 hours of registered nurse time. Because of sickness, 30 hours of registered nurse time is available. Two registered nurses are on duty. According to NICE SG1, is this a nursing red flag event?
o: Yes, because any shortfall in registered nurse time is a red flag
No, because the shortfall is exactly 25% and not more than 25%
Yes, because the 10-hour shortfall is more than 8 hours
No, because two registered nurses are present on the ward
9.w: NICE SG1 Box 2: a red flag is a shortfall of more than 8 hours or 25% of registered nurse time, whichever is reached first, compared with the requirement for the shift. Working: shortfall = 40 - 30 = 10 hours. 10 hours is more than 8 hours, so the red flag is triggered even though 10/40 is exactly 25% (SG1 gives 40 hours with under 32 available as its example).

n.0: SG1 sets thresholds; a shortfall below 8 hours and 25% is not itself a red flag.
n.1: The 8-hour limit is reached first; 'whichever is reached first' means the 25% figure does not need to be exceeded.
n.3: Having at least two registered nurses avoids a different red flag; it does not cancel the shortfall red flag.

10.q: A ward pharmacist explains to nursing staff how NICE judges whether a new medicine is cost-effective in its technology appraisals. Since April 2026, what is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold?
o: £100,000 to £300,000 per QALY gained
£20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
10.w: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold in technology appraisals rose from £20,000-£30,000 to £25,000-£35,000 per QALY gained from April 2026 (NICE, Changes to NICE's cost-effectiveness thresholds; P7.4 implications of current health policy).

n.0: This higher range applies to highly specialised technologies for ultra-rare diseases, not the standard threshold.
n.1: This was the threshold before April 2026.
n.2: This is not a NICE threshold range.

10.q: Tariq, 8, has anaphylaxis after eating peanuts at a hospital clinic. What dose of IM adrenaline should be given?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 mg/mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL)
100 micrograms (0.1 mL of 1 mg/mL)
10.w: RCUK anaphylaxis doses (1 mg/mL): over 12 years 500 micrograms; 6-12 years 300 micrograms; 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 500 micrograms is for adults and children over 12.
n.3: 100 micrograms is within the range for infants under 6 months.

10.q: Hilda, 84, with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide and an eGFR of 28, had a hypo of 2.8 mmol/L on admission that was treated successfully. She is now eating. What is the most important ongoing nursing action?
o: Recheck glucose when she reports symptoms of a hypo
Recheck glucose once at 1 hour, then resume her usual checks
Give her usual gliclazide dose with breakfast tomorrow
Continue regular glucose monitoring for at least 24 to 48 hours
10.w: JBDS 01 (2023): hypoglycaemia from a sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin may persist or recur for up to 24 to 36 hours, especially with renal impairment, so capillary monitoring should continue for at least 24 to 48 hours and the prescriber should review the dose.

n.0: Older people often have reduced warning symptoms, so waiting for symptoms is unsafe.
n.1: A single recheck misses recurrent hypoglycaemia from a long-acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment.
n.2: The dose active at the time of the hypo should be reviewed before it is given again.

10.q: Daniel, 45, is on an intensive care unit in England after a catastrophic brain haemorrhage. Treatment is to be withdrawn. He has lived in England all his life and has not recorded a donation decision on the NHS Organ Donor Register. What happens about organ donation?
o: His organs are retrieved without discussion because his consent is deemed
His family are approached to find out whether he held any views about donation
The consultant decides on donation at a best interests meeting
Donation cannot proceed because he did not register as an organ donor
10.w: NHS Organ Donation, Organ donation law in England (opt out from 20 May 2020): adults are considered to agree to donate unless they recorded a decision not to donate or are in an excluded group, and families are still consulted when donation is a possibility, to share any knowledge of the person's decision.

n.0: Under the opt-out law the family are still consulted when donation is possible; retrieval does not proceed without that discussion.
n.2: Donation decisions follow the deemed consent law and the person's known views, not a clinical best interests meeting.
n.3: In England, adults not in an excluded group are considered to agree unless they opted out; registration is not required.

10.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
10.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

10.q: Kofi raised a patient safety concern with his manager and then with the trust's director of nursing. Three months later nothing has changed and patients remain at risk. Under NMC guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record his concerns in his reflective accounts for revalidation
Raise the concern again with his manager in writing
Contact a national newspaper to make the risk public
Raise the concern with a regulator such as the CQC
10.w: NMC Raising concerns guidance stage 4: if internal routes have not worked, raise the concern with a regulator or helpline, for example the CQC in England. Code 16.1.

n.0: Reflection does not escalate the risk to anyone able to act.
n.1: He has already used the internal stages without result; repeating stage 1 delays action.
n.2: Media disclosure is not a stage in NMC guidance and may lose legal protection.

10.q: Bernard, 69, has a suspected stroke. He reports that his symptoms began with a sudden, very severe headache. His GCS is 15. When should brain imaging be done?
o: Within 24 hours
Within 4 hours
Immediately
Within 12 hours
10.w: NICE NG128 1.3.2: severe headache at onset of stroke symptoms is an indication for immediate non-enhanced CT, as it suggests possible haemorrhage. NG128 defines 'immediately' as ideally the next slot and definitely within 1 hour, whichever is sooner.

n.0: 24 hours applies when no immediate criterion is present.
n.1: Severe headache at onset needs immediate CT, which NICE defines as the next slot and definitely within 1 hour; 4 hours is too long.
n.3: 12 hours is not an NG128 imaging timeframe.

10.q: Winifred, 76, has newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation and treated hypertension. She has no other conditions. What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score and the recommended action?
o: Score 4: offer a DOAC
Score 4: offer aspirin
Score 3: offer a DOAC
Score 2: consider a DOAC
10.w: Two steps: age 75 or over = 2, female sex = 1, hypertension = 1, total 4. NICE NG196 1.6.3: offer anticoagulation with a DOAC if CHA2DS2-VASc is 2 or above, taking bleeding risk into account.

n.1: NICE says do not offer aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention in AF.
n.2: Age 75 or over scores 2, not 1, so the total is 4.
n.3: Her total is 4, and at 2 or above a DOAC is offered, not considered.

10.q: Mark, 52, has chronic primary pain and has taken codeine 60 mg four times a day for two years. He says it helps very little and makes him drowsy at work. What is the most appropriate approach, in line with NICE NG193?
o: Advise him to stop the codeine today as it has no evidence
Ask the GP to change to modified-release morphine for better effect
Explain the risks and support a plan to reduce and stop it
Continue the current dose because he has taken it for two years
10.w: NG193 1.2.11-1.2.12: if a person is already taking a medicine on the 'do not initiate' list and reports little benefit or significant harm, explain the risks of continuing and encourage and support them to reduce and stop, discussing withdrawal problems.

n.0: Abrupt cessation after two years risks withdrawal; NG193 asks for a supported, shared plan.
n.1: Switching to a stronger opioid adds risk without evidence of benefit for chronic primary pain.
n.3: Long use does not justify continuing a medicine giving little benefit and significant harm.

10.q: Callum, 39, has an asthma attack. His PEF is 55% of best, respiratory rate 22/min, heart rate 114/min and he completes sentences. SpO2 is 96%. How should this attack be classified?
o: Acute severe asthma
Mild asthma with no severe features
Moderate asthma attack
Life-threatening asthma
10.w: SIGN 158: any one feature (PEF 33-50%, RR 25/min or more, HR 110/min or more, unable to complete sentences) classifies an attack as acute severe.

n.1: His heart rate of 114/min is a severe feature.
n.2: His PEF fits moderate, but a heart rate of 110/min or more is an acute severe feature.
n.3: There are no life-threatening features such as SpO2 below 92% or PEF below 33%.

10.q: A newly qualified nurse on a surgical ward asks which patients should be offered an enhanced recovery programme. According to NICE perioperative care guidance, which answer is correct?
o: People having elective major or complex surgery
People having emergency surgery out of hours
People having day-case surgery under local anaesthetic
People aged 65 and over having any operation
10.w: NICE NG180 (1.2.1-1.2.2) recommends offering an enhanced recovery programme to people having elective major or complex surgery, with preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative components.

n.1: NG180 recommends enhanced recovery for elective major or complex surgery, not by time of day.
n.2: Day-case local anaesthetic procedures are not the group NG180 targets for enhanced recovery.
n.3: Eligibility is based on the type of surgery, not age.

10.q: Elif, a ward manager, is preparing a business case for an additional registered nurse on night shifts. Which evidence would most strengthen her case?
o: Comments from staff that the ward has felt busier over recent months
The staffing levels of a similar ward in a neighbouring hospital trust
Red flag reports, acuity data and safe nursing indicators, linked to costs
The number of complaints she has personally received about night care
10.w: A basic business case sets out the problem with objective evidence, the options and their costs and benefits (P7.12 develop a basic business case using finance, resources and safe staffing). NICE SG1 recommends recording red flag events and safe nursing indicators so they can inform establishment reviews.

n.0: Staff impressions are useful context but are subjective and not linked to patient need or cost.
n.1: Another ward's staffing does not show this ward's patients' needs.
n.3: Complaint numbers are a partial measure and do not demonstrate the staffing requirement or its cost.

10.q: Joan, 74, has lower back pain after a fall at home and is being cared for on a frailty unit. Her care plan lists several pain-relieving interventions. Which of these is a non-pharmacological intervention?
o: A rectal paracetamol suppository
A topical lidocaine plaster
Patient-controlled analgesia pump
Repositioning using pillows
10.w: Non-pharmacological measures include repositioning, heat or cold where appropriate, distraction, relaxation, reassurance and explanation. NICE NG31 gives repositioning as an example (Annexe B 3.5).

n.0: A suppository is a route for giving a drug.
n.1: A lidocaine plaster delivers a drug and is pharmacological.
n.2: PCA delivers opioid medicine and is pharmacological.

10.q: Brian, 54, has alcohol-related cirrhosis and is admitted vomiting large amounts of fresh blood. Pulse 118, BP 96/60. Variceal bleeding is suspected. Alongside resuscitation, which medicines should be given at presentation?
o: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics
Prophylactic antibiotics and propranolol
Terlipressin and vitamin K
Omeprazole and tranexamic acid
10.w: NICE CG141 (1.5.1-1.5.2): offer terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation to people with suspected variceal bleeding, followed by band ligation for oesophageal varices.

n.1: Propranolol lowers blood pressure in a shocked patient and is used later for prophylaxis, not at presentation.
n.2: Vitamin K is not the recommended presentation treatment; antibiotics are.
n.3: Pre-endoscopy acid suppression is not recommended and neither drug is the NICE treatment for variceal bleeding.

10.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
10.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

10.q: Your close colleague, going through a divorce, asks you not to mention that she has given several time-critical medicines over an hour late this week. She promises it will stop. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Agree to keep it confidential if she promises to improve
Offer support but explain you must tell the nurse in charge
Give her time-critical medicines for her so the delays stop
Report her to the NMC without speaking to anyone locally
10.w: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but this must never compromise patient safety. Code 16.1: raise and escalate safety concerns; 19.1 reduce harm.

n.0: Code 8.7 says support must not compromise patient safety; late time-critical medicines need escalating.
n.2: Covering for her hides the problem and leaves the risk unmanaged.
n.3: Local escalation and support should come first; referral is not the immediate proportionate step.

10.q: A nurse is preparing for a structured multimorbidity review with Ahmed, 77, who takes 13 regular medicines. Following the NICE NG56 sequence, which step should come before reviewing his medicines?
o: Deciding who will coordinate his ongoing care
Arranging the timing of his follow-up review
Agreeing his individualised management plan
Establishing his goals, values and priorities
10.w: NG56 1.5.2 order: discuss the purpose of the approach, establish disease and treatment burden, establish goals, values and priorities, review medicines and other treatments, then agree an individualised plan (including coordination and follow-up).

n.0: Coordination of care is set within the final management plan.
n.1: Follow-up timing is part of the plan agreed at the end.
n.2: The management plan is agreed after the medicines review.

10.q: Frank, 88, is CFS 7 at baseline after a stroke two years ago and is fully dependent for personal care. He has a chest infection and is improving. A healthcare assistant says Frank 'must be dying' because CFS 7 is near the top of the scale. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: CFS 7 shows he is approaching the end of life and cannot recover
CFS 7 means dependency, but he appears stable and not likely dying soon
CFS 7 means life expectancy is usually under six months
CFS 7 should prompt a referral to the hospital end of life care team today
10.w: CFS v2.0 level 7 (living with severe frailty) describes people completely dependent for personal care who seem stable and not at high risk of dying within about 6 months. Levels 8 (very severe frailty, approaching end of life) and 9 (terminally ill, life expectancy under 6 months) describe approaching death.

n.0: Approaching end of life and unable to recover from minor illness describes level 8.
n.2: Life expectancy under 6 months describes level 9, terminally ill.
n.3: An end of life referral is not indicated by CFS 7 when he is stable and improving.

10.q: Tom, 34, attends an acute medical unit with a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and sepsis is suspected. Under NICE NG253 (2025), within what time should broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics be given?
o: Within 3 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 6 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 4 hours of arrival in the department
10.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.3: for people at high risk (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score.

n.0: Up to 3 hours is the deferral window a clinician may use for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6).
n.2: Up to 6 hours is the deferral window for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.3: A 4-hour arrival target is not a sepsis treatment standard.

10.q: Frederick, 87, was living independently last week. Today he is very drowsy, keeps falling asleep mid-sentence and cannot attempt the orientation questions or the months backwards. A colleague says the 4AT 'cannot be done' and should be left blank. What should the nurse do?
o: Use the Abbreviated Mental Test 10 instead of the 4AT today
Leave the 4AT blank and repeat it once he is more awake
Record a 4AT of 4 for drowsiness and leave the other items blank
Score each untestable item 2 and complete the 4AT
10.w: The 4AT can always be scored: untestable AMT4 and attention items score 2 each, clearly abnormal alertness scores 4, and acute change from his independent baseline scores 4 (total 12). A score of 4 or more suggests delirium, which should prompt urgent clinical assessment (4AT user guide; CG103 1.6.1).

n.0: CG103 1.6.1 names the 4AT for assessment outside critical care, and he cannot attempt an AMT10 either.
n.1: Leaving it blank delays recognising delirium, a medical emergency; the 4AT is designed to score drowsy patients.
n.2: The remaining items must also be scored; untestable items score 2 and acute change scores 4.

10.q: Jorge, 61, is prescribed potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours. The ward has no ready-mixed bags. A colleague suggests adding concentrated potassium chloride from an ampoule to a bag of saline. What should the nurse do?
o: Run plain saline now and add the potassium when the bag is changed
Obtain a ready-mixed bag from pharmacy or another area per policy
Give the concentrated potassium chloride as a slow IV bolus instead
Add the ampoule to the bag and invert it several times to mix
10.w: Mis-selection of a strong potassium solution is a Never Event (2018 list, updated 2021); national guidance requires ready-diluted potassium infusions wherever possible, with concentrated ampoules restricted. Potassium is a high-risk medicine (P4.15).

n.0: Delaying and then adding concentrate later carries the same mis-selection risk.
n.2: Concentrated potassium must not be given as a bolus; it can cause cardiac arrest.
n.3: Ward addition of concentrated potassium risks mis-selection and poor mixing, causing fatal hyperkalaemia.

10.q: Mr Carter died on the ward last week. A local journalist phones, saying she is writing a tribute, and asks the nurse what illness he died from. His family have not given any permission. How should the nurse respond?
o: Confirm the details if the journalist knew him personally
Share general details but not the diagnosis itself
Share the cause of death, as he can no longer be harmed
Decline to share, as confidentiality continues after death
10.w: Code 5.3: make sure that people's confidentiality is respected after they have died. There is no lawful basis to disclose his health information to a journalist.

n.0: Knowing the patient personally gives no right to confidential information.
n.1: Any health details about Mr Carter remain confidential; partial disclosure is still a breach.
n.2: Confidentiality does not end at death (Code 5.3).

10.q: Victor, 66, has COPD. He tells you he has to stop for breath after walking about 100 metres on level ground but can still dress himself and leave the house. What is his MRC dyspnoea grade?
o: Grade 5
Grade 2
Grade 3
Grade 4
10.w: NICE NG115 Table 1 (MRC dyspnoea scale): grade 4 = stops for breath after walking about 100 metres or after a few minutes on level ground.

n.0: Grade 5 is too breathless to leave the house or breathless when dressing.
n.1: Grade 2 is breathlessness when hurrying or walking up a slight hill.
n.2: Grade 3 is walking slower than contemporaries or stopping at own pace on the level.

10.q: For three weeks the call bells in one bay on Kemi's ward have failed intermittently. Each failure has been reported as an incident, but estates staff say a full replacement needs trust funding. What is the most appropriate next step for Kemi as the nurse in charge?
o: Move patients who cannot use a call bell to beds nearer the nurses' station each shift
Keep reporting each failure as an incident until the estates team replaces the system
Write to the local newspaper about the delay to replacing the call bell system
Escalate to the ward manager so the risk can be assessed and added to the risk register
10.w: A persistent risk that cannot be fixed at ward level should be escalated so it is formally assessed, recorded on the organisation's risk register with an owner and controls, and reviewed (P6.3 local and national frameworks for managing and reporting risk; Code 16.1 and 25.1). Interim measures continue alongside escalation.

n.0: Moving patients is a sensible interim control but does not get the underlying risk managed or funded.
n.1: Incident reports record events; they do not on their own place a known, ongoing risk under managed review with an owner.
n.2: Going to the media before using internal escalation routes is not consistent with NMC raising concerns guidance.

10.q: Wendy, 60, develops stridor, facial swelling and a blotchy rash after a wasp sting in the hospital garden. A colleague has called for help and brought the emergency box with adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should you inject the intramuscular adrenaline?
o: Deltoid muscle of the non-dominant arm
Anterolateral middle third of the thigh
Subcutaneous tissue of the abdomen
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
10.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline: IM adrenaline is given into the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh, which gives reliable absorption.

n.0: The deltoid is not the recommended site for anaphylaxis.
n.2: Subcutaneous injection gives slower, less reliable absorption.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended and risks injection into fat or the sciatic area.

10.q: Mr Ito, 38, has a head injury. On assessment his eyes open to pressure on the fingertip, he is talking but disorientated about time and place, and he localises to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
10.w: GCS: eye opening to pressure = 2; confused speech = 4; localising = 5. Total 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 out of 15 (range 3-15). Any fall in GCS after head injury needs urgent escalation.

n.0: Orientated speech scores 5 and obeying commands 6; he is confused and localises.
n.1: Eye opening to speech scores 3; he opens his eyes only to pressure, which scores 2.
n.2: Inappropriate words score 3; he is talking in sentences but confused, which scores 4.

10.q: Carol, 41, tells the nurse at a health check that she drinks most weekends: about 7 units on Friday night and 7 units on Saturday night, and nothing during the week. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Her drinking is above the weekly guideline, which is 10 units for women
Her drinking is low risk because her weekly total is within 14 units
Spread drinking over 3 or more days, as heavy sessions raise her risk
She should drink a small amount daily, as this protects her heart
10.w: UK Chief Medical Officers' low risk drinking guidelines (2016): it is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, for men and women; if drinking as much as 14 units a week, spread it evenly over 3 or more days, as one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase the risk of death from long-term illness and from accidents and injuries.

n.0: The CMO guideline is 14 units a week for both men and women.
n.1: The CMOs advise that one or two heavy drinking episodes a week increase risks of long-term illness, accidents and injuries.
n.3: The CMOs do not advise drinking for health; risk rises with regular drinking.

10.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
10.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

10.q: Jean, 48, is nil by mouth for 24 hours before planned surgery and has no cardiac, renal or nutritional problems. The junior doctor asks you to check the volume she is prescribing for routine maintenance. Under NICE CG174, what is the daily routine maintenance water requirement for an adult?
o: 60-70 mL/kg/day
40-50 mL/kg/day
10-15 mL/kg/day
25-30 mL/kg/day
10.w: NICE CG174: routine maintenance is 25-30 mL/kg/day of water, about 1 mmol/kg/day each of potassium, sodium and chloride, and 50-100 g/day of glucose.

n.0: 60-70 mL/kg/day risks fluid overload.
n.1: 40-50 mL/kg/day exceeds adult maintenance needs.
n.2: 10-15 mL/kg/day would cause dehydration in most adults.

10.q: A ward manager is reviewing staffing on an acute adult medical ward. Which statement about nurse-to-patient ratios reflects NICE SG1 (2014)?
o: A ratio of one registered nurse to six patients applies on all wards, day and night
A ratio of one registered nurse to eight patients is a legal minimum in England
There is no single ratio, but over 8 patients per nurse by day is linked to harm
Staffing ratios for adult wards are set by the NMC for each type of hospital ward
10.w: NICE SG1 rec 1.5.3: there is no single nursing staff-to-patient ratio for all acute adult wards, but there is evidence of increased risk of harm when a registered nurse cares for more than 8 patients on day shifts, which should prompt close monitoring of red flags and safe nursing indicators.

n.0: SG1 does not set a 1:6 ratio; it uses patients' nursing needs and professional judgement.
n.1: The 1:8 figure is an evidence threshold for monitoring, not a legal minimum in England.
n.3: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not set ward staffing ratios.

10.q: An occupational health nurse is giving an intradermal tuberculin skin test into the inner forearm of Leila, 24. Which finding confirms that the injection has been placed correctly?
o: The fluid flows freely and leaves no mark on the skin
Blood flashback is seen in the hub of the syringe
A small pale bleb forms raising the skin at the site
A bruise appears at the site within a few minutes
10.w: Intradermal injections are given at a shallow angle of about 10-15 degrees with the bevel up, just under the epidermis; correct placement raises a small pale bleb (AnnexB.11.7). No bleb suggests a deeper, subcutaneous injection.

n.0: Free flow with no bleb suggests the fluid has gone into subcutaneous tissue.
n.1: Flashback indicates the needle is in a blood vessel, not the dermis.
n.3: Bruising suggests trauma to vessels, not correct dermal placement.

10.q: Preparing the 14:00 dose, nurse Tamsin sees that Edna, 88, has been prescribed oral morphine solution 50 mg four-hourly. Edna is opioid-naive and her previous doses were 5 mg. Tamsin suspects a tenfold prescribing error. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold it, have the prescription corrected and report a near miss
Withhold it and ask for an amendment; reporting is not needed as no harm
Amend the chart to 5 mg, initial the change and give the dose
Give 5 mg, as this was clearly intended, then tell the prescriber
10.w: A prescribing error intercepted before reaching the patient is a near miss and should be reported so learning can be shared (P6.8). The nurse checks that the prescription is unambiguous and appropriate before administration (RPS/RCN 2019 para 15) and raises concerns with the prescriber without delay.

n.1: Near misses are reported; no-harm events still reveal system weaknesses.
n.2: Nurses cannot amend a prescription; that is a prescribing act.
n.3: Giving a dose different from the written prescription is administering without a valid prescription.

10.q: Dennis, 60, has an ECG showing STEMI. He has had two doses of sublingual GTN but still reports severe central chest pain. What pain relief is recommended next?
o: A third GTN dose with no further drug
An intravenous opioid such as morphine
Oral paracetamol and codeine
Intramuscular morphine into the deltoid
10.w: NICE CG95 1.2.3.1: offer pain relief as soon as possible, with GTN (sublingual or buccal) and an intravenous opioid such as morphine, particularly if an acute MI is suspected.

n.0: Persisting pain after GTN in suspected MI calls for an IV opioid.
n.2: Oral analgesia is too slow and weak for suspected MI pain.
n.3: IV is preferred; IM absorption is unpredictable and can interfere with later investigations.

10.q: Samuel, 79, is in the last days of life. Yesterday a trial of subcutaneous fluids was started because he was thirsty and slightly confused. Today the nurse notes new crackles at both lung bases and increasing ankle swelling. He is more breathless. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give 'as required' midazolam for breathlessness and continue the fluids
Increase the infusion rate because his thirst is still present
Continue the fluids and reassess them at tomorrow's daily review
Reduce or stop the fluids and inform the team of signs of fluid overload
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.4.9: for a person started on clinically assisted hydration, monitor at least every 12 hours for benefit or harm; continue if there is clinical benefit and reduce or stop it if there are signs of possible harm such as fluid overload, or if the person no longer wants it.

n.0: Sedating him without removing the cause of the overload is not appropriate; the fluids are causing harm.
n.1: Increasing fluid would worsen the overload; thirst is managed with mouth care and sips (rec 1.4.2).
n.2: NG31 rec 1.4.9 says reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if there are signs of harm such as fluid overload.

10.q: Tomasz, a community nurse, is planning CPD for revalidation. Which activity would count as participatory learning under the NMC requirements?
o: Completing a self-directed e-learning module on sepsis
A live online workshop discussing cases with other nurses
Watching a recorded conference lecture on wound care
Reading a systematic review and writing summary notes
10.w: NMC CPD guidance: participatory learning means activity involving interaction with one or more other professionals, in a physical or virtual environment; you do not have to be in the same room.

n.0: E-learning completed alone involves no interaction with other professionals, so it is non-participatory.
n.2: A recording watched alone has no interaction; participatory learning needs engagement with others.
n.3: Independent reading is valuable CPD but does not involve interaction with another professional.

10.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
10.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

10.q: During a patient safety study day, a nurse asks what makes an incident a Never Event rather than another serious incident. Which statement is correct?
o: It is any incident that causes harm lasting 28 days or more to a patient
It is wholly preventable because national barriers should be in place
It is any incident that a coroner later finds was caused by staff error
It is any incident in which a patient dies as a direct result of their care
10.w: NHS England's Never Events policy and framework (2018, list updated 2021) defines Never Events as patient safety incidents that are wholly preventable because guidance or safety recommendations providing strong systemic protective barriers are available nationally and should have been implemented by all providers. They are recorded on LFPSE with a learning response under PSIRF.

n.0: Twenty-eight days is the duration used for prolonged pain or psychological harm in the statutory candour definitions, not the Never Event test.
n.2: A coroner's finding does not define the category; it is defined by the national barriers that should have prevented it.
n.3: Death is not the defining feature; a Never Event may cause no harm, and many deaths are not Never Events.

10.q: Mr Rowe, 74, is recovering from a hip fracture. The nurse and Mr Rowe are agreeing a mobility goal. Which goal is most appropriate?
o: Improve his mobility as much as possible before discharge
Walk to the day room with his frame by Friday, as he chose
Follow the physiotherapy plan written for all hip patients
Walk 200 metres unaided by tomorrow, as set by the team
10.w: Proficiency P3.4: apply a person-centred approach to shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting. Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This is vague and not measurable or time-bound.
n.2: A standard plan is not a personal, shared goal.
n.3: This is set for him, not with him, and may be unrealistic.

10.q: Bernard, 77, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is receiving oxygen at 4 L/min via nasal cannulae. On your round he is drowsy and difficult to rouse, and his SpO2 is 99%. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Sit him upright and repeat the observations in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen to reach 88-92% and request urgent blood gases
Continue the current flow because his saturation is satisfactory
Stop the oxygen straight away and recheck his saturation
10.w: Assess then act: drowsiness with SpO2 above target in an at-risk patient suggests hypercapnic respiratory failure. BTS 2017 advises stepping oxygen down to the target range (not stopping it suddenly) and urgent blood gases with medical review.

n.0: New drowsiness with high saturation needs urgent action and blood gases, not routine monitoring.
n.2: 99% is above his target; with new drowsiness this suggests hypercapnia from excess oxygen.
n.3: Sudden withdrawal can cause rebound hypoxaemia; oxygen should be stepped down to the target, not stopped abruptly.

10.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
10.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

10.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
10.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

10.q: Graham, 63, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide twice daily and metformin twice daily. He is first on the morning theatre list tomorrow and will miss breakfast only. What does the JBDS perioperative guideline advise for tomorrow morning?
o: Take gliclazide as normal and omit metformin
Omit gliclazide and take metformin as normal
Take both gliclazide and metformin as normal
Omit both gliclazide and metformin
10.w: JBDS 03 (2022) medicines table: for a morning list, omit the sulfonylurea on the morning of surgery (hypoglycaemia risk while fasting) and take once- or twice-daily metformin as normal, provided eGFR is above 60 and no contrast is planned.

n.0: This reverses the advice: the sulfonylurea is the drug to omit.
n.2: Gliclazide while fasting risks hypoglycaemia, so it is omitted that morning.
n.3: Twice-daily metformin is taken as normal on the day of a morning list under JBDS 03.

10.q: Walter, 81, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He slipped in the ward bathroom 20 minutes ago and hit his forehead. He is alert with a GCS of 15, has not vomited and has no other indication for imaging. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue routine observations and scan if his GCS falls
Request a CT head scan within 1 hour of the fall
Escalate so a CT head scan can be considered within 8 hours
Arrange a CT head scan within 24 hours if he develops a headache
10.w: NICE NG232 1.5.13: for people on anticoagulants (including DOACs such as apixaban) with no other indication for CT, consider a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury, or within 1 hour if they present more than 8 hours after it. NG249 links inpatient falls care to this guidance.

n.0: Relying on a GCS drop misses bleeding that can be detected earlier on CT in people taking anticoagulants.
n.1: The 1-hour timing applies to people on anticoagulants presenting more than 8 hours after the injury, or those with other high-risk features.
n.3: Waiting for a headache and a 24-hour window is too late for someone on an anticoagulant.

10.q: After hearing his cancer has spread, Mr Ward, 70, falls silent and starts to cry. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Step out of the room and return once he is calmer
Reassure him that many people live for years with this
Stay with him, allow silence and acknowledge his feelings
Explain the treatment options to him while he takes it in
10.w: Annexe A 2.9 convey compassion during difficult conversations; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; P1.12 support people who are emotionally vulnerable.

n.0: Leaving may feel like abandonment at a vulnerable moment.
n.1: This may be inaccurate and closes down his emotions.
n.3: Giving more information while he is distressed is unlikely to be absorbed.

10.q: At a training session on restrictive practice, a nurse asks which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 is engaged when a person who lacks capacity is deprived of their liberty in a care home. Which Article should the trainer name?
o: Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
10.w: Article 5 (HRA 1998 Sch 1) protects the right to liberty and security and requires lawful procedures for any deprivation of liberty. DoLS exist to provide those safeguards for people lacking capacity.

n.0: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of other rights; it is not the liberty right itself.
n.1: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not lawful authority for deprivation of liberty.
n.3: Article 8 may be relevant to care arrangements, but deprivation of liberty engages Article 5.

10.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
10.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

10.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside the bed of Thomas, 66. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on non-sterile gloves and an apron. What should the nurse do next?
o: Cover with paper towels and apply 70% alcohol to the towels
Apply 1,000 ppm chlorine solution and mop the area straight away
Wipe it up with paper towels and clean the area with detergent
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
10.w: NIPCM appendix 9: for blood or high-risk body fluid spills apply chlorine-releasing granules (or towels soaked in 10,000 ppm available chlorine), follow the contact time (or 3 minutes), discard the waste as healthcare waste, then wash with detergent and dry.

n.0: Alcohol is not the NIPCM agent for blood spills.
n.1: 1,000 ppm is for urine, faeces or vomit spills; blood needs granules or 10,000 ppm, with contact time.
n.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill, which may contain blood-borne viruses.

10.q: Oliver, 38, is prescribed an intramuscular injection into the ventrogluteal site. He has an average build. The nurse has located the site, cleaned it according to policy and stretched the skin. At what angle should the needle be inserted?
o: 30 degrees, angled towards the iliac crest
90 degrees to the skin, in a dart-like motion
10 to 15 degrees with the bevel facing up
45 degrees into a pinched fold of skin
10.w: Intramuscular injections are given at 90 degrees to the skin so that the needle reaches muscle beneath the subcutaneous tissue (AnnexB.11.7). Lower angles deposit medicine in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, changing absorption and causing tissue damage.

n.0: A shallow angle risks depositing the drug subcutaneously, not intramuscularly.
n.2: 10 to 15 degrees is the angle for an intradermal injection.
n.3: 45 degrees into a pinched fold is a subcutaneous technique.

10.q: Brenda, 73, has an exacerbation of COPD. Her blood gases show pH 7.32 and PaCO2 7.6 kPa. A salbutamol nebuliser is prescribed. How should the nebuliser be given?
o: Driven by compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae alongside
Through a spacer instead, because nebulisers are unsafe here
Driven by compressed air, with oxygen stopped during the dose
Driven by oxygen at 8 L/min through the nebuliser mask
10.w: NICE NG115: if a person is hypercapnic or acidotic, nebulisers should be driven by compressed air; if oxygen is needed it is given simultaneously by nasal cannulae (BTS 2017 agrees).

n.1: Nebulisers can be used; the issue is the driving gas, not the device.
n.2: Stopping oxygen during the nebuliser risks hypoxaemia; oxygen continues by cannulae.
n.3: Oxygen-driven nebulisers can worsen hypercapnia when PaCO2 is raised and pH is low.

10.q: Pharmacy has not yet collected four out-of-date diamorphine ampoules from a ward's CD cupboard. A nurse suggests destroying them in a denaturing kit with another registered nurse to tidy the cupboard before an audit. What is the correct action?
o: Destroy them in a denaturing kit with a second registered nurse
Keep them segregated and recorded until an authorised witness attends
Destroy them and record it once the ward manager has countersigned
Return them to pharmacy in the sealed internal post
10.w: NICE NG46: stock Schedule 2 controlled drugs may only be destroyed in the presence of an authorised witness (for example someone appointed by the CD accountable officer). Until then they stay in the CD cupboard, clearly segregated and recorded.

n.0: A colleague who is not an authorised witness cannot witness destruction of stock Schedule 2 CDs.
n.2: A ward manager is not an authorised witness by virtue of the role, and recording after the event does not fix this.
n.3: Internal post is not a secure, auditable transport route for Schedule 2 CDs.

10.q: Walter, 74, has type 2 diabetes and is admitted to a medical ward with pneumonia. He says his feet are fine. What foot assessment should the admitting nurse ensure is completed?
o: Examine both feet with shoes, socks and dressings removed
Arrange foot screening at his next annual diabetes review
Record his report that he has no current foot problems
Examine the feet once he is well enough to mobilise
10.w: NICE NG19 advises examining both feet of a person with diabetes on any admission to hospital, with shoes, socks, bandages and dressings removed, to identify risk and any active problem early.
