n.1: Inpatients need examination on admission; deferring to primary care leaves risk unidentified.
n.2: Self-report misses neuropathic ulcers that the person may not feel.
n.3: Immobile and acutely unwell patients are at highest risk of heel ulceration, so examination cannot wait.

10.q: Sophie is about to insert a peripheral intravenous cannula into the forearm of Malik, 45. She has selected the vein and performed hand hygiene. According to NICE CG139, how should she prepare the skin at the insertion site?
o: Clean with a 70% alcohol wipe, then palpate the vein again
Clean with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride and pat the skin dry with gauze
Apply povidone-iodine and wipe it off before inserting
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
10.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate the skin at the insertion site with chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. The solution must dry to work, and the cleaned site is not re-palpated.

n.0: Re-palpating the vein after cleaning contaminates the Key-Site, and alcohol alone is not the CG139 product.
n.1: Saline cleans but does not decontaminate the skin.
n.2: CG139 specifies chlorhexidine in alcohol; wiping antiseptic off before it has acted also defeats it.

10.q: Doreen, 70, with type 2 diabetes, is an inpatient after a fall. On admission foot examination the nurse finds a small, clean, shallow ulcer on her left big toe. She is afebrile, with no spreading redness and warm feet with palpable pulses. What is the most appropriate referral?
o: Refer to the foot protection service for review within 2 to 4 weeks
Refer to the community podiatrist at discharge
Refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours
Refer to the vascular team as an emergency
10.w: NICE NG19 (1.1.3) says refer an inpatient with a diabetic foot problem to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of the initial examination of the feet.

n.0: 2 to 4 weeks is the NG19 referral time for people at high risk without an active problem.
n.1: An active ulcer needs specialist assessment during the admission, not after discharge.
n.3: There are no signs of limb-threatening ischaemia or infection needing emergency vascular input.

10.q: Ella, 14, is in school Year 9. The school nurse assesses her as Gillick competent, and Ella consents to her MenACWY vaccine. Her mother has returned a form refusing the vaccine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the vaccine, as a parent cannot override a Gillick competent child's consent
Delay the vaccine until Ella is 16 and can legally consent for herself
Ask the head teacher to decide whether the vaccine should be given
Withhold the vaccine, because a parent's refusal takes priority under age 16
10.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): children under 16 who understand fully what is involved (Gillick competent) can give consent, ideally with parental involvement; where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent. UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: MenACWY at 14 years (school Year 9).

n.1: Gillick competent children under 16 can consent, so waiting is unnecessary.
n.2: The head teacher has no role in consent to Ella's treatment.
n.3: The Green Book states that where a Gillick competent child consents, a parent cannot override that consent.

10.q: Nurse Adebayo nearly gives insulin to the wrong patient but notices at the bedside check, so no dose is given. A colleague says there is no need to report it because nothing happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss it at the next team meeting without making a report
Make a note in her own reflective log for revalidation
Tell the patient about the near miss and make no further record
Report the near miss through the local incident reporting system
10.w: The NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (refreshed December 2024) covers openness within organisations, including reporting adverse incidents and near misses. Code 19.1 requires action to reduce the likelihood of mistakes and near misses.

n.0: Discussion helps learning, but candour guidance expects near misses to be reported formally so the system can learn.
n.1: Personal reflection is useful but does not replace organisational reporting of the near miss.
n.2: Telling the patient is not enough; the near miss must still be documented and reported (Code 14.3, 19.1).

10.q: Agnes, the nurse in charge of a busy surgical ward, wants the whole team to share the same understanding of which patients are at risk at the start of each shift. Which practice best supports this?
o: Each nurse reads the full medical notes of all patients before starting
Staff ask the nurse in charge about any patient they are worried about
A brief safety huddle after handover to share key risks and plans
The nurse in charge keeps a written list of risks in the ward office
10.w: Shared situational awareness, the team's common understanding of what is happening and what may happen next, is supported by short structured safety huddles where risks (deteriorating patients, falls, staffing) are discussed and actions agreed (human factors; P5.2; P6.6).

n.0: Reading all notes is impractical on a busy ward and does not create a shared team picture or agreed actions.
n.1: Relying on individuals to ask means risks are shared reactively and unevenly.
n.3: A list kept by one person does not share awareness across the team.

10.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
10.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

10.q: Mrs Shah, 58, asks a practice nurse whether a herbal supplement she has bought online will help her blood pressure alongside her prescribed amlodipine. The nurse is unsure. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her that nurses cannot discuss non-prescribed products
Check a reliable source or the pharmacist before advising her
Advise her that herbal products are natural and safe to take
Advise her to stop the amlodipine while she tries the supplement
10.w: Code 6.1: information or advice must be evidence-based, including about health products; Code 18.3: check compatibility with other treatment, including over-the-counter medicines; Code 13.3 seek help when unsure.

n.0: Code 18.3 expects compatibility with other treatments, including over-the-counter products, to be checked.
n.2: This is not evidence-based and ignores possible interactions (Code 6.1, 18.3).
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review could be harmful and is outside the nurse's evidence base.

10.q: Gareth, 37, is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion for DKA. Over the last hour his blood ketones have fallen from 4.6 to 4.4 mmol/L and glucose has barely changed. What should the nurse do first?
o: Check the pump and line, then inform the prescriber
Increase the infusion by 1 unit/hour and recheck in an hour
Give a subcutaneous bolus of rapid-acting insulin
Recheck ketones in 2 hours, as early falls are often slow
10.w: Two steps: JBDS 02 targets a ketone fall of at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour. The nursing guide says if ketones and glucose are not falling as expected, first check the pump is working and connected, then call a prescribing clinician to increase the rate.

n.1: The rate is increased by the prescribing clinician after equipment problems are excluded.
n.2: Extra subcutaneous insulin is not part of the JBDS DKA protocol.
n.3: JBDS expects at least 0.5 mmol/L/hour; waiting 2 hours delays correcting a failing treatment.

10.q: Daniel, 41, is prescribed a 3 mL deep intramuscular injection. He is of average build and has no contraindications at any site. The nurse is choosing between the available sites. Which site is preferred for this volume?
o: The abdomen, at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
The ventrogluteal site over the gluteus medius
The dorsogluteal site in the upper outer buttock
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
10.w: The ventrogluteal site is the preferred IM site for larger volumes in adults: the muscle is thick, the subcutaneous layer is relatively thin and it is away from major nerves and vessels (AnnexB.11.7). The deltoid takes small volumes, and the dorsogluteal site risks sciatic nerve injury.

n.0: The abdomen is a subcutaneous site, not an intramuscular one.
n.2: The dorsogluteal site carries a risk of sciatic nerve and gluteal artery injury.
n.3: The deltoid is a small muscle used for small volumes such as vaccines, not 3 mL.

10.q: Ian, 35, has type 1 diabetes and is shaky and sweaty at a community clinic. He is alert and able to swallow. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. After giving 15-20 g of glucose tablets, his symptoms are no better at 15 minutes. What should you do?
o: Give a further 15-20 g of oral glucose
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give him a meal containing complex carbohydrate
Recheck his blood glucose again in 30 minutes
10.w: RCUK first aid 2025: treat hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L) in a person who can swallow with 15-20 g glucose; repeat if symptoms persist after 15 minutes; give a snack once recovered.

n.1: He is alert and swallowing, so oral treatment is repeated before an emergency call.
n.2: A snack follows recovery; complex carbohydrate alone is too slow while still hypoglycaemic.
n.3: Waiting another 30 minutes leaves hypoglycaemia untreated.

10.q: Lionel, 75, has CKD with an eGFR of 26 and takes ramipril. He is booked for a non-urgent contrast-enhanced CT as an inpatient tomorrow. Which preparation should the nurse discuss with the team?
o: Keep him nil by mouth for 6 hours before the scan
Cancel the scan because contrast is unsafe with an eGFR below 30
Encourage oral fluids and ask whether ramipril should be paused
Ask for a loop diuretic dose before the scan
10.w: NICE NG148 (1.2.7-1.2.9) advises encouraging oral hydration before and after contrast in people at increased risk, considering IV volume expansion if eGFR is below 30, and considering temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs if eGFR is below 30.

n.0: Fluid restriction before contrast increases the risk of contrast-associated AKI.
n.1: Contrast is not prohibited; NG148 asks for risk discussion and preventive measures.
n.3: Diuretics cause volume depletion and increase the risk of kidney injury.

10.q: Before a short handover, Graham, a staff nurse, needs to ask a healthcare assistant to monitor Mr Okafor, 70, who had a hypotensive episode earlier. Which instruction is clearest?
o: 'Please check Mr Okafor's BP and pulse at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is under 100.'
'Please keep an eye on Mr Okafor this afternoon and let me know how he gets on.'
'Please do the usual observations on everyone in bay 2, including Mr Okafor, this afternoon.'
'Please do Mr Okafor's observations when you have time and tell me if anything looks off.'
10.w: AnnexA.1.11 requires clear verbal, digital or written information and instructions when delegating or handing over. An instruction stating what to do, when, and exactly what to report and when removes ambiguity (Code 11.2; AnnexA.4.1.2).

n.1: 'Keep an eye on' does not specify what to measure, when, or what to report.
n.2: A general bay instruction does not flag Mr Okafor's specific risk or what to report.
n.3: There is no time set or threshold for reporting; 'anything off' depends on the assistant's interpretation.

10.q: Lewis, 70, was admitted an hour ago with an acute stroke. He has not yet had a swallow screen. He asks for a cup of tea and says he feels fine. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Offer small sips of tea while you watch him closely for coughing
Explain he needs a swallow screen before anything to eat or drink
Offer the tea once he is sitting fully upright
Offer the tea thickened to reduce the choking risk
10.w: NICE NG128 1.6.1: people with acute stroke should have their swallowing screened by a specially trained healthcare professional before being given any oral food, fluid or medication.

n.0: Even small sips are oral intake and can be aspirated silently.
n.2: Positioning does not replace a swallow screen.
n.3: Thickening is guided by a specialist assessment; nothing is given before the screen.

10.q: Lillian, 89, has dementia and gets out of bed at night. Her son asks for bed rails to be put up to stop her falling. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Assess the risks first, as rails can harm her if she climbs
Put the rails up and add a lap belt in her chair by day
Refuse the request because bed rails are not allowed
Put the rails up straight away, as her son has asked
10.w: Annexe B 7.4: use safety devices appropriately. Bed rails must be individually risk-assessed; for a person with dementia who mobilises, they may cause entrapment or a higher fall from climbing over. Alternatives include a low bed, crash mat or sensor alarm, discussed with her and her family.

n.1: A lap belt is a restriction needing capacity and best-interests consideration, not a routine add-on.
n.2: Bed rails can be used after individual assessment.
n.3: A relative's request does not replace an individual risk assessment.

10.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
10.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

10.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
10.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

10.q: Lucy brings her 1-year-old son for his MMRV vaccine. Her neighbour's baby is too young to be vaccinated, and Lucy asks how vaccinating her son could help that baby. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Vaccinating children means adults in the area no longer need vaccines
Her son will pass vaccine antibodies to other children he plays with
Vaccinated people are less likely to pass the infection on to others
The vaccine gives lifelong protection, so the disease disappears locally
10.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, Immunity and how vaccines work (January 2021): vaccinated individuals are less likely to be a source of infection to others, reducing the risk of exposure for unvaccinated individuals, so people who cannot be vaccinated still benefit. This is population (or 'herd') immunity.

n.0: Population immunity does not replace the adult programme; adults are still offered vaccines.
n.1: Antibodies are not passed between children; protection of others comes from reduced transmission.
n.3: No vaccine offers 100% protection, and disease can return if coverage falls.

10.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
10.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

10.q: Winston, 73, has a red area over his sacrum. You want to check whether it is blanching. Which method is recommended by NICE CG179?
o: Applying a barrier cream and checking in a week
Measuring the area's temperature with a probe
Rubbing the area firmly to restore circulation
Finger palpation or diascopy with a clear disc
10.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy (pressing a transparent disc onto the skin) to test whether erythema blanches. Non-blanching erythema can present as colour change or discolouration in darker skin tones.

n.0: Barrier cream does not assess blanching and a week's delay misses early damage.
n.1: Temperature probes are not the CG179 method for testing blanching.
n.2: Skin massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179 and can cause damage.

10.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
10.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

10.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
10.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

10.q: Bridget, 77, is admitted with an acute ischaemic stroke and is immobile. The healthcare assistant asks whether to fit anti-embolism stockings. What is the most appropriate VTE prevention?
o: Thigh-length anti-embolism stockings on both legs
Intermittent pneumatic compression to both legs
Leg elevation and ankle exercises with no device
Knee-length anti-embolism stockings on the weak leg
10.w: NICE NG89 1.4.2-1.4.3: do not offer anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis to people admitted for acute stroke; consider intermittent pneumatic compression for those who are immobile.

n.0: NICE advises not to offer anti-embolism stockings for VTE prevention after stroke.
n.2: IPC is recommended for immobile stroke patients; exercises alone are not enough.
n.3: Stockings of any length are not recommended for VTE prevention in acute stroke.

10.q: On a ward for older people, a nurse uses old photographs, wartime songs and conversation about his working life with Mr Black, 89, who has dementia. Which therapeutic intervention is this?
o: Positive behaviour support
Distraction and diversion
Reminiscence therapy
Solution-focused therapy
10.w: Annexe A 3.3: reminiscence therapies use memories, photographs and music to support wellbeing and identity.

n.0: PBS is a framework for understanding behaviour that challenges.
n.1: Distraction redirects attention from a stressor; this is planned recall of life history.
n.3: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and future goals.

10.q: Mrs Brennan, 66, has heart failure and wants to stay well at home. Which nursing action best supports her self-management?
o: Agree a written plan with her, including when to seek help
Tell her to rest and avoid activity until her next review
Arrange for a carer to manage her medicines at home
Ask her to phone the ward whenever she feels unwell
10.w: Proficiency P4.2: work in partnership to encourage shared decision making and support people to manage their own care. Code 2.1-2.3.

n.1: This is not person-centred and may not reflect her condition or goals.
n.2: Taking over her medicines reduces self-management without a reason to do so.
n.3: This keeps her dependent and does not build her own management skills.

10.q: Brian, 75, has advanced prostate cancer and wishes to die in the local hospice. He is now in the last days of life, and the hospice confirms no bed will be available this week. Brian asks the nurse whether he will be moving soon. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange discharge home as the next best setting and inform him afterwards
Defer the conversation until the hospice confirms a date for admission
Reassure him that a bed will be found soon so that he does not become distressed
Explain honestly why no hospice bed is available and agree another plan
10.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.3.8: when a dying person's wishes cannot be met, explain the reason to them and those important to them. Rec 1.2.4: give accurate information and avoid false optimism. The plan is then revised with Brian (rec 1.3.7).

n.0: Deciding a new setting without Brian breaches shared decision-making (NG31 1.3.1) and Code 4.
n.1: Delay leaves Brian uncertain in his last days; NG31 rec 1.3.8 says explain why a wish cannot be met.
n.2: This offers false hope; NG31 rec 1.2.4 asks for accurate information that avoids false optimism.

10.q: Mia, 6, is due her annual flu vaccine at school. Her parents tell the school nurse they decline the nasal spray vaccine because it contains porcine gelatine, which conflicts with their beliefs, but they want her protected. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that children under 9 must have the nasal vaccine to be protected
Give the nasal vaccine, explaining that gelatine is an inactive ingredient
Discuss the injected inactivated flu vaccine as an alternative for Mia
Advise them that Mia can have a flu vaccine once she reaches adulthood
10.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: the live attenuated influenza vaccine (Fluenz, nasal) contains porcine gelatine; if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used (Green Book chapter 19). UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent must be given freely by an appropriately informed person.

n.0: The schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used.
n.1: Giving it against the parents' refusal would be without valid consent (Green Book chapter 2).
n.3: An inactivated alternative is available now, so she need not go unprotected.

10.q: Nurse Holly has been asked to support a doctor who will tell Mr Pearce, 61, that his biopsy shows cancer. Which preparation is most appropriate?
o: Tell Mr Pearce the result first so the doctor can focus on treatment
Arrange a private room and hand her bleep to a colleague
Ask a relative to break the news before the doctor arrives
Use the bay with curtains drawn to save time
10.w: Annexe A 2.9: engage in difficult conversations including breaking bad news. Code 1.1 dignity, 5.1 privacy and 2.6 respond compassionately to distress.

n.0: Delivering the diagnosis outside the planned conversation risks giving it without support.
n.2: Results should be given by the clinical team, with the patient's consent to involve others.
n.3: Curtains do not give privacy; a private room protects dignity and confidentiality.

10.q: Vera, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and is keen to return home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker suggests giving her a full bed bath to save time. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone her wash until she can manage it without help
Set her up to wash what she can and help with the rest
Give her a full bed bath so that she can rest afterwards
Ask her daughter to wash her during the afternoon visit
10.w: Annexe B 4.3: assist with washing and dressing in a way that promotes independence. Encouraging Vera to do what she can, with help for the rest, maintains her abilities and dignity and supports her goal of going home (Code 1.2, 2.1).

n.0: Postponing hygiene leaves her needs unmet and risks skin problems.
n.2: A full bed bath removes the independence she needs to regain.
n.3: Hygiene is a fundamental of care that the nursing team is responsible for providing.

10.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
10.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

10.q: Victor, 81, has been taking clindamycin for 5 days for cellulitis. He now has four episodes of watery diarrhoea in 12 hours and is in a four-bed bay. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop the clindamycin and keep him in the bay with curtains drawn
Isolate him, send a stool sample and ask for an antibiotic review
Give loperamide and review his bowels at the end of the day
Send a stool sample and keep him in the bay until the result returns
10.w: NICE NG15 rec 1.1.35 highlights the risk of selecting for C. difficile with certain antibiotics. New diarrhoea on antibiotics should prompt isolation on suspicion (NIPCM ch 2.1), a stool sample and a prescriber review of the antibiotic.

n.0: Changing antibiotics is a prescriber decision, and staying in the bay exposes other patients.
n.2: Antimotility drugs are inappropriate in suspected C. difficile and delay diagnosis.
n.3: Isolation should not wait for the result, as C. difficile spreads to others in the bay.

10.q: Mr Price, 79, was alert this morning. At 14:00 his eyes are closed and he opens them and answers when the nurse speaks to him, but then drifts off again. His other observations are unchanged from earlier. How should his level of consciousness be recorded and scored on NEWS2?
o: V on ACVPU, scoring 1
V on ACVPU, scoring 3
A on ACVPU, scoring 0
P on ACVPU, scoring 3
10.w: ACVPU: Alert, new Confusion, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive. He responds to voice, so V. NEWS2 Chart 1 scores any of C, V, P or U as 3, which also triggers at least hourly monitoring and informing the medical team.

n.0: V is correct, but any score other than Alert scores 3 on NEWS2, not 1.
n.2: He is not alert, as his eyes are closed until he is spoken to.
n.3: He responds to voice, so a pain stimulus was not needed; P overstates the level.

10.q: Tessa, 45, is admitted with mild acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. She is not vomiting and says she is hungry. Her care plan was written as nil by mouth by default. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Request parenteral nutrition while she is in hospital
Offer clear fluids for 48 hours before any food
Ask for review, as food is not withheld without a clear reason
Keep her nil by mouth until her amylase level has returned to normal
10.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.5) says ensure people with acute pancreatitis are not made nil by mouth and do not have food withheld unless there is a clear reason, such as vomiting.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is for severe disease where enteral feeding has failed or is contraindicated.
n.1: Routine restriction to clear fluids is still withholding food without a clear reason.
n.3: NG104 advises against routine nil by mouth; normalising amylase is not a condition for eating.

10.q: Ms Ford, 50, is due to have surgery this afternoon. She is restless, keeps asking the same questions and says she cannot stop thinking she will not wake up. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
o: Give her a leaflet about the operation and leave her to rest
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe a sedative premedication
Tell her that modern anaesthetics are very safe and move on
Sit with her, explore her fears and explain what will happen
10.w: NMC proficiency P4.8 requires nurses to initiate interventions for common symptoms including anxiety. Listening, exploring specific fears and giving clear information are first-line, person-centred interventions for pre-operative anxiety.

n.0: A leaflet without discussion leaves her specific fears unexplored.
n.1: Medication may be considered later, but non-drug measures come first for anxiety with normal observations.
n.2: Brief reassurance without exploring her fears does not address her anxiety.

10.q: A nurse is carrying out a whole-body systems assessment of Mr Burns, 80, who has been bedbound for several days. On the skin review she finds a red area over his sacrum that does not blanch with light finger pressure. What should she do?
o: Record it as a category 2 pressure ulcer and apply a dressing
Reassess it at his next weekly skin inspection
Massage the area to restore its circulation and recheck it tomorrow
Start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck the skin at least 2-hourly
10.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy to test blanching; if non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved. A systems assessment includes skin (Annexe B 2.7).

n.0: Intact non-blanching erythema is a category 1 finding, not category 2, which involves partial-thickness skin loss.
n.1: Weekly review is too infrequent; CG179 requires at least 2-hourly reassessment.
n.2: Massaging pressure-damaged skin can cause further harm, and a day's delay is too long.

10.q: Annette, 64, has COPD with MRC grade 3 breathlessness. She has stopped going to the shops because she feels too breathless and sees herself as limited. She is on LAMA+LABA with good technique. Which referral is most appropriate?
o: Home non-invasive ventilation assessment
Respiratory physiotherapy for airway clearance
Long-term oxygen therapy assessment
Pulmonary rehabilitation
10.w: NICE NG115: offer pulmonary rehabilitation to people with COPD who view themselves as functionally disabled, usually MRC grade 3 and above.

n.0: Home NIV is for chronic hypercapnic failure, which is not described here.
n.1: Airway clearance helps sputum problems; it is not the structured programme she needs.
n.2: LTOT is assessed on blood gas criteria, not on functional disability alone.

10.q: During a teaching session on health economics, a student nurse asks what a quality-adjusted life year (QALY) measures. Which answer is correct?
o: A patient's own rating of their satisfaction with care, scored from 0 to 1
Length of life adjusted for its quality, where 1 is a year in full health
The cost to the NHS of keeping one person in hospital for a year
The number of years a person lives after receiving a treatment
10.w: A QALY combines quantity and quality of life: one year in perfect health counts as 1 QALY, and years lived in poorer health are weighted below 1. NICE uses cost per QALY gained to judge cost-effectiveness (P7.3 principles of health economics; FACTS S-NICETH).

n.0: A QALY uses health-related quality of life, not satisfaction with care.
n.2: This is a cost measure; a QALY measures health benefit, not cost.
n.3: Survival alone ignores quality of life, which the QALY adjusts for.

10.q: Ellen, 77, who had C. difficile infection, has been discharged home from a single room. The domestic team asks the nurse what terminal cleaning is required. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Use detergent wipes on surfaces and send the curtains as used linen
Clean with a 10,000 ppm available chlorine solution and leave the curtains in place
Clean with neutral detergent and change the curtains at the next routine change
Remove the curtains as infectious linen and clean with 1,000 ppm available chlorine
10.w: NIPCM ch 2.3 terminal decontamination: bag and remove waste, manage curtains and bedding as infectious linen, decontaminate equipment, then clean with a combined detergent and 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or detergent followed by 1,000 ppm), working from high to low and least to most contaminated.

n.0: Curtains from an infectious patient's room are infectious linen, and wipes alone are not a terminal clean.
n.1: 10,000 ppm is the strength for blood spills; terminal cleaning uses 1,000 ppm, and curtains are removed.
n.2: Detergent alone does not meet the terminal clean standard, and curtains from an isolation room are removed as infectious linen.

10.q: A community nurse is identifying people on her caseload who meet the NICE NG56 definition of multimorbidity. Which person meets the definition?
o: Carol, 58, who has well-controlled type 1 diabetes
Derek, 71, recovering from a wrist fracture and a chest infection
Elaine, 63, who has hypertension treated with three medicines
Brian, 66, who has hearing loss and chronic back pain
10.w: NG56 1.1.1: multimorbidity is 2 or more long-term health conditions, which can include sensory impairment such as hearing loss and symptom complexes such as chronic pain. Brian has two long-term conditions.

n.0: Carol has one long-term condition.
n.1: A healing fracture and a chest infection are acute problems, not long-term conditions.
n.2: Several medicines for one condition is still a single long-term condition.

10.q: Joan, 79, has taken alendronic acid for osteoporosis for 3 years. She has multimorbidity and asks the practice nurse whether she must keep taking it. What should the nurse explain, in line with NICE NG56?
o: It must continue lifelong to keep protecting her bones from fracture
Further benefit after 3 years is unproven, so discuss stopping
It should stop now, because 3 years is the maximum licensed course
It should continue for 10 years before any review is considered
10.w: NG56 1.6.16: tell people who have taken a bisphosphonate for at least 3 years that there is no consistent evidence of further benefit from continuing for another 3 years, or of harm from stopping; discuss stopping, including patient choice, fracture risk and life expectancy.

n.0: NG56 specifically suggests discussing stopping after 3 years.
n.2: Stopping is a shared decision based on fracture risk and choice, not a fixed maximum.
n.3: NG56 sets the discussion at 3 years, not 10.

10.q: Edna, 68, has fatigue and mild breathlessness. Her NT-proBNP is 850 ng/L. What is the appropriate referral timeframe for specialist assessment and echocardiography?
o: Within 2 weeks
Within 6 weeks
No referral, as heart failure is excluded
Within 24 hours
10.w: NICE NG106: NT-proBNP between 400 and 2,000 ng/L, refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks.

n.0: 2 weeks is for NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L.
n.2: Heart failure is unlikely below 400 ng/L; 850 ng/L needs referral.
n.3: This is not an NG106 timeframe for suspected chronic heart failure.

10.q: Ali, 64, weighs 80 kg and has sepsis from a chest infection. He has a catheter, and his NEWS2 is 3 with no change in the last hour. His urine output has been 25, 22 and 20 mL in the last 3 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Flush the catheter and recheck output in 4 hours
Escalate the falling urine output to the medical team now
Increase his oral fluid encouragement and recheck at handover
Wait until he has been below 40 mL/hour for 6 hours
10.w: Two steps: his threshold is 0.5 x 80 = 40 mL/hour and output is well below it and falling. NICE NG148 (1.2.2) requires systems to recognise and respond to oliguria because NEWS2 does not score urine output, and sepsis is an AKI risk factor; prompt escalation allows treatment before AKI is established.

n.0: Checking for a blocked catheter is reasonable, but a 4-hour delay before escalation is unsafe.
n.2: Oral fluids may help but a falling output in sepsis needs medical review, not deferral to handover.
n.3: The 6-hour figure defines AKI; waiting for it delays treatment of a deteriorating septic patient.

10.q: An integrated frailty service involves a hospital, community nursing, social care and a voluntary sector partner. The service lead, Ade, wants to evaluate the quality of people's experience of care across the whole pathway. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Measure the average length of hospital stay for people in the service
Compare each organisation's complaint numbers separately for the past year
Ask people and families for feedback on their whole journey across services
Survey staff in each organisation about how well they work together
10.w: Evaluating the experience of complex care means asking the people who receive it, and their families, about the whole journey, including transitions between services (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Length of stay is an efficiency measure, not a measure of people's experience.
n.1: Complaints in separate organisations show only part of the picture and miss the transitions between services.
n.3: Staff views are useful but do not describe the experience of people using the service.

10.q: Arthur, 79, has taken regular co-codamol 30/500 for back pain for two years. At a medication review he says he is unsure it helps and has been badly constipated. Which next step reflects NICE NG56?
o: Continue it and add a regular laxative to treat the constipation
Discuss reducing or stopping it and plan a review of the effects
Switch to an equivalent dose of tramadol to reduce constipation
Stop it today because he is unsure whether it is helping him
10.w: NG56 1.6.12: ask whether symptom-relieving treatments give benefit or harm. If the person is unsure of benefit or is experiencing harm, discuss reducing or stopping the treatment and plan a review of any changes, including whether to restart.

n.0: Adding a laxative adds to his treatment burden without addressing doubtful benefit.
n.2: Tramadol is also an opioid with constipation and other risks, and does not address the lack of benefit.
n.3: Stopping abruptly without discussion or a planned review risks withdrawal and loses shared decision making.

10.q: In a GP surgery waiting room, the practice nurse notices Colin, 56, coughing repeatedly into his hands. He has a fever and says he has no tissues. Other patients are seated close by. Which action best applies respiratory and cough hygiene?
o: Give tissues, a bin and a facemask, and seat him at least 1 metre from others
Ask him to cough into his hands and seat him at least 2 metres from others
Give him an FFP3 respirator to wear until he is called in for his appointment
Ask him to wait outside the building in his car until the nurse is ready to see him
10.w: NIPCM ch 1.3 and ch 2: cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue, dispose of it promptly and clean hands; outpatients with respiratory symptoms should be asked to wear a facemask if tolerated and be separated from others by at least 1 metre. Prioritising his appointment also helps.

n.1: Coughing into hands contaminates them; the crook of the arm is the fallback, and the NIPCM distance is 1 metre, not the pandemic-era 2 metres.
n.2: NIPCM states an FFP3 respirator must not be worn by an infectious patient, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
n.3: Sending a febrile patient to wait outside delays assessment and is not a standard respiratory hygiene measure.

10.q: Mr Albert King, 81, has heart failure, type 2 diabetes, COPD and osteoarthritis. He takes 14 different medicines and has had two falls this month. The community nurse visits. What is the most appropriate next step to address his complex needs?
o: Remove the medicines he finds hardest to swallow from his list
Advise him to stop his diuretic on days when he feels dizzy
Request a structured medication review with his GP or pharmacist
Refer him to the falls clinic and leave the medicines unchanged
10.w: Polypharmacy with multiple long-term conditions increases the risk of falls and adverse effects. A structured medication review, including psychotropic and cardiovascular drugs, is part of falls assessment (NICE NG249; NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation; P7.5 comorbidities and complex needs).

n.0: Nurses without prescribing responsibility for him must not stop prescribed medicines on swallowing difficulty alone; the issue needs review.
n.1: Advising him to stop a diuretic without prescriber review risks fluid overload.
n.3: A falls referral is reasonable, but leaving medicines unreviewed ignores a likely contributing factor.

10.q: A nurse is preparing a teaching session on how childhood adversity affects adult health. In the Welsh ACE study, how much more likely were adults with four or more ACEs to be high-risk drinkers than adults with no ACEs?
o: About 4 times
About 20 times
About 2 times
About 11 times
10.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): compared with people with no ACEs, those with 4+ ACEs were 4 times more likely to be a high-risk drinker, 6 times more likely to smoke, 11 times more likely to have smoked cannabis and 20 times more likely to have been incarcerated.

n.1: Twenty times relates to having been incarcerated, not high-risk drinking.
n.2: The study reported a fourfold, not twofold, increase in high-risk drinking.
n.3: Eleven times relates to having smoked cannabis, not high-risk drinking.

10.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
10.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

10.q: Mr Hussain, 69, has died on a medical ward after an expected death. The death is not being referred to the coroner. His family tell the nurse that their faith requires family members to wash his body and that they would like to do this themselves. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that hospital policy requires staff to wash all deceased patients
Leave the washing to the family and support them with the rest of his care
Ask the mortuary staff to wash him before he is released to the family
Wash him before the family arrive so that they are spared any distress
10.w: Hospice UK Care after death guidance (edition 5.2, 2025): wash the deceased unless requested not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons, or the death is being referred to the coroner; key contacts may wish to assist and should be supported. NMC Code 1.3 and 1.5: recognise diversity and individual choice, and respect and uphold people's human rights.

n.0: Care after death guidance says wash the deceased unless asked not to for spiritual, religious or cultural reasons.
n.2: Washing by mortuary staff would also override the family's wish to carry out the washing themselves.
n.3: This disregards the family's stated religious wishes, which the guidance says must be respected.

10.q: Ida, 79, is being fed through a nasogastric tube. During the feed she starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
o: Slow the feed rate and recheck her saturation
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Check the tube length mark and continue feeding
10.w: Sudden coughing, breathlessness and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or tube misplacement. Stop the feed, sit her upright, give oxygen and get urgent help (Annexe B 5.7; misplaced tubes are a Never Event).

n.0: Continuing a slower feed risks further aspiration.
n.1: Flushing adds more fluid to a possibly misplaced tube.
n.3: Continuing feeding is unsafe until the cause is established.

11.q: Code standard 19.2 asks nurses to take account of current evidence and knowledge about human factors. During preceptorship, Jade is asked which definition of human factors the Code refers to. Which is correct?
o: The physical and mental health conditions that may affect a registrant's fitness to practise safely
The personal values and beliefs that staff bring to their work and that can influence patient care
The study of individual mistakes so that staff responsible for errors can be identified and retrained
Environmental, organisational and job factors, and individual characteristics that affect behaviour at work
11.w: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors refer to environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way which can affect health and safety (P5.2).

n.0: Health and fitness to practise is covered by Code 20.9 and NMC processes, not by the definition of human factors.
n.1: Personal beliefs are addressed by Code 20.7; the human factors definition is wider and centres on work systems.
n.2: Human factors looks at how systems shape performance, not at singling out individuals for blame or retraining.

11.q: A ward manager has designed a new bedside safety checklist and wants every ward in the hospital to start using it next Monday. Arjun, the ward's quality improvement lead, is asked for advice. Which approach best reflects improvement methodology?
o: Pilot it on one ward for a year before deciding whether to use it more widely
Introduce it on all wards on Monday and audit compliance in six months
Test it with a few patients on one ward, measure, adapt and then scale up
Ask each ward manager to decide whether to adopt the checklist locally
11.w: The Model for Improvement uses rapid, small-scale PDSA cycles: test a change with a few patients or one shift, measure the effect, adapt, and build up to wider implementation once it works. This limits risk and builds learning and ownership (NHS England improvement guidance; P6.4, P6.6).

n.0: A single year-long pilot is slow; PDSA relies on short, repeated cycles that allow rapid adaptation.
n.1: Hospital-wide launch without testing risks spreading an untested change, and a six-month delay in measurement slows learning.
n.3: Leaving adoption to individual choice produces inconsistent practice without any evidence that the checklist works.

11.q: Mr Peter Clarke, 73, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. He can wash his face and upper body himself, although it takes him 20 minutes. A healthcare assistant suggests washing him to save time. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Agree for weekdays and let Mr Clarke wash himself at weekends when it is quieter
Ask the occupational therapist to decide whether Mr Clarke should wash himself
Agree, as it reduces the risk that Mr Clarke becomes tired before therapy
Encourage Mr Clarke to wash what he can, with prompts and help where needed
11.w: Nurses support people to maintain independence and avoid unnecessary interventions (P7.8). Doing for a person what they can do for themselves reduces function and dignity; rehabilitation depends on practice with support where needed (Code 1.2 fundamentals of care; Code 2).

n.0: Inconsistent practice slows recovery and is driven by staff convenience.
n.1: The occupational therapist may advise, but supporting independence in daily care is part of the nurse's role now.
n.2: Fatigue can be managed through planning; removing the activity undermines his rehabilitation.

11.q: Hilda, 77, has been admitted to a medical ward with a urinary tract infection. The nurse begins the NICE NG249 comprehensive falls assessment. Which assessment does NG249 include for hospital inpatients that it does not list for people in community settings?
o: Assessment for delirium
A structured medication review
Examination of footwear and feet
Assessment of visual impairment
11.w: NG249 1.2.2 lists delirium assessment for hospital inpatient and residential care settings only. Vision, medication review and footwear and foot condition are part of the comprehensive assessment in every setting.

n.1: Medication review is part of the comprehensive falls assessment in all settings.
n.2: Footwear and foot condition are assessed in all settings.
n.3: Visual impairment is assessed in all settings, not inpatients alone.

11.q: Mrs Joan Pike, 90, has social care needs and has been in hospital for a week with heart failure. Several professionals are involved and her daughter is confused about who to contact about discharge plans. According to NICE NG27, what should be in place?
o: A weekly letter to the daughter from the consultant in charge
A named discharge coordinator as the central point of contact
A rule that her daughter contacts the ward sister each morning
A referral to the hospital complaints team to manage contact
11.w: NICE NG27 (2015) recommends a hospital-based multidisciplinary team and a named discharge coordinator who is the central point of contact for the person and their family during discharge planning (P7.10; P4.18).

n.0: A weekly letter is too infrequent and does not provide a single coordinating contact.
n.2: This places responsibility on the family rather than giving them a coordinator.
n.3: Her daughter's confusion is a coordination problem, not a complaint to be managed.

11.q: Bill, 70, has diabetes, heart failure, COPD and gout. At his annual review the practice nurse counts 16 regular prescribed medicines. He manages them himself and has had no recent admissions. What does NICE NG56 advise?
o: Use it, because 15 or more regular medicines puts him at higher risk
Consider it, because 10 to 14 medicines is the trigger range
Defer it until he has an adverse event from a medicine
Use it, because the NG56 threshold is 12 or more regular medicines
11.w: NG56 1.3.4: use an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity for adults of any age prescribed 15 or more regular medicines, because they are likely to be at higher risk of adverse events and interactions. For 10 to 14 it is 'consider' (1.3.5).

n.1: 10 to 14 medicines leads to 'consider'; at 16 NG56 says 'use' the approach.
n.2: NG56 is proactive; waiting for harm defeats the purpose.
n.3: There is no 12-medicine threshold; the bands are 15 or more, and 10 to 14.

11.q: During a weekly stock check, two nurses find that the oxycodone 5 mg capsule count is one lower than the balance in the controlled drugs register. They have rechecked the cupboard and the most recent entries. What should they do next?
o: Report the discrepancy to the nurse in charge and pharmacy
Wait for the next weekly check to see if the count resolves
Borrow a capsule from another ward to restore the balance
Correct the register balance to match the stock and initial it
11.w: NICE NG46: stock check SOPs include reporting and managing discrepancies between stock and records. Once rechecked, unresolved discrepancies are reported promptly to the person in charge and pharmacy (and the CD accountable officer as required) and an incident is recorded.

n.1: Delaying a week loses the trail needed to investigate a possible diversion or error.
n.2: Borrowing stock conceals the loss and creates a second unrecorded transfer.
n.3: Altering a balance to hide a discrepancy falsifies a legal record.

11.q: Maureen, 87, lacks capacity and has life-threatening pneumonia. Her daughter holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney (LPA). The LPA does not contain express authority over life-sustaining treatment. Her daughter says she refuses intravenous antibiotics. How should the team proceed?
o: Delay treatment until the Court of Protection has confirmed that the LPA is valid
Ask the daughter to agree as nearest relative, which overrides the terms of the LPA
Follow the daughter's refusal, as the LPA is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
Decide in her best interests, consulting her daughter, who cannot refuse this treatment
11.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s9 (an LPA must be registered) and s11(7)-(8): a health and welfare attorney can give or refuse consent to treatment when the person lacks capacity, but this does not extend to life-sustaining treatment unless the LPA contains express provision. The team decide in Maureen's best interests (s4), consulting her daughter.

n.0: The registered LPA does not need court confirmation, and delaying antibiotics would put Maureen's life at risk.
n.1: There is no 'nearest relative' power under the MCA; decisions are made in Maureen's best interests.
n.2: Registration is required, but under MCA s11(8) an attorney cannot refuse life-sustaining treatment without express authority in the LPA.

11.q: Doreen, 70, with type 2 diabetes, is an inpatient after a fall. On admission foot examination the nurse finds a small, clean, shallow ulcer on her left big toe. She is afebrile, with no spreading redness and warm feet with palpable pulses. What is the most appropriate referral?
o: Refer to the foot protection service for review within 2 to 4 weeks
Refer to the community podiatrist at discharge
Refer to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours
Refer to the vascular team as an emergency
11.w: NICE NG19 (1.1.3) says refer an inpatient with a diabetic foot problem to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of the initial examination of the feet.

n.0: 2 to 4 weeks is the NG19 referral time for people at high risk without an active problem.
n.1: An active ulcer needs specialist assessment during the admission, not after discharge.
n.3: There are no signs of limb-threatening ischaemia or infection needing emergency vascular input.

11.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
11.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

11.q: Mr Mensah, 59, has Black African heritage and is recovering from pneumonia. His pulse oximeter reads 94% on air. He is a little more breathless than earlier. Which consideration is most important when interpreting this reading?
o: Oximeters underestimate saturations in people with dark skin
Oximeters can overestimate saturations in people with dark skin
His reading is within target, so his breathlessness is not significant
An SpO2 of 94% on air means oxygen therapy should be started
11.w: NICE NG253 (practical information on pulse oximeters): some oximeters underestimate or overestimate saturations, especially when borderline, and overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. His true saturation may be lower, so the reading should be interpreted with his clinical picture and escalated if concerned.

n.0: The reported error in people with dark skin is overestimation, not underestimation.
n.2: Increasing breathlessness is significant even when the oximeter reading is within target.
n.3: 94% on air is within the 94-98% target for most adults; starting oxygen is not indicated by the number alone.

11.q: Albert, 85, dies at home with his wife present at 02:10. The community nurse arrives at 03:30 and completes verification of his expected death at 03:45. His wife asks what time will be recorded as the time of death. What should the nurse tell her?
o: 03:30, when the nurse arrived at the house
02:10, when she noticed that he had stopped breathing
The time the doctor completes the death certificate
03:45, when verification of death was completed
11.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the time of verification is recognised as the official time of death and is recorded when verification is completed, not when the death is first reported. Families should be advised there may be a difference between the time of the last breath and the official time of death.

n.0: Arrival time is not the time of death; it is recorded when verification is completed.
n.1: The guidance says families should be told that the time of the last breath may differ from the official time of death.
n.2: The MCCD is completed later by a medical practitioner; the official time of death is the time of verification.

11.q: Iris, 74, has had a stroke and her swallow screen is not yet done. Her usual oral medicines, including atorvastatin and amlodipine, are due on the morning round. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the tablets with thickened fluid
Give the tablets with small sips of water
Crush the tablets and give them in a spoonful of yoghurt instead
Withhold oral doses, arrange the screen and ask about other routes
11.w: NICE NG128 1.6.1: no oral food, fluid or medication before a swallow screen. Withhold, document the reason, arrange the screen promptly and discuss essential medicines and alternative routes with the prescriber.

n.0: Thickened fluids are not used before a screen and specialist advice.
n.1: No oral medication is given before the swallow screen.
n.2: Crushing changes the medicine and is still oral intake before the screen.

11.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
11.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

11.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
11.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

11.q: Reg, 72, is admitted with three days of diarrhoea and vomiting and a creatinine rise from 90 to 150 micromol/L. His regular medicines are ramipril, omeprazole, atorvastatin and paracetamol. Which medicine should the nurse query with the prescriber first?
o: Atorvastatin
Ramipril
Omeprazole
Paracetamol
11.w: NICE NG148 (1.1.1, 1.2.14) lists ACE inhibitors among drugs that can cause or worsen AKI and advises considering temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in people with diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis until stable. Pharmacist advice on dosing is also recommended (1.2.13).

n.0: Atorvastatin does not reduce renal perfusion and is not in the NG148 list.
n.2: Omeprazole is not among the nephrotoxic drugs NICE asks to be paused in acute dehydrating illness.
n.3: Paracetamol at normal doses is not among the nephrotoxic drugs listed in NG148.

11.q: Doreen, 70, gave consent for a two-dose shingles vaccine course at her first appointment. She now attends for the second dose. Nothing has changed in her health and no new information about the vaccine has emerged. What should the nurse do about consent?
o: Check that she is still happy to proceed, then give the second dose
Obtain fresh written consent from her before giving the second dose
Ask her GP to confirm the consent given at her first appointment
Give the dose without discussion, as consent covers the whole course
11.w: UKHSA Green Book chapter 2, Consent (27 October 2025): consent is a process; it may be withdrawn at any time. Where consent has been obtained for a full course it is not necessary to seek consent again for each vaccine unless new information has come to light, but it is good practice to check the person is content to proceed at each stage.

n.1: Where consent was obtained for a full course, it need not be sought again for each dose unless new information arises.
n.2: Consent is between Doreen and the person giving the vaccine; GP confirmation is not required.
n.3: The Green Book says it is good practice to check the person is content to proceed at each stage.

11.q: Gary, 52, tells the nurse he is thinking of paying for a private 'full body' screening scan because 'the NHS does not screen for enough things'. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: NHS programmes are offered where benefits are judged to outweigh harms
Private screening tests are more accurate than NHS screening tests
All private screening tests are approved by the UK National Screening Committee
Each GP practice chooses which screening tests to offer its patients
11.w: NHS website, NHS screening (England): the UK National Screening Committee advises the NHS on which screening programmes to offer and recommends screening only when the benefits to the group offered outweigh the harms; some commercial tests are not recommended because it is not clear that benefits outweigh harms.

n.1: There is no basis for this; some private tests are not recommended because benefits may not outweigh harms.
n.2: Some private tests are not recommended by the UK NSC.
n.3: The UK NSC advises the NHS in all four nations on which screening programmes to offer.

11.q: Hassan, 54, is prescribed 7.5 mg of an intramuscular medicine. The ampoule contains 10 mg in 2 mL. The nurse works out the volume to draw up and a colleague is available. What volume is needed, and what should happen before administration?
o: 1.5 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
2.67 mL, then ask the colleague to check the calculation independently
0.75 mL, then give it straight away as the colleague is busy
3.75 mL, then record the calculation in the notes and give it
11.w: Volume = (dose required / stock strength) x stock volume = (7.5 / 10) x 2 = 1.5 mL. RPS/RCN guidance (2019) para 15 says any calculations needed are double checked, where practicable, by a second person.

n.1: 2.67 mL inverts the fraction (10 / 7.5 x 2); a check would catch it, but the volume is wrong.
n.2: 0.75 mL omits multiplying by the 2 mL volume, and skipping an available second check is unsafe.
n.3: 3.75 mL comes from dividing the dose by the stock volume (7.5 / 2) instead of using the formula, and no second check is made.

11.q: George, 80, lives in a care home and has been assessed as having capacity to make decisions about his medicines. He refuses his atorvastatin, saying he does not want it at his age. His daughter asks the nurse to crush it into his yoghurt without telling him. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a best interests meeting about covert administration
Agree after the GP signs a covert administration form
Respect his refusal, record it and inform the prescriber
Agree, as the statin is in his long-term interests
11.w: Covert administration is used only for people who actively refuse medication and lack capacity, under an agreed plan (RPS/RCN 2019 para 21; NICE SC1). George has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (MCA 2005 s1(4): an unwise decision does not mean lack of capacity), documented and shared with the prescriber.

n.0: A best interests process applies to people who lack capacity; George has capacity.
n.1: A GP's signature cannot authorise covert administration to a person who has capacity.
n.3: Giving medicine covertly to a person with capacity is unlawful, whatever the benefit.

11.q: A practice nurse is preparing a short presentation for a safeguarding update and reads the 2015 Welsh study of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) among adults. Roughly what proportion of the adults surveyed reported four or more ACEs?
o: About 47%
About 30%
About 5%
About 14%
11.w: Public Health Wales/LJMU, Adverse Childhood Experiences and their impact on health-harming behaviours in the Welsh adult population (Bellis et al., 2015): 47% of Welsh adults reported at least one ACE and 14% reported four or more.

n.0: Forty-seven per cent reported at least one ACE, not four or more.
n.1: Thirty per cent is not a figure from the study for 4+ ACEs.
n.2: Five per cent was the prevalence of individual ACEs such as parental drug use or incarceration.

11.q: Mr Doyle, 55, tells his community mental health nurse that he has been saving his prescribed tablets and has a large supply at home, as he 'might need them one day'. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Remove the tablets from his home while he is out of the room
Tell his GP to reduce his prescription at the next medication review
Note his comment in the record and review it at the next visit
Discuss removing the tablets with him and agree a plan to keep him safe
11.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with therapeutic collaboration or negotiation to keep the person safe. A stockpile with this comment is an immediate safety concern needing collaborative action and escalation.

n.0: Covert removal undermines trust; NG225 describes collaborative negotiation, not unilateral action.
n.1: Waiting for a future review leaves the means available now.
n.2: Delaying to the next visit fails to act on an immediate safety concern.

11.q: Nadia is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound for Doreen, 81. Splashing of wound fluid towards her face is likely. There are no full-face visors on the ward. Which facial protection should Nadia wear?
o: A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection
A Type II surgical mask and her own prescription glasses
A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask without eye protection
An FFP3 respirator without separate eye protection
11.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: where splashing of blood or body fluids onto the face is anticipated and a full-face visor is not available, wear a Type IIR FRSM with eye protection. Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.

n.1: A Type II mask is not fluid resistant, and corrective spectacles do not count as eye protection.
n.2: The mask protects the nose and mouth, but the eyes remain exposed to the expected splashes.
n.3: An FFP3 respirator protects against airborne particles; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.

11.q: Nadia, 23, is being treated for DKA. Her first litre of 0.9% sodium chloride has run in. The next litre is due and her serum potassium is now 4.2 mmol/L. According to the JBDS protocol, how much potassium chloride should the next litre contain?
o: 20 mmol
None
40 mmol
Senior review for additional potassium
11.w: JBDS 02 (2023) potassium guide: above 5.5 mmol/L give none; 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L give 40 mmol per litre; below 3.5 mmol/L senior review because more is needed. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so levels fall during treatment.

n.0: 20 mmol per litre is not the JBDS replacement for a potassium of 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L.
n.1: No potassium is added when the level is above 5.5 mmol/L.
n.3: Senior review for extra potassium applies when the level falls below 3.5 mmol/L.

11.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
11.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

11.q: Peter, 74, has pancreatic cancer and is in the last days of life at home. He can no longer swallow tablets. Over the past 24 hours the community nurse has given three 'as required' subcutaneous doses of morphine for pain, each giving relief for a few hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue 'as required' doses and review the plan in 72 hours
Ask his wife to give oral morphine solution between visits
Discuss with the prescriber starting a continuous syringe pump
Give the next 'as required' doses by intramuscular injection
11.w: NICE NG31 (2015) rec 1.5.6: consider a syringe pump to deliver medicines for continuous symptom control if more than 2 or 3 doses of any 'as required' medicine have been given within 24 hours. Rec 1.5.5: avoid intramuscular injections.

n.0: Needing more than 2 or 3 doses in 24 hours is the NG31 trigger to consider a syringe pump; waiting 72 hours leaves pain poorly controlled.
n.1: Peter can no longer swallow safely, so the oral route is unsuitable (NG31 rec 1.5.4).
n.3: NICE NG31 rec 1.5.5 advises avoiding intramuscular injections in the last days of life; subcutaneous or intravenous routes are used.

11.q: A nurse consultant plans to randomly allocate patients to two different mouth care regimens to find out which reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia, aiming to publish the results. What does this project need before it starts?
o: Approval from the ward manager as a service evaluation
Registration as a clinical audit with the trust audit team
Informal agreement from patients at the bedside
Approval as research, normally with NHS ethics committee review
11.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (2022): research aims to produce generalisable or transferable new knowledge, may involve randomisation to interventions and normally requires NHS REC review.

n.0: Service evaluation does not allocate patients to interventions; this design is research.
n.1: Random allocation to interventions to produce generalisable findings makes it research, not audit.
n.2: Research needs formal approval and documented informed consent, not informal agreement.

11.q: Sophie is about to insert a peripheral intravenous cannula into the forearm of Malik, 45. She has selected the vein and performed hand hygiene. According to NICE CG139, how should she prepare the skin at the insertion site?
o: Clean with a 70% alcohol wipe, then palpate the vein again
Clean with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride and pat the skin dry with gauze
Apply povidone-iodine and wipe it off before inserting
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
11.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate the skin at the insertion site with chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. The solution must dry to work, and the cleaned site is not re-palpated.

n.0: Re-palpating the vein after cleaning contaminates the Key-Site, and alcohol alone is not the CG139 product.
n.1: Saline cleans but does not decontaminate the skin.
n.2: CG139 specifies chlorhexidine in alcohol; wiping antiseptic off before it has acted also defeats it.

11.q: Leah, 34, attends the emergency department after self-harm. A colleague completes a self-harm risk scale, which places her at low risk, and suggests she can be discharged on that basis. According to NICE NG225, what should happen?
o: Assess Leah's needs and agree a safety plan with her, not using the scale
Repeat the scale in four hours and discharge Leah if it is unchanged
Discharge Leah, as the scale places her in the low-risk group
Admit Leah for observation until a medium-risk score can be ruled out
11.w: NICE NG225 (2022) advises not to use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Care is based on a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan developed with the person.

n.1: Repeating an invalid tool does not make it a valid basis for discharge.
n.2: NG225 says scales must not be used to decide discharge; a low score gives false reassurance.
n.3: NG225 advises against global low, medium or high risk stratification; admission is decided by assessed needs, not a score band.

11.q: Lorraine, 61, has a chronic productive cough and exertional breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry is performed. Which result confirms airflow obstruction consistent with COPD?
o: FEV1/FVC ratio above 0.8
FeNO level of 50 ppb or more
FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7
FEV1 increase of 12% after bronchodilator
11.w: NICE NG115: airflow obstruction is defined as a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7, interpreted with the clinical picture.

n.0: A ratio above 0.8 is within the normal range and does not show obstruction.
n.1: A raised FeNO supports a diagnosis of asthma, not COPD.
n.3: Significant reversibility suggests asthma rather than confirming COPD.

11.q: Marta, a registered nurse, asks Lewis, a healthcare assistant who is trained and assessed in clinical observations, to record observations on three stable patients in her bay. What must Marta do to delegate this task appropriately?
o: Tell Lewis which patients to observe and leave the escalation decisions to him
Explain what to report and when, check he understands and review the results
Ask Lewis to record the observations and to calculate the NEWS2 for each patient
Ask Lewis to observe the patients if he feels confident and has time this morning
11.w: Code 11.1-11.3: delegate only within the other person's competence, make sure they understand the instructions and are supervised and supported, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. AnnexA.4.1.2 requires clear instructions and checking understanding when delegating. Marta remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for reviewing findings.

n.0: Escalation decisions require registered nurse assessment; leaving them to Lewis passes on responsibility Marta cannot delegate in this way.
n.2: Recording a score without clear thresholds for reporting and review does not meet Code 11.2-11.3.
n.3: Delegation must be clear and planned; leaving it to his confidence and time does not ensure the care is done.

11.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Send them by WhatsApp to the community nurse's phone
Print them and post them by second class mail
Email them from her personal account as it is faster
Send them through an approved, secure NHS system
11.w: Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; Caldicott principles; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

n.0: Personal messaging apps are not approved secure systems for clinical data.
n.1: Post is slower and less secure than approved electronic routes.
n.2: Personal email breaches data security (Code 10.5).

11.q: Hamid, 34, has a history suggestive of asthma. His blood eosinophil count is normal and his FeNO is 56 ppb. How does this result guide diagnosis under NG245?
o: It needs a bronchial challenge test to confirm
It confirms asthma without further testing
