It is a normal result, so asthma is unlikely
It needs bronchodilator reversibility testing to confirm
11.w: NG245 (2024): in adults, diagnose asthma if the blood eosinophil count is above the reference range or FeNO is 50 ppb or more. If neither confirms it, measure bronchodilator reversibility, then PEF variability, then bronchial challenge.

n.0: Challenge testing comes later in the sequence, after reversibility and peak flow variability.
n.2: In adults, 50 ppb or more is raised and supports asthma.
n.3: Reversibility testing is the next step when eosinophils and FeNO do not confirm asthma.

11.q: A ward manager wants to check whether patients' falls risk assessments are completed within 6 hours of admission, as the trust policy requires, by reviewing 50 sets of notes. How should this project be classified?
o: Research, which needs NHS research ethics committee review
Health surveillance, which tracks outbreaks and health threats
Service evaluation, which judges a service without a standard
Clinical audit, which measures practice against a set standard
11.w: HRA 'Defining research' table (October 2022): clinical audit answers 'Does this service reach a predetermined standard?', uses care already in use and does not require REC review.

n.0: It tests no hypothesis and seeks no generalisable knowledge; it compares practice with an existing standard.
n.1: Surveillance monitors threats to population health, not compliance with a ward policy.
n.2: Service evaluation does not measure against a predetermined standard; this project does.

11.q: Daniel Morgan, 32, has a learning disability and is very anxious about needles. He missed his last two blood test appointments at a busy GP practice clinic. Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate for the practice nurse to offer?
o: Offer the first appointment of the day with extra time and easy read information
Ask his support worker to bring him in and stay outside the room during the test
Arrange for the test to be done when he next attends hospital as an inpatient
Book him into the next routine clinic slot and send a standard reminder letter
11.w: Equality Act 2010 s20 places a duty to make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people are not at a substantial disadvantage. A quiet first appointment, extra time and accessible information reduce anxiety and support his access (P3.7 principles of reasonable adjustments; P7.9; Accessible Information Standard).

n.1: A familiar support worker can help, but asking them to wait outside removes the support he may need.
n.2: Waiting for an unplanned admission denies him timely, equitable access to routine care.
n.3: Repeating the arrangement that has failed twice makes no adjustment for his disability.

11.q: Norman, 79, has severe COPD and is about to start NIV for hypercapnic respiratory failure. His notes contain no plan about what will happen if NIV does not work. He has capacity. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the medical team to agree and record a ceiling of care with him
Ask his daughter to decide what should happen if NIV fails
Record him as not for resuscitation because he has severe COPD
Start NIV and leave escalation planning until it has had time to work
11.w: NICE NG115: before starting NIV there should be a clear plan covering what to do if it fails, with the ceiling of treatment agreed and documented, involving the person (MCA: a person with capacity makes their own decisions).

n.1: He has capacity, so the discussion is with him; family do not decide for him.
n.2: Severity alone does not set a ceiling; decisions are made with him and the senior team.
n.3: NICE expects the plan, including what happens if NIV fails, to be agreed at the start.

11.q: Mrs Ali, 76, has delirium from a urinary infection. She can repeat back what the nurse has told her about a proposed blood transfusion, but she cannot relate the risks and benefits to her own situation when making a choice. Which part of the functional test of capacity is she unable to meet?
o: Communicating her decision to staff
Retaining the information
Understanding the information
Using or weighing the information
11.w: MCA 2005 s3(1): a person is unable to make a decision if unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the information, or communicate the decision. Mrs Ali understands and retains it but cannot use or weigh it in reaching a decision.

n.0: She can speak and express choices; the difficulty is in weighing the information.
n.1: She can recall the information when asked, so retention is not the problem described.
n.2: She can repeat back what she was told, which suggests she understands the information.

11.q: Rashid, 56, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes last year. He manages it with diet and modified-release metformin and has had no hypoglycaemia. He asks the practice nurse what HbA1c he should aim for. Which target is recommended?
o: 58 mmol/mol (7.5%)
53 mmol/mol (7.0%)
48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
64 mmol/mol (8.0%)
11.w: NICE NG28 (1.5.7, amended 2026) supports adults managed by diet and healthy living, with or without medicines not associated with hypoglycaemia such as metformin, to aim for an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%).

n.0: 58 mmol/mol is the level at which NG28 advises intensifying treatment, not the target.
n.1: 53 mmol/mol applies to people taking a medicine associated with hypoglycaemia, such as a sulfonylurea or insulin.
n.3: 64 mmol/mol is not an NG28 target; it would leave Rashid at higher risk of complications.

11.q: Albert, 86, has heart failure, COPD and osteoarthritis. He was admitted 6 hours ago with an acute exacerbation, is breathless at rest and drowsy. A student nurse wants to do a 4-metre gait speed test to complete his frailty assessment. What should the nurse advise?
o: Use a gait speed test now but halve the walking distance to 2 metres
Do the 4-metre gait test now while two staff are present to observe
Defer performance tests and gather his baseline history from family
Record him as CFS 8 based on how dependent he is today
11.w: NICE NG56 1.4.2-1.4.3: be cautious about assessing frailty in a person who is acutely unwell and do not use a physical performance tool in that situation. The CFS is scored on baseline function, so history from Albert's family about the previous 2 weeks is the safer source.

n.0: Shortening the walk still uses a physical performance tool during acute illness and is not a validated measure.
n.1: NG56 1.4.3 advises against physical performance tools while acutely unwell, and testing a breathless drowsy man risks a fall.
n.3: CFS reflects baseline about 2 weeks before illness, not current dependency, so scoring today overstates frailty.

11.q: Mr Price, 69, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and depression. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on air and he is struggling to finish sentences; his capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L. Which need should the nurse prioritise first?
o: His dietary intake and weight
His raised blood glucose
His low mood and anxiety
His breathing and oxygenation
11.w: When prioritising care for a person with comorbidities (P3.13), immediate threats to life come first. Severe hypoxaemia and breathlessness are an airway and breathing priority needing escalation and oxygen to a prescribed target; the other needs are addressed once he is stable.

n.0: Nutrition is important for recovery but is not the immediate priority.
n.1: A glucose of 11.2 mmol/L needs monitoring but is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxaemia.
n.2: His mood matters but is not the most urgent need while he is hypoxic.

11.q: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, Martin, 70, develops rigors, lower back pain and a temperature of 38.9°C (baseline 37.0°C). His blood pressure has fallen from 132/80 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the transfusion, keep venous access, recheck identity and call for urgent review
Continue the transfusion and give a prescribed antihistamine for the rigors
Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, remove the cannula and dispose of the unit in clinical waste
11.w: Features of a severe acute transfusion reaction (rigors, fever, loin pain, hypotension, possible ABO incompatibility) require the transfusion to be stopped immediately, venous access maintained for treatment, the patient's identity and unit rechecked, an ABCDE assessment and urgent medical review (NICE NG24 1.13; BSH). The unit is kept for investigation.

n.1: Continuing risks a fatal haemolytic reaction; antihistamines do not treat this.
n.2: Slowing the transfusion continues exposure to a possibly incompatible unit.
n.3: Venous access is needed for treatment, and the unit must be kept for laboratory investigation.

11.q: Leo, 19, is autistic and attends a busy emergency department with a wrist injury. He is covering his ears, rocking and becoming more distressed in the noisy waiting room. His triage category means he may wait two hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Suggest he returns tomorrow when the department is likely to be quieter
Move him up the triage queue ahead of patients with more urgent needs
Ask him to wait outside the department until a cubicle becomes free
Offer a quieter space to wait and explain clearly what will happen next
11.w: Reasonable adjustments remove disadvantage arising from disability without compromising others' safety: a quieter waiting space and clear, predictable information reduce sensory overload while clinical priority is maintained (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7; P7.9). Two steps: recognise sensory distress, then select a proportionate adjustment.

n.0: Delaying treatment of an injury is not a reasonable adjustment and may worsen the outcome.
n.1: Triage order is based on clinical urgency; changing it could harm patients with more urgent needs.
n.2: Sending him outside removes him from observation and is not an adjustment that maintains his care.

11.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium. He is shouting, pulling at his cannula and swinging his arms at staff. No one has been hurt yet. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request haloperidol as the first step to calm him down quickly
Restrain his arms so the cannula is not pulled out
Ask security to stay with him until he settles down
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and look for causes
11.w: NICE CG103: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk to themselves or others, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation; consider short-term haloperidol if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate. Underlying causes such as pain, retention or hypoxia should be sought (Annexe B 1.1.5).

n.0: Medication is considered when de-escalation fails or is inappropriate, not as the first step.
n.1: Physical restraint is a last resort and may worsen agitation and delirium.
n.2: Security presence is restrictive and does not address his distress or its cause.

11.q: Clive, 80, had an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) that was still active when he died on a cardiology ward. The registered nurse has verified his expected death. Which action relating to the device is the nurse's responsibility?
o: Instigate deactivation and tell the mortuary or funeral director about the device
Record the device in the notes, as no further action is needed after death
Ask his family to inform the funeral director that a device is present
Remove the device before Clive is transferred to the mortuary
11.w: Hospice UK/RCN RNVoEAD guidance (6th edition, 2024): the RN must instigate the process for deactivation of an implantable cardiac defibrillator where applicable, and must notify the funeral director or mortuary of any infections, radioactive implants, implantable devices and whether an ICD is still active.

n.1: An active ICD remains a hazard to people handling the body, so deactivation must be arranged.
n.2: Notifying the mortuary or funeral director is the verifying nurse's responsibility, not the family's.
n.3: Ward nurses do not remove implanted devices; the RN instigates deactivation and passes on the information.

11.q: Harold, 67, has stable heart failure after a recent admission. He is keen to get fitter but worried exercise will strain his heart. What should the nurse discuss with him?
o: Avoiding exercise until his ejection fraction has improved
A personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme
Bed rest for 6 weeks to reduce cardiac workload
Unsupervised gym training at the highest intensity he can
11.w: NICE NG106 1.11.1: offer people with heart failure a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme with psychological and educational components.

n.0: NICE recommends exercise-based rehabilitation rather than avoiding activity.
n.2: Prolonged rest leads to deconditioning and is not recommended.
n.3: Rehab is personalised and structured, not unsupervised maximal training.

11.q: Bill, 85, has advanced dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces, groans and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
o: A visual analogue scale explained slowly to him
A behavioural pain tool such as the Abbey pain scale
A 0-10 numerical rating scale completed by Bill himself
His daughter's estimate of his pain on a 0-10 scale
11.w: Where a person cannot reliably self-report, for example because of dementia or a learning disability, use a validated behavioural or observational pain assessment tool such as the Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (NICE NG31 principle; Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue scale still needs him to self-report, which he cannot reliably do.
n.2: Numerical self-report relies on abilities Bill no longer has.
n.3: Family insight is valuable, but a proxy number is not a validated assessment.

11.q: Lionel, 79, has had a stroke and cannot reposition himself. He is incontinent and his assessment shows he is at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer. His skin is currently intact. Under NICE CG179, what is the minimum frequency at which he should be helped to change position?
o: At least every 8 hours
At least every 6 hours
At least every 12 hours
At least every 4 hours
11.w: NICE CG179: reposition adults at risk at least every 6 hours, and adults at high risk at least every 4 hours.

n.0: Every 8 hours is longer than any CG179 interval.
n.1: Every 6 hours is the minimum for adults at risk, not high risk.
n.2: Every 12 hours is far longer than CG179 recommends.

11.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
11.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

11.q: Hilda, 74, has had a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. You aspirate gastric contents and test them on CE-marked pH paper. Which reading confirms gastric placement so that feeding can start?
o: pH 8.5 or above
pH 6.0 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 5.5 or below
11.w: NICE CG32: gastric tube position is confirmed by pH 5.5 or below on pH paper. Position must be confirmed after placement and before each use by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary (rec 1.7.17).

n.0: pH 8.5 is alkaline and suggests a non-gastric position.
n.1: pH 6.0 is above the 5.5 threshold and does not confirm gastric placement.
n.2: pH 7 or above may indicate the tube is in the lung or intestine.

11.q: Mrs Webb, 72, takes ibuprofen for arthritis. She vomits a moderate amount of dark brown material that looks like coffee grounds. Her pulse is 108 and her blood pressure is lower than earlier. What should the nurse do?
o: Send a stool sample to the laboratory for testing
Dispose of the vomit and offer her mouth care and a drink
Give an antiemetic and recheck all her observations in 4 hours
Escalate urgently as a possible upper GI bleed and keep a record
11.w: Coffee-ground vomit suggests partly digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed; NSAID use is a risk factor. With a rising pulse and falling blood pressure she needs urgent escalation (P3.12) and accurate recording of the amount and appearance (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: A stool sample does not address an acute bleed with haemodynamic change.
n.1: Disposing of it without escalation ignores a possible bleed; oral fluids may need withholding pending review.
n.2: An antiemetic does not address a possible bleed, and 4-hourly observations are too infrequent.

11.q: Chloe, a staff nurse, receives a police caution for shoplifting. It is not a protected caution. She is worried about her job. According to the Code, what must Chloe do?
o: Tell her employer, who will decide whether to inform the NMC
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell the NMC if the matter later leads to a criminal conviction
Declare it on her next revalidation health and character declaration
11.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, a conditional discharge or a finding of guilt for a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction).

n.0: Code 23.2 requires her to tell both the NMC and any employers herself.
n.2: Code 23.2 covers cautions and charges as well as convictions, so the duty arises now.
n.3: Waiting until revalidation could be years away; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as she can.

11.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
11.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

11.q: A community mental health nurse asks Leon, 27, "Think of a day recently when things were a little better. What was different about that day?" Which approach is the nurse using?
o: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Motivational interviewing
Reminiscence therapy
11.w: Annexe A 3.2: solution-focused therapies. Asking about exceptions, when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths.

n.0: CBT works on links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
n.2: MI explores ambivalence about change.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories to support wellbeing, mainly in older adults.

11.q: Joanne is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and is preparing to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she show over the three-year period?
o: 900 hours, including 450 for each registration
675 hours, as half of the second registration counts
1,350 hours, including 450 for each registration
450 hours across both registrations combined
11.w: NMC revalidation, practice hours (page updated 26/05/2021): 450 hours for one registration, 900 hours for nurse and midwife (450 each), 1,350 for triple registration.

n.1: There is no pro rata reduction; each registration needs its own 450 hours.
n.2: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as nurse, midwife and nursing associate.
n.3: 450 hours is the figure for a single registration; dual nurse and midwife registration requires 900.

11.q: Ben, a staff nurse on a respiratory ward, has developed red, cracked skin across the backs of both hands after several weeks of frequent hand hygiene. He asks his ward manager for advice. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Use soap and water instead of handrub for routine care until his hands heal
Seek occupational health advice and use his own emollient regularly, including on breaks
Apply hand cream from the communal tub in the staff room after each patient contact
Wear non-sterile gloves for routine care tasks so his skin is protected
11.w: NIPCM ch 1.2 skin care: dry hands thoroughly, use an emollient hand cream regularly (for example during breaks and off duty), do not use communal tubs, and staff with skin problems should seek advice from occupational health or their GP. Damaged skin harbours organisms and may need further intervention or reporting.

n.0: Alcohol handrub is recommended for routine hand hygiene and is generally less drying than repeated soap and water.
n.2: NIPCM advises against communal tubs of hand cream because they can become contaminated.
n.3: Gloves are not recommended where no body fluid exposure is anticipated; overuse increases infection risk and does not replace hand hygiene.

11.q: Molly, 34, takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and is booked for elective major knee surgery in 6 weeks. At her preoperative assessment, what advice about the pill should the nurse discuss?
o: Consider stopping it 4 weeks before, with other contraception
Stop it 2 weeks before surgery and use no contraception
Stop it on the morning of surgery and restart it on discharge
Continue it, as surgery does not change her VTE risk
11.w: NICE NG89 (1.3.13) advises people to consider stopping oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives or HRT 4 weeks before elective surgery because of VTE risk, and to give advice on alternative contraception if stopped.

n.1: 2 weeks is shorter than NICE advises, and stopping without contraception risks pregnancy.
n.2: Stopping on the day does not reduce the oestrogen-related clotting risk in time.
n.3: Oestrogen-containing contraception adds to the VTE risk from surgery and immobility.

11.q: Grace, 66, attends the emergency department feeling unwell with rigors. Her last dose of chemotherapy was 3 weeks ago. The triage healthcare assistant says neutropenic sepsis is unlikely because treatment 'was too long ago'. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Suspect it, as treatment within the last 48 hours counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 7 days counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 14 days counts
Suspect it, as treatment within the last 30 days counts
11.w: NICE NG253 1.1.10: suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell and are having or have had systemic anticancer treatment within the last 30 days. Grace's chemotherapy was 21 days ago.

n.0: 48 hours is far shorter than the 30-day window.
n.1: 7 days is not the NG253 window, and Grace's treatment would wrongly fall outside it.
n.2: 14 days is not the NG253 window, and her treatment would wrongly fall outside it.

11.q: Fiona, 26, knows her best peak flow is 500 L/min. During an attack her PEF is 150 L/min. She can speak in full sentences and her SpO2 is 95%. What is her PEF as a percentage of best, and how is this classified?
o: 30%, which is life-threatening
30%, which is classed as acute severe
33%, which is classed as acute severe
40%, which is classed as acute severe
11.w: Two steps: 150 / 500 x 100 = 30%. SIGN 158: PEF below 33% best or predicted is a life-threatening feature.

n.1: Acute severe is PEF 33-50%; 30% is below 33% and so is life-threatening.
n.3: The calculation is wrong: 150/500 x 100 = 30%.

11.q: Clive, 62, is eating, drinking and taking tablets on day 1 after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His chart shows intravenous paracetamol 1 g four times daily. What is the most appropriate action by the nurse?
o: Ask the prescriber to review a switch to oral paracetamol
Give the IV dose, as it works faster than oral paracetamol
Omit paracetamol, as he can now take ibuprofen instead
Give the IV dose and add oral paracetamol for breakthrough pain
11.w: NICE NG180 (1.6.6) says do not offer intravenous paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine. Clive can swallow, so the route should be reviewed with the prescriber.

n.1: Speed of onset does not justify IV use when oral medicines can be taken, per NG180.
n.2: NG180 uses paracetamol and an NSAID together in multimodal analgesia, not one in place of the other.
n.3: Combining IV and oral paracetamol risks exceeding the maximum daily dose.

11.q: A community nursing team wants to improve the written information given to people after a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Which approach best involves people who use the service in this improvement?
o: Adapt a leaflet that a neighbouring trust has used for several years
Co-design the information with people who have recently been diagnosed
Ask the diabetes consultant to approve the content before it is printed
Ask the team's nurses to agree the content at the next team meeting
11.w: P6.9 requires nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience of the service makes information relevant, accessible and person-centred (Code 2.1 work in partnership).

n.0: Borrowing another organisation's leaflet may help, but it does not involve local service users in the improvement.
n.2: Clinical approval checks accuracy but does not involve people who use the service.
n.3: Staff agreement alone excludes the people the information is for.

11.q: Priya, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant and attends her antenatal appointment in October, during the flu season. She has had no vaccines in this pregnancy. According to the UKHSA schedule, which vaccines should she be offered now?
o: Flu, pertussis and RSV vaccines, all at this appointment
Pertussis vaccine now, with the flu vaccine after the birth
RSV vaccine now, with the pertussis vaccine from 28 weeks
Inactivated flu vaccine and the pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
11.w: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule from 1 September 2026: in pregnancy, inactivated flu vaccine at any stage during the flu season; pertussis (Tdap) from 16 weeks (ideally before 32 weeks but may be given later); RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks.

n.0: RSV vaccine is offered from 28 weeks of pregnancy, so it is not due at 20 weeks.
n.1: Inactivated flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season.
n.2: This reverses the timings: pertussis is from 16 weeks and RSV from 28 weeks.

11.q: Harriet, 70, has an acute ischaemic stroke confirmed on CT, with haemorrhage excluded. Her symptoms started 3 hours ago. What is the time limit for giving thrombolysis?
o: 24 hours from onset
3 hours from onset
4.5 hours from onset
6 hours from onset
11.w: NICE NG128 1.4 and TA990: thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of known onset once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded.

n.0: 24 hours is the extended thrombectomy window for selected people.
n.1: The licensed window was extended to 4.5 hours.
n.3: 6 hours is the standard thrombectomy window, not thrombolysis.

11.q: Mr Brennan, 74, was assessed last month as lacking capacity to manage his complex investments. Today he tells the nurse he would like fish rather than chicken for lunch and wants to wear his own clothes. Which statement is correct?
o: His financial attorney should make these choices on his behalf
He lacks capacity for all decisions until a new assessment is completed
He can choose his lunch but not his clothing without an assessment
He may be able to make these decisions, as capacity is decision-specific
11.w: MCA 2005 s2(1): lack of capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time. Being unable to manage complex investments says nothing about everyday choices, which he is presumed able to make (s1(2)).

n.0: A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over personal welfare choices such as food or clothing.
n.1: Incapacity is not global; a finding about one decision does not transfer to others.
n.2: There is no basis for treating clothing differently from food; both are everyday choices he is presumed able to make.

11.q: Cyril, 82, has heart failure and is on intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily. His morning bloods show potassium 3.1 mmol/L (previously 4.0). He feels weak. What best explains this result, and what should the nurse do?
o: IV furosemide dilutes the blood; increase his oral fluid intake
Loop diuretics cause potassium retention; repeat the bloods tomorrow
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; inform the prescriber now
Loop diuretics raise urinary potassium loss; give a banana with lunch
11.w: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urinary sodium and potassium excretion, so hypokalaemia is an expected effect (P4.17, applying pharmacology). A fall to 3.1 mmol/L with weakness needs prompt prescriber review for replacement and dose review; low potassium increases arrhythmia risk in heart failure.

n.0: Dilution is not the mechanism, and extra fluid may worsen heart failure.
n.1: Loop diuretics cause potassium loss, not retention, and a day's delay is unsafe.
n.3: Dietary potassium will not correct this promptly and the prescriber still needs to know.

11.q: Roger, 61, is on an oncology ward having chemotherapy. He says he feels nauseated before each meal and has been leaving most of his food. He has a prescription for a regular antiemetic. Which nursing action is most appropriate first?
o: Encourage large meals to settle his stomach
Withhold all food until the nausea fully resolves
Give the prescribed antiemetic before meals and review it
Offer strong-smelling hot food to stimulate appetite
11.w: Annexe B 5.5: identify and manage nausea and vomiting. Give prescribed antiemetics at a time that covers meals, assess the response, and use measures such as small frequent meals and reducing food odours.

n.0: Large meals worsen nausea; small frequent meals are better tolerated.
n.1: Withholding all food risks malnutrition.
n.3: Strong food smells often worsen nausea.

11.q: While giving a subcutaneous injection to Peter, 61, who has hepatitis C, nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury to her finger through her glove. The needle has been used. What should Hana do immediately?
o: Let it bleed without squeezing, wash with soap and running water, then report
Squeeze the wound firmly to express blood, then apply an alcohol wipe
Suck the wound, cover it with a plaster and report it after the drug round
Scrub the wound with a nail brush and chlorhexidine, then apply a dressing
11.w: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed but do not squeeze, do not suck, and wash with warm running water and non-antimicrobial soap. The incident is then reported urgently so that occupational health or A&E can assess the need for post-exposure management; the Sharps Regulations 2013 require all sharps injuries to be reported.

n.1: Squeezing can push contaminated material deeper into tissue; NIPCM says allow bleeding without squeezing.
n.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against, and reporting must be prompt so treatment is not delayed.
n.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and may increase uptake; gentle washing under running water is advised.

11.q: Tom, 74, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis. During a multimorbidity review he says he has 'given up', rarely leaves the house and has stopped seeing friends. What should the nurse do next?
o: Refer him to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme straight away
Focus the review on his inhaler technique and blood glucose
Assess him for depression and anxiety and act on the findings
Reassure him that low mood is normal with long-term conditions
11.w: NG56 1.6.5: be alert to the possibility of depression and anxiety and consider identifying, assessing and managing these in line with NICE guidance on common mental health problems; 1.6.3 includes mental health when establishing disease burden.

n.0: Rehabilitation may help later, but his mood needs assessing first.
n.1: Concentrating on physical measures misses possible depression, which affects all his self-management.
n.3: Normalising low mood risks missing treatable depression.

11.q: During a ward teaching session on transmission-based precautions, a student nurse asks which route of transmission is responsible for most cross-infection in care settings, including spread via equipment and the patient's surroundings. Which answer is correct?
o: Airborne transmission via aerosols
Droplet transmission over short distances
Blood-borne transmission via sharps injuries
Contact transmission, direct or indirect
11.w: NIPCM ch 2 defines contact precautions as preventing spread by direct contact with the patient or indirectly from the immediate care environment, including care equipment, and states this is the most common route of cross-infection transmission.

n.0: Airborne spread applies to a smaller group of organisms such as measles and TB.
n.1: Droplet spread is important for respiratory pathogens but NIPCM names contact as the most common route.
n.2: Sharps injuries carry blood-borne virus risk to staff, but are not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

11.q: Edna, 80, is admitted to a medical ward from home after a fall. She has limited mobility and a previous sacral pressure ulcer. Under NICE CG179, when should her pressure ulcer risk be assessed and documented?
o: When a skin change is first noticed
Within 72 hours of admission
At the first weekly skin review
On admission to the ward
11.w: NICE CG179 (2014): assess and document pressure ulcer risk for adults on admission to secondary care or care homes, and reassess if clinical status changes.

n.0: Waiting for skin change means prevention starts after damage has begun.
n.1: 72 hours delays prevention in someone at risk, contrary to CG179.
n.2: A weekly review would leave her unassessed during the high-risk early period.

11.q: Ada, 88, has been sleeping poorly. She dozes most of the afternoon, is woken for observations at 02:00 and 06:00, and has a NEWS2 of 0. She says she is tired all day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Review her observation times with the team to protect her sleep
Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her to take at night
Wake her more often in the afternoon so that she sleeps at night
Leave her plan unchanged, as observations have to be done at night
11.w: With a NEWS2 of 0 the minimum frequency is 12-hourly (RCP 2017), so night-time waking may be avoidable. Reviewing the care plan to cluster care and protect sleep supports rest (Annexe B 3.1, 3.6).

n.1: Sedatives are not first line and increase falls risk in older people.
n.2: Repeatedly waking her during the day adds fatigue rather than addressing the night-time disturbance.
n.3: Observation timing is a clinical decision and can be reviewed when the score is 0.

11.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
11.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

11.q: Tara, 22, tells the nurse, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which technique is this?
o: A cognitive behavioural therapy method
A motivational interviewing technique
A distraction and diversion technique
A reminiscence therapy based technique
11.w: Annexe A 3.6: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques. Examining evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is cognitive restructuring.

n.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not evidence for thoughts.
n.2: Distraction moves attention away; this examines the thought directly.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories for wellbeing, not testing thoughts.

11.q: Ella, 30, has been treated for DKA for 14 hours. Her latest venous gas and capillary results are reviewed by the nurse before the next medical round. Which results show that the DKA has resolved?
o: Ketones 1.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.32
Bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 9.4 mmol/L
Glucose 7.8 mmol/L, eating and drinking
Ketones 0.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.35
11.w: JBDS 02 (2023) defines resolution as blood ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH above 7.3. Bicarbonate alone and glucose are not used to judge resolution.

n.0: Ketones of 1.2 mmol/L are above the 0.6 mmol/L resolution threshold.
n.1: Bicarbonate can stay low from hyperchloraemia, and glucose does not reflect acidosis clearance.
n.2: Glucose and eating do not confirm that ketoacidosis has cleared.

11.q: Eileen, 59, has type 2 diabetes. The practice nurse is arranging her annual kidney check, which includes a test to detect and quantify protein in the urine. Which urine test does NICE recommend?
o: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR)
Reagent strip for protein on a random sample
24-hour urine protein collection
Urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR)
11.w: NICE NG203 (1.1.12-1.1.13) recommends urine ACR rather than PCR to detect and identify proteinuria, because it is more sensitive at low levels; an ACR of 3 mg/mmol or more is clinically important.

n.1: Reagent strips are not reliable for quantifying albuminuria.
n.2: 24-hour collections are impractical and are not the recommended test.
n.3: NICE recommends ACR rather than PCR for detecting and quantifying proteinuria.

11.q: You are performing chest compressions on Alan, 60, who has collapsed in a hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what compression depth and rate are correct for an adult?
o: 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute
6-7 cm at 80-100 per minute
4-5 cm at 100-120 per minute
5-6 cm at 120-140 per minute
11.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress on the lower half of the sternum to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil.

n.1: 6-7 cm is too deep and 80-100 per minute is too slow.
n.2: 4-5 cm is too shallow for an adult.
n.3: 120-140 per minute is faster than the recommended maximum of 120.

11.q: Glenys, 72, is admitted for a hip replacement. She has type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy and reduced sensation in both feet. She is due to be measured for anti-embolism stockings. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Check her ankle brachial pressure index, then fit if normal
Do not fit stockings and discuss other prophylaxis with the team
Fit knee-length stockings to reduce pressure on her feet
Fit thigh-length stockings and check her skin each day
11.w: NICE NG89 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with peripheral neuropathy or other causes of sensory impairment (or peripheral arterial disease, severe oedema, local skin conditions). Discuss alternative mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis.

n.0: A normal ABPI excludes arterial disease but not her neuropathy.
n.2: Stockings of any length are contraindicated with sensory impairment.
n.3: Peripheral neuropathy is a contraindication; daily checks do not remove the risk.

11.q: Leanne, a staff nurse, is asked by the nurse in charge to remove a patient's chest drain because the doctors are busy. Leanne has read about the procedure but has never been trained or assessed in it. What should Leanne do first?
o: Watch an online video of the procedure and then remove the drain
Remove the drain with the nurse in charge talking her through it
Remove the drain and record that she did so on the instruction given
Explain she is untrained and ask a competent practitioner to do it
11.w: Code 13.3: ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for any procedure beyond your competence; 13.5: complete training first; 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Safe evidence-based practice in procedures (P1.20) depends on this.

n.0: Self-directed viewing is not training or assessment; Code 13.5 requires the necessary training before a new role or procedure.
n.1: Verbal guidance from someone not supervising hands-on does not make her competent; she would be practising beyond her competence (Code 13.3).
n.2: Being instructed does not transfer accountability; each registrant is accountable for working within competence (Code 13).

11.q: Tessa, 45, is admitted with mild acute pancreatitis due to gallstones. She is not vomiting and says she is hungry. Her care plan was written as nil by mouth by default. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Request parenteral nutrition while she is in hospital
Offer clear fluids for 48 hours before any food
Ask for review, as food is not withheld without a clear reason
Keep her nil by mouth until her amylase level has returned to normal
11.w: NICE NG104 (1.2.5) says ensure people with acute pancreatitis are not made nil by mouth and do not have food withheld unless there is a clear reason, such as vomiting.

n.0: Parenteral nutrition is for severe disease where enteral feeding has failed or is contraindicated.
n.1: Routine restriction to clear fluids is still withholding food without a clear reason.
n.3: NG104 advises against routine nil by mouth; normalising amylase is not a condition for eating.

11.q: Ms Ward, 72, is breathless with heart failure and has gained 3 kg in 4 days. On chest auscultation, which finding would the nurse most expect and report?
o: A pleural rub over the left upper zone
Fine crackles at both lung bases
Absent sounds over the whole right lung
High-pitched stridor on inspiration
11.w: Fluid overload in heart failure causes pulmonary oedema, heard as fine crackles, usually at both bases. This fits her rapid weight gain and breathlessness (Annexe B 2.8: undertake chest auscultation and interpret findings).

n.0: A pleural rub indicates inflamed pleura, for example pleurisy, not fluid overload.
n.2: Absent sounds over one whole lung suggest pneumothorax, large effusion or collapse, not the typical bilateral picture.
n.3: Stridor is an upper airway sound suggesting obstruction, not pulmonary oedema.

11.q: Ruth, 64, has lung cancer and has developed new numbness in both legs and a band of pain around her chest. The MSCC coordinator has been contacted. Within what time frame should her MRI be performed, according to NICE NG234?
o: Within 48 hours, at the regional spinal surgery centre
Within 1 week, as an urgent outpatient
As soon as possible, and always within 24 hours
Within 72 hours, once she is pain controlled
11.w: NG234 1.5.2: offer MRI to people with suspected MSCC as soon as possible and always within 24 hours, at the local hospital or appropriate centre with direct access to imaging.

n.0: 48 hours is too long, and transfer is used if local MRI is not possible.
n.1: A week's delay risks permanent neurological loss.
n.3: Imaging should not wait for pain control, and 72 hours exceeds the limit.

11.q: A ward manager, Leon, has noticed over three weeks that a staff nurse, Abi, regularly completes her patients' records several hours after care. Patient care has otherwise been good. What is Leon's most appropriate first step?
o: Start a formal capability process with a written warning
Meet Abi privately, give examples, explore reasons and agree a plan
Refer Abi to the NMC for failing to keep records as required
Move Abi to a different ward with a lighter workload
11.w: Performance management starts with an informal, supportive conversation using specific examples, exploring causes (for example workload or skills) and agreeing objectives, support and a review date, escalating to formal processes only if problems continue (P5.3 principles and processes of performance management; Code 10.1 records completed at the time or as soon as possible after).

n.0: Formal processes are disproportionate before an informal discussion and support have been tried.
n.2: This is a local performance issue, not a fitness to practise concern at this stage.
n.3: Moving her does not address the reasons for the delay or support her improvement.

11.q: Margaret, 83, has mixed dementia and no history of epilepsy or bipolar disorder. She has become verbally aggressive in the evenings. A locum doctor suggests starting sodium valproate to calm her. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as NICE advises against valproate for agitation in dementia
Give it, as valproate is safer than antipsychotics in older people
Give it, then check her valproate blood level after the first week
Give it, as mood stabilisers are first-line for agitation in dementia
11.w: NG97 1.7.10: do not offer valproate to manage agitation or aggression in people living with dementia, unless it is indicated for another condition. Code 18 and 19 require nurses to question medicines that may cause harm.

n.1: NICE does not recommend valproate as an alternative to antipsychotics for this purpose.
n.2: Monitoring levels does not address that valproate should not be started for this indication.
n.3: First-line management is a structured assessment and psychosocial interventions, not mood stabilisers.

11.q: Over two months, Zara has noticed her usually cheerful colleague has become withdrawn, irritable with patients and has had several short-term absences. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Speak to her privately, voice concern and signpost support
Avoid raising it in case it causes her more stress
Suggest she takes annual leave to recover from stress
Report her absence pattern to the ward manager at once
11.w: Proficiency P1.5: recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to health. Code 8.7 support colleagues; escalate if patient safety becomes affected.

n.1: Avoiding the issue fails to support a colleague showing signs of vulnerability (P1.5).
n.2: Advising leave without understanding the problem may not meet her needs.
n.3: Raising it with the manager may follow, but a supportive conversation is the appropriate first step when there is no immediate safety risk.

11.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
11.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

11.q: Thomas, 68, is being assessed for thrombolysis after an ischaemic stroke. His blood pressure is 196/112 mmHg. What blood pressure should be achieved before thrombolysis?
o: 140/90 mmHg or lower
220/120 mmHg or lower
160/100 mmHg or lower
185/110 mmHg or lower
11.w: NICE NG128 1.5.10: consider blood pressure reduction to 185/110 mmHg or lower in people who are candidates for thrombolysis.

n.0: This is a long-term target, not the pre-thrombolysis threshold.
n.1: This is above the NG128 threshold for thrombolysis.
n.2: This is lower than NG128 requires before thrombolysis.

11.q: Owen, a staff nurse, realises he gave Ruth Price, 76, 10 mg of morphine instead of the prescribed 2.5 mg. She becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. The doctor has reviewed her and naloxone has been given. Which action best meets Owen's professional duty of candour?
o: Tell Mrs Price's daughter what happened and leave her to explain it to her mother
Ask the doctor to decide whether Mrs Price needs to be told about the overdose
Wait until the incident review is complete before telling Mrs Price what happened
Tell Mrs Price promptly what happened, apologise, and explain what is being done
11.w: Code 14.1-14.3 and the NMC/GMC professional duty of candour guidance (2024): when something goes wrong, tell the person (or their advocate) promptly, apologise, explain what happened and the likely effects, put matters right where possible, and record and report the incident (P1.3).

n.0: Mrs Price is the person affected; information goes to her unless she lacks capacity or asks for it to be shared.
n.1: The professional duty of candour belongs to each registrant; Owen cannot pass the decision to another clinician.
n.2: Candour is prompt; waiting for a review delays information the person is entitled to now.

11.q: Ruth, 83, lives alone and is CFS 5 at baseline. She is being discharged after a fall-related admission. She sees a GP, a heart failure nurse, a diabetes clinic and a community physiotherapist. Her daughter is unsure who to contact. Which discharge action best supports safe coordination of care?
o: Give Ruth a list of every service telephone number to keep
Ask the daughter to phone each of the services weekly to check on her progress
Book Ruth into the ward follow-up clinic for all future concerns
Agree a care plan naming who coordinates care and share it with services
11.w: NG56 1.5.2 and 1.6.17 require an individualised management plan stating who is responsible for coordinating care, and that this is communicated to all professionals involved (with consent). This supports safe transitions between services (Platform 7).

n.0: A list of numbers leaves Ruth and her daughter to coordinate several services themselves.
n.1: Transferring coordination to the daughter is not a care plan and may not reflect Ruth's wishes.
n.2: A ward clinic cannot coordinate all community services and adds another appointment to her burden.

11.q: A ward wants to evaluate how well it plans discharges for people with complex care needs who go home with new support. Which approach would best capture the quality of their experience?
o: Count the number of discharges completed before midday each week
Review the ward's length-of-stay figures against other medical wards
Phone people and carers after discharge to ask about their experience
Audit how many discharge letters reached GPs within 24 hours
11.w: The quality of people's experience of complex care is best evaluated by asking them and their carers directly about the discharge and transition, including whether support started as planned (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Discharge timing is a process measure that says little about the person's experience.
n.1: Length of stay measures efficiency, not experience.
n.3: Letter timeliness is an important process measure but does not capture the experience of people and carers.

11.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
11.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

11.q: Derek, 70, has COPD and has been admitted twice this winter with exacerbations. He tells the nurse that his flat is damp and that he cannot afford to heat it. Which action by the nurse best addresses the factors affecting his health?
o: Ask the prescriber to increase his inhaler dose for the winter months
Refer or signpost him to local housing and energy support services
Advise him to spend more time in bed to conserve his energy
Record the housing issue and note it is outside the nursing role
11.w: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) P2.2 and P2.7: understand the wider determinants of health and explain the contribution of social influences and circumstances to health outcomes. NICE PH49 (2014): assess the context in which people live, including their physical, economic and social environment.

n.0: Medicines do not address the damp, cold housing that is affecting his health.
n.2: This does not address the housing problem and reduces his activity.
n.3: NMC P2.7 expects nurses to recognise social circumstances as influences on health and act on them.

11.q: Henry, 69, takes aspirin 75 mg after a previous heart attack and naproxen for knee pain. He has had a bleeding duodenal ulcer treated at endoscopy and haemostasis is achieved. Which medicines plan is consistent with NICE guidance?
o: Continue naproxen and stop aspirin until the ulcer heals
Continue both with added proton pump inhibitor cover
Stop both aspirin and naproxen for at least 3 months
Continue aspirin and stop naproxen during the acute phase
11.w: NICE CG141 (1.6.1-1.6.2): continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention of vascular events once haemostasis is achieved, and stop other NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors, during the acute phase.

n.0: Naproxen is the NSAID to stop; aspirin for secondary prevention continues.
n.1: Other NSAIDs are stopped in the acute phase, not continued under PPI cover.
n.2: Stopping secondary-prevention aspirin raises his risk of further cardiovascular events.

11.q: Amira, 29, is admitted to a gynaecology ward. Her notes record a history of sexual assault. When the nurse reaches to hold her hand during an examination, Amira flinches. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop, ask whether touch is acceptable and explain each step first
Ask a colleague to hold her hand in place of the nurse
Continue gently, as touch is a recognised comforting technique
Stop all communication until the examination is finished
11.w: Annexe A 1.3: use appropriate non-verbal communication, including touch, eye contact and personal space. Code 1.1 and 4.2: treat with respect and gain consent before any action.

n.1: Changing who touches her does not address whether she wants touch at all.
n.2: Comforting touch is only therapeutic when welcome; her reaction shows it is not.
n.3: Withdrawing communication leaves her anxious and unsupported.

11.q: Ravi, 55, is a day after a hernia repair. He is anxious and says he 'cannot catch his breath'. RR 26, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 128/80, alert, temperature 37.2°C. You have called for help. Which action best reflects the ABCDE approach?
o: Start oxygen, then continue to C and D while reassessing his breathing
Complete C, D and E fully before deciding whether he needs oxygen
Reassure him that anxiety is common after surgery and observe hourly
Wait for the doctor to examine him before giving any treatment
11.w: ABCDE treats each life-threatening problem as it is found and then reassesses. Hypoxaemia (93% with RR 26) is a B problem: start oxygen to a target of 94-98% (BTS; NG253 rec 1.10.1), then continue through C, D and E, re-evaluating after each intervention.

n.1: Completing the rest of the assessment first delays treatment of a breathing problem already identified.
n.2: Attributing tachypnoea and low saturation to anxiety risks missing a pulmonary embolism or other serious cause.
n.3: Nurses start initial treatment within competence while help arrives; waiting delays care (Code 15).

11.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
11.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

11.q: Sandra, 58, is admitted with sepsis. She is pale and clammy, her SpO2 is 82% on air and her blood pressure is 84/50 mmHg. She has no chronic lung disease. Which oxygen delivery is most appropriate initially?
o: Nasal cannulae at 4 L/min
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 5 L/min
28% Venturi mask at 4 L/min
11.w: BTS 2017: in critical illness (shock, sepsis, major trauma) or SpO2 below 85%, start a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate down to 94-98% once stable.

n.0: Nasal cannulae suit mild hypoxaemia; critical illness with SpO2 below 85% needs a reservoir mask.
n.2: A simple mask delivers a lower and variable concentration than she needs in critical illness.
n.3: Controlled low-concentration oxygen is for people at risk of hypercapnia, not critical illness.

11.q: Ellie qualified six weeks ago. At the start of a night shift she is told she will be the only registered nurse for 28 patients on an unfamiliar ward, and has never taken charge. What should she do first?
o: Accept the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Raise her concerns at once with the person in charge and record it
Leave the ward and return to her own ward for safety
Accept the shift and phone her own ward manager at home
11.w: Code 16.2: raise your concerns immediately if you are being asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training. Code 13.3 and NMC Raising concerns guidance support escalation and keeping a record.

n.0: Delaying until the morning leaves patients at risk; Code 16.2 requires her to raise concerns immediately.
n.2: Leaving abandons patients; she must raise the concern so safe cover is arranged.
n.3: Her absent manager cannot change tonight's staffing; the site lead or person in charge must be told now.

11.q: Hamid, 74, takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. His INR today is 8.5 (target 2.5 to 3.5). He has no bleeding, bruising or other symptoms, and his 18:00 dose is due. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the usual dose, as he has no signs of bleeding
Give oral vitamin K from ward stock to lower the INR
Withhold the warfarin and inform the prescriber urgently
Give half the usual dose and recheck the INR tomorrow
11.w: An INR well above target raises the risk of serious bleeding. Anticoagulants are high-risk medicines (P4.15): the dose is withheld and the prescriber informed promptly, who decides on dose changes or reversal such as vitamin K.

n.0: No bleeding now does not remove the high bleeding risk at INR 8.5.
n.1: Vitamin K must be prescribed; giving it from stock without a prescription is unlawful.
n.3: Altering the warfarin dose is a prescriber decision.

11.q: George Hall, 80, has a NEWS2 score of 1. His nurse, Precious, feels uneasy: he is quieter than usual and has not eaten, though nothing specific is abnormal. She is unsure whether to act on this feeling. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase his observations and discuss her concern with the medical team
Ask the healthcare assistant to repeat the observations at the next round
Record her impression and continue observations at the planned frequency
Wait until his score reaches 5 so that escalation is clearly justified
11.w: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement (RCP 2017; NICE NG253). For scores of 1-4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation. Acting on clinical concern under uncertainty, by increasing monitoring and escalating, is safe practice (P6.11 accept and manage uncertainty; Code 13.3 ask for help).

n.1: Repeating routine observations later does not address her clinical concern now.
n.2: Recording a concern without acting on it leaves a possible deterioration unaddressed.
n.3: Waiting for a threshold ignores the nurse's assessment and may delay recognition of deterioration.

11.q: Reginald, 66, attends the practice with a headache. His clinic blood pressure is 188/124 mmHg on repeat. His wife says he has been confused since this morning. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange same-day specialist assessment
Offer ABPM to confirm the diagnosis
Start amlodipine and recheck in 1 week
Recheck his blood pressure after 1 hour of rest
11.w: Two steps: 188/124 is severe hypertension (180/120 or higher); new confusion is a life-threatening symptom. NICE NG136 1.5.1: refer for same-day specialist assessment.

n.1: ABPM delays care; severe hypertension with red flags is managed urgently.
n.2: New confusion with severe hypertension is a life-threatening symptom needing same-day assessment.
n.3: Resting and rechecking delays urgent review of a possible hypertensive emergency.

11.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
11.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

12.q: A nurse is planning patient information for an outpatient clinic and wants to account for health literacy across the local population. Which statement about health literacy in England is supported by Public Health England evidence?
o: Up to 61% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
Health literacy is measured by a person's highest school qualification
Difficulty understanding health information mainly affects people over 80
About 10% of working-age adults do not routinely understand health information
12.w: NHS England, Health literacy (personalised care): a Public Health England report found that up to 61% of the English working-age population do not routinely understand the health and wellbeing information they are given. Health literacy (WHO) is the personal characteristics and social resources needed to access, understand, appraise and use information to make health decisions.

n.1: Health literacy is the ability to access, understand, appraise and use information, not a qualification level.
n.2: Low health literacy is common across working-age adults, not mainly in the oldest age groups.
n.3: The figure is far higher; PHE found up to 61% of the working-age population struggle.

12.q: Glenys, 72, is admitted for a hip replacement. She has type 2 diabetes with peripheral neuropathy and reduced sensation in both feet. She is due to be measured for anti-embolism stockings. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Check her ankle brachial pressure index, then fit if normal
Do not fit stockings and discuss other prophylaxis with the team
Fit knee-length stockings to reduce pressure on her feet
Fit thigh-length stockings and check her skin each day
12.w: NICE NG89 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with peripheral neuropathy or other causes of sensory impairment (or peripheral arterial disease, severe oedema, local skin conditions). Discuss alternative mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis.

n.0: A normal ABPI excludes arterial disease but not her neuropathy.
n.2: Stockings of any length are contraindicated with sensory impairment.
n.3: Peripheral neuropathy is a contraindication; daily checks do not remove the risk.

12.q: Gloria, 72, has been prescribed oral nutritional supplements twice daily. On the ward round you notice the supplement bottles are left unopened on her table each day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to bring in food from home and stop recording intake
Stop the supplements because she clearly does not want them
Sign the chart for the supplements because they were supplied
Explore why with her and review the plan with the dietitian
12.w: Effective nutrition support requires monitoring that it is actually taken (NICE CG32 monitoring). Explore reasons (taste, fullness, opening the bottle, timing) and review with Gloria and the dietitian. Recording a supplement as taken when it was not would be inaccurate (Code 10.3).

n.0: Food from home may help, but intake must still be monitored and recorded.
n.1: Stopping without exploring reasons or involving the dietitian may leave her malnourished.
n.2: Recording unopened supplements as given falsifies the record.

12.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
o: Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00; her NEWS2 rose to 4
She was admitted four days ago from her own home
She enjoyed her lunch and watched television all afternoon
Her daughter visited during the afternoon
12.w: Annexe A 1.11: provide clear information when handing over care. Code 10.2 identify risks and problems; Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed.

n.1: Admission date is less urgent than outstanding care and deterioration.
n.2: Social details matter less than risks and time-critical care.
n.3: Visitor details are not the priority for safe handover.

12.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
12.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

12.q: Winifred, 90, has hyperactive delirium. Her daughter is upset and asks, 'Has Mum gone mad? Will she be like this for ever?' Which response by the nurse best reflects NICE CG103?
o: It will clear within 24 hours now her antibiotics have started
It would help her settle if visits stopped until she is calmer
It is common and usually temporary; please tell us about sudden changes
It is probably the start of dementia, so you should plan for more care at home
12.w: CG103 1.8.1: inform people and families that delirium is common and usually temporary, describe the experience, and encourage them to tell staff about any sudden changes or fluctuations. CG103 1.4.4 and 1.7.2 also support family visits to help reorientation.

n.0: Promising resolution within 24 hours is inaccurate; recovery time varies.
n.1: Family visits help reorientation; CG103 encourages involving family and friends.
n.3: Delirium is not dementia; suggesting this without assessment causes alarm and is inaccurate.

12.q: Jorge, 61, is prescribed potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously over 8 hours. The ward has no ready-mixed bags. A colleague suggests adding concentrated potassium chloride from an ampoule to a bag of saline. What should the nurse do?
o: Run plain saline now and add the potassium when the bag is changed
Obtain a ready-mixed bag from pharmacy or another area per policy
Give the concentrated potassium chloride as a slow IV bolus instead
Add the ampoule to the bag and invert it several times to mix
12.w: Mis-selection of a strong potassium solution is a Never Event (2018 list, updated 2021); national guidance requires ready-diluted potassium infusions wherever possible, with concentrated ampoules restricted. Potassium is a high-risk medicine (P4.15).

n.0: Delaying and then adding concentrate later carries the same mis-selection risk.
n.2: Concentrated potassium must not be given as a bolus; it can cause cardiac arrest.
n.3: Ward addition of concentrated potassium risks mis-selection and poor mixing, causing fatal hyperkalaemia.

12.q: Ernest, 84, lacks capacity to decide about his medicines and actively refuses his antiepileptic. The care home manager arranges a best interests meeting about covert administration. According to NICE SC1, who should be involved?
o: The prescriber, the care home manager and the senior carer
Care staff, prescriber, pharmacist and a family member or advocate
The care home manager and the registered nurse on duty that day
The family, who make the final decision as his next of kin
12.w: NICE SC1 (1.15) and RPS/RCN 2019: covert administration follows a best interests meeting involving care home staff, the health professional prescribing, a pharmacist and a family member or advocate, with a documented management plan.

n.0: Without a pharmacist and a family member or advocate the decision lacks key input.
n.2: The prescriber and pharmacist must also be involved, as must family or an advocate.
n.3: Next of kin have no legal power to decide unless they hold a relevant LPA or are deputies; the decision is made by the team in his best interests.

12.q: Ms Reid, 38, has a learning disability, epilepsy and type 1 diabetes. She has missed three diabetes clinic appointments, and her carer says the waiting room makes her very anxious. What is the most appropriate response by the community nurse?
o: Write to her to say that further missed appointments will be noted
Discharge her from clinic, as she has not attended three times
Ask her carer to attend the clinic in her place to collect advice
Arrange reasonable adjustments such as a first or quiet appointment
12.w: P7.5 requires responding to the challenges of person-centred care for people with complex needs, and the Equality Act 2010 s20 imposes a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Adjusting the appointment removes the barrier to her care.

n.0: A warning letter does not address the cause of her non-attendance.
n.1: Discharging her penalises her for a barrier the service can adjust, worsening inequality.
n.2: Her carer cannot receive her care or examinations for her; she needs to be seen.

12.q: Pauline, 73, has an MRSA-colonised leg ulcer. The nurse removes a dressing heavily soaked with wound exudate. In an acute hospital in England, which waste stream should the used dressing go into?
o: Yellow and black striped offensive waste bag
Orange bag for infectious clinical waste
Black domestic waste bag
Purple bag for cytotoxic waste
12.w: NIPCM ch 1.9 (HTM 07-01): clinical waste that is infectious, for example from a patient known or suspected to be infected or colonised, goes in a UN-approved orange bag. Offensive (tiger) waste is for non-infectious waste containing body fluids.

n.0: Tiger bags are for offensive waste that is not infectious; this dressing is from a colonised wound.
n.2: Domestic bags are for non-healthcare general waste, not soiled dressings.
n.3: Purple is for waste contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines.

12.q: Lucy, 40, is on air. Observations: RR 22, SpO2 95%, BP 116/70, pulse 96, alert, temperature 38.3°C. What is her NEWS2 score?
12.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): RR 21-24 = 2; SpO2 94-95% = 1; air = 0; systolic 111-219 = 0; pulse 91-110 = 1; alert = 0; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1. Total 2+1+1+1 = 5, which is the key threshold for an urgent response.

n.1: 6 overscores; temperature 38.3°C scores 1, not 2 (2 starts at 39.1°C).
n.2: 3 omits two parameters, for example SpO2 95% and pulse 96, which each score 1.
n.3: 4 omits one of the scoring parameters (RR 2, SpO2 1, pulse 1, temperature 1).

12.q: Kamala, 54, has CKD with an ACR of 95 mg/mmol. Her clinic blood pressure is 136/84 mmHg on current treatment. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: It is within her target of below 150/90 for proteinuric CKD
It is above her target of below 130/80, so treatment review is needed
It is within her target of below 140/90, so no change is needed
It needs confirming by home readings above 145/85 first
12.w: NICE NG203 sets a target systolic below 130 mmHg (range 120 to 129) and diastolic below 80 mmHg when ACR is 70 mg/mmol or more. At 136/84 she is above target.

n.0: Below 150/90 is not a CKD target.
n.2: Below 140/90 applies to people with an ACR below 70 mg/mmol.
n.3: Her clinic reading already exceeds her target; 145/85 is an ABPM figure for people aged 80 and over.

12.q: After an unsuccessful resuscitation attempt on a medical ward, Sofia, the nurse in charge, arranges a short team debrief once the immediate tasks are complete. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: Identify which member of staff made an error so that it can be dealt with formally
Reflect together on what went well and what could improve, and support staff
Complete the incident report and the statutory notification to the regulator
Decide as a team what information the family should and should not be given
12.w: Team reflection and debriefing support staff wellbeing and turn experience into learning for future practice (P5.10 contribute to supervision and team reflection; Code 8 work cooperatively; human factors and just culture principles).

n.0: A debrief is a supportive learning discussion, not a disciplinary process; a blame focus discourages openness.
n.2: Reporting is a separate governance step and is not the purpose of a team debrief.
n.3: Communication with the family is guided by candour and the person's wishes, not by a team agreement to withhold information.

12.q: Bernard, 77, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is receiving oxygen at 4 L/min via nasal cannulae. On your round he is drowsy and difficult to rouse, and his SpO2 is 99%. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Sit him upright and repeat the observations in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen to reach 88-92% and request urgent blood gases
Continue the current flow because his saturation is satisfactory
Stop the oxygen straight away and recheck his saturation
12.w: Assess then act: drowsiness with SpO2 above target in an at-risk patient suggests hypercapnic respiratory failure. BTS 2017 advises stepping oxygen down to the target range (not stopping it suddenly) and urgent blood gases with medical review.

n.0: New drowsiness with high saturation needs urgent action and blood gases, not routine monitoring.
n.2: 99% is above his target; with new drowsiness this suggests hypercapnia from excess oxygen.
n.3: Sudden withdrawal can cause rebound hypoxaemia; oxygen should be stepped down to the target, not stopped abruptly.

12.q: Edith, 90, is frail, weighs 45 kg and has chronic kidney disease. Routine IV maintenance fluids are prescribed at 30 mL/kg/day. What should the nurse do?
o: Double the rate to protect her kidneys from dehydration
Give the fluids as prescribed, as this is the standard rate
Query the prescription, as a lower rate may be needed
Change her to oral fluids without consulting the prescriber
12.w: NICE CG174: consider prescribing less fluid (for example 20-25 mL/kg/day) for people who are older or frail, or who have renal or cardiac impairment. Raising a concern about a prescription supports safe practice (Code 18, RPS/RCN 2019).

n.0: Doubling the rate risks serious fluid overload.
n.1: Standard rates may cause overload in frail people with renal impairment.
n.3: Changing the route without the prescriber is outside a nurse's authority.

12.q: Sarah, 41, is two hours after an appendicectomy. She rates her pain at 8 out of 10 and was given prescribed oral morphine 30 minutes ago. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give a second dose of morphine because her pain is still 8
Reassess her pain and document the effect of the morphine
Encourage her to walk around the ward to ease the pain
Wait until the next scheduled observations in four hours
12.w: Pain management is a cycle of assessment, intervention and reassessment. Reassess at the expected time of peak effect (around 30-60 minutes after oral analgesia), document the response, and escalate if relief is inadequate (Annexe B 3.5, P4.8).

n.0: Repeating the dose without reassessment or a prescription for a further dose risks opioid toxicity.
n.2: Mobilising with severe uncontrolled pain is inappropriate and distressing.
n.3: Four hours is too long to leave severe pain without reassessing the response.

12.q: Yusuf, 50, is prescribed co-amoxiclav 1.2 g by slow intravenous injection over 3 to 4 minutes via his peripheral cannula. The second check is complete. The ward is busy and his maintenance fluids are running. How should the nurse give the dose?
o: Add it to the maintenance fluid bag and let it run in with the fluids
Flush to confirm patency, give over 3 to 4 minutes, then flush again
Give it by rapid push over 30 seconds, then flush with saline
Give it without a flush, as the cannula was used this morning
12.w: Safe IV administration via a vascular access device (AnnexB.11.9; NICE CG139 flushing with 0.9% sodium chloride): check patency and the site with a flush, give the drug at the prescribed rate, observe for reactions, then flush to clear the line.

n.0: Adding drugs to a bag changes the prescribed route and rate and risks incompatibility.
n.2: Giving faster than prescribed risks adverse reactions and does not follow the prescription.
